title: Capstone: Soil Carbon and Cropland of Every Great Plains County
text:
Overview

The question
Soil organic carbon (SOC) is the largest terrestrial store of carbon and a measure of soil health. Cultivation usually lowers it, while climate and vegetation set its overall level: wetter, cooler and greener places hold more. A county-level picture of SOC next to cropland share is the kind of summary that carbon accounting, conservation programmes and soil health initiatives start from, and it needs exactly the operations of this chapter.


The pipeline









Stage
Data
Operations (notebook)
Scale




1. Cropland by county
2025 CDL, 10 m
lazy read (02), lookup-table reclassification (03), zonal sums (05)
21 billion pixels


2. Training table
570 SOC samples, 12 covariates
grid alignment (02), point extraction (05)
570 x 12


3. Model
training table
spatial cross-validation, XGBoost on CPU and GPU (09)
561 rows


4. SOC map
12 covariates, 90 m
chunked prediction (09), COG output (02)
262 million pixels


5. County summaries
SOC map, covariates
zonal statistics (05)
225 zones x 4 rasters


6. Spatial patterns
county table
weights, Moran’s I, LISA, G* (06)
225 counties





What counts as done
The final products are a county GeoParquet file with cropland areas, mean predicted SOC, climate and terrain summaries and hot spot statistics; a SOC map as a COG; and a timing table showing where the time went.

title: Capstone: Soil Carbon and Cropland of Every Great Plains County
text:
The Capstone with GeoLattice
All stages use the functions of the previous notebooks: dd.cdl, dd.gp_raster and dd.gp_stack (lazy readers, grids aligned), pdist.raster.map_tiles, pdist.zonal_stats, pdist.extract_values, pdist.ml.fit, pdist.ml.predict_raster, pdist.write_raster, pdist.analysis.weights, morans_i, local_morans, getis_ord_local and pdist.vector.sjoin. The GPU is used where notebooks 03 to 09 showed it pays off (model prediction, zonal partial sums); I/O-bound stages stay on the CPU.

Learning objectives

Plan a multi-stage spatial pipeline and choose CPU or GPU per stage from earlier measurements.
Summarize 21 billion 10 m pixels by county out of core.
Build, validate and apply a soil carbon model to 262 million pixels.
Combine raster and vector results into a county table and analyse its spatial patterns.
Time each stage and write analysis-ready outputs.



Data







Dataset
Content




2025 CDL
10 m crop codes, Great Plains window of 154,776 x 137,219 pixels


Great Plains covariates
12 continuous 90 m rasters, aligned to the elevation grid


Great Plains SOC samples
570 points, kg m-2


Great Plains counties and states
225 counties, 4 states (EPSG:5070)



Outputs go to outputs/capstone/: counties_soc_cropland.parquet and soc_map_cog.tif.


Contents

Setup
Stage 1: cropland by county from the 10 m CDL
Stage 2: the training table
Stage 3: a validated soil carbon model
Stage 4: the soil carbon map
Stage 5: county summaries
Stage 6: spatial patterns
Outputs and the time budget
Summary and exercises

import geolattice.distributed as pdist  # distributed and GPU spatial computing
import dist_data as dd  # chapter helper: paths, cached downloads, timers

title: Capstone: Soil Carbon and Cropland of Every Great Plains County
section: Stage 1: cropland by county from the 10 m CDL
text:
Stage 1: cropland by county from the 10 m CDL
A lazy three-band flag raster (all cropland, wheat, corn) is built from the CDL with lookup tables, and pdist.zonal_stats sums it within each county (notebook 05). Reading and decompressing 21 billion pixels is CPU work, so this stage runs on the CPU.


Code
gp = counties.total_bounds  # extent of the counties
cdl = dd.cdl(chunks={"y": 4096, "x": 4096}).sel(x=slice(gp[0], gp[2]), y=slice(gp[3], gp[1]))  # lazy 10 m window; 4096 chunks bound memory (notebook 05)
luts = {}  # lookup table per flag
for band, groups in [("crop", dd.CROP_GROUPS), ("wheat", ["Wheat"]), ("corn", ["Corn"])]:  # three flags
    lut = np.zeros(256, np.float32)  # 0 elsewhere
    for gname in groups:  # codes of the groups
        lut[dd.CDL_GROUPS[gname]] = 1.0  # 1 for them
    lut[0] = np.nan  # no data
    luts[band] = lut  # keep
flags = xr.concat([pdist.raster.map_tiles(cdl, lambda b, xp, l=l: xp.asarray(l)[b], dtype="float32", compute="cpu")  # one band per flag
                   for l in luts.values()], dim="band").assign_coords(band=list(luts))  # (3, y, x)
with dd.PeakMemory() as pm:  # watch memory
    t0 = time.perf_counter()  # start
    crop = pdist.zonal_stats(counties[["FIPS", "geometry"]], flags, stats=["count", "sum"], compute="cpu")  # one pass
    budget["1 cropland by county (21 billion pixels)"] = time.perf_counter() - t0  # time
km2 = 100 / 1e6  # one 10 m pixel in km2
counties["mapped_km2"] = crop["count_crop"].values * km2  # mapped land
for band in luts:  # areas
    counties[f"{band}_km2"] = crop[f"sum_{band}"].values * km2  # km2 of each flag
counties["crop_share"] = counties.crop_km2 / counties.mapped_km2  # cropland share
print(f"{budget['1 cropland by county (21 billion pixels)'] / 60:.1f} min, peak memory {pm.peak_gb:.1f} GB; "  # time and memory
      f"cropland {counties.crop_km2.sum():,.0f} km2 ({counties.crop_km2.sum() / counties.mapped_km2.sum():.1%} of the land)")  # totals


6.4 min, peak memory 23.4 GB; cropland 117,687 km2 (11.2% of the land)

title: Capstone: Soil Carbon and Cropland of Every Great Plains County
text:
Stage 2: the training table
The 12 covariates are aligned to the elevation grid by dd.gp_stack (notebook 02 found the files on five slightly different grids) and extracted at the 570 sampling points.


Code
t0 = time.perf_counter()  # start
stack = dd.gp_stack()  # lazy (12, y, x)
soc = dd.gp_points()  # 570 points
table = pdist.extract_values(soc, stack, name="v")  # covariates at the points
table = table.rename(columns=lambda c: c[2:] if c.startswith("v_") else c).dropna(subset=dd.PREDICTORS)  # complete rows
X = table[dd.PREDICTORS].to_numpy(np.float32)  # predictors
y = np.log(table.SOC.to_numpy())  # log SOC
budget["2 training table"] = time.perf_counter() - t0  # time
print(f"{len(table)} samples; SOC median {np.median(table.SOC):.2f} kg m-2, range {table.SOC.min():.2f} to {table.SOC.max():.2f}")  # summary


561 samples; SOC median 4.73 kg m-2, range 0.15 to 30.47

title: Capstone: Soil Carbon and Cropland of Every Great Plains County
section: Stage 3: a validated soil carbon model
text:
Stage 3: a validated soil carbon model
XGBoost with spatial cross-validation (5 blocks of the sample coordinates), then a final fit on all samples. Training 561 rows is quick on either target; the GPU model is used because stage 4 predicts on the GPU.


Code
t0 = time.perf_counter()  # start
params = dict(n_estimators=400, learning_rate=0.03, max_depth=4, subsample=0.8, colsample_bytree=0.8)  # settings from notebook 09
blocks = KMeans(5, random_state=0, n_init=10).fit_predict(np.column_stack([table.geometry.x, table.geometry.y]))  # spatial blocks
pred = np.empty_like(y)  # held-out predictions
for b in range(5):  # each block
    m = pdist.ml.fit("xgb", X[blocks != b], y[blocks != b], task="regression", compute=gpu, **params)  # fit without it
    pred[blocks == b] = np.asarray(m.predict(X[blocks == b])).ravel()  # predict it
model = pdist.ml.fit("xgb", X, y, task="regression", compute=gpu, **params)  # final model on all samples
budget["3 model and spatial cross-validation"] = time.perf_counter() - t0  # time
print(f"spatial CV: R2 {r2_score(y, pred):.2f}, RMSE {mean_squared_error(y, pred) ** 0.5:.2f} (log units); engine {model.geolattice_engine}")  # accuracy


spatial CV: R2 0.45, RMSE 0.70 (log units); engine xgboost-cuda

text:
Stage 4: the soil carbon map
pdist.ml.predict_raster predicts every pixel chunk by chunk; the map is back-transformed to kg m-2 and written as a COG.


Code
t0 = time.perf_counter()  # start
log_map = pdist.ml.predict_raster(model, stack)  # lazy (y, x) log SOC
soc_map = np.exp(log_map).astype("float32").rename("soc").rio.write_crs(5070)  # kg m-2, still lazy
soc_map = soc_map.compute()  # predict once and keep the 1 GB map in memory for stages 4 and 5
budget["4a predict 262 million pixels"] = time.perf_counter() - t0  # time
t0 = time.perf_counter()  # start
pdist.write_raster(soc_map.chunk({"y": 2048, "x": 2048}), CAP / "soc_map_cog.tif", format="cog")  # Cloud-Optimized GeoTIFF
budget["4b write the map as a COG"] = time.perf_counter() - t0  # time
print(f"predicted pixels: {int(np.isfinite(soc_map.values).sum()):,}; COG {(CAP / 'soc_map_cog.tif').stat().st_size / 1e6:.0f} MB")  # outputs

Stage 5: county summaries
Mean predicted SOC, NDVI, precipitation, temperature and slope per county, in one zonal pass over a five-band stack. Zone labels are burned per chunk and partial statistics combined (notebook 05); the partial sums run on the GPU.

title: Capstone: Soil Carbon and Cropland of Every Great Plains County
text:
Stage 6: spatial patterns
Is county SOC spatially clustered, and does cropland share explain it once climate is accounted for? Queen weights, Moran’s I, LISA and G* (notebook 06) on the county means, then a simple regression of county SOC on cropland share, precipitation and temperature.


Code
t0 = time.perf_counter()  # start
w = pdist.analysis.weights(counties, "queen")  # queen contiguity
mi = pdist.analysis.morans_i(counties.soc_mean.values, w, permutations=999, seed=0, compute=gpu)  # global
lisa = pdist.analysis.local_morans(counties.soc_mean.values, w, permutations=999, seed=0, compute=gpu)  # local
gstar = pdist.analysis.getis_ord_local(counties.soc_mean.values, w)  # hot spots
counties["lisa_q"] = np.where(lisa.p_sim < 0.05, lisa.q.map({1: "HH", 2: "LH", 3: "LL", 4: "HL"}), "ns")  # significant quadrants
counties["gstar_z"] = gstar.Zs.values  # z-scores
Z = np.column_stack([np.ones(len(counties)), counties.crop_share, counties.preci_mean / 100, counties.temp_mean])  # design matrix
beta, *_ = np.linalg.lstsq(Z, counties.soc_mean.values, rcond=None)  # least squares
fit = Z @ beta  # fitted values
resid = counties.soc_mean.values - fit  # residuals
mi_res = pdist.analysis.morans_i(resid, w, permutations=999, seed=0)  # are residuals still clustered?
budget["6 spatial statistics and regression"] = time.perf_counter() - t0  # time
print(f"Moran's I of county SOC {mi.statistic:.2f} (p_sim {mi.p_sim:.3f}); LISA clusters: {counties.lisa_q.value_counts().to_dict()}")  # global and local
print("SOC = {:.2f} + {:.2f} crop share + {:.2f} per 100 mm precipitation + {:.2f} per degree C; R2 {:.2f}".format(*beta, r2_score(counties.soc_mean, fit)))  # regression
print(f"Moran's I of the residuals {mi_res.statistic:.2f} (p_sim {mi_res.p_sim:.3f})")  # remaining clustering


Moran's I of county SOC 0.78 (p_sim 0.001); LISA clusters: {'ns': 115, 'HH': 59, 'LL': 51}
SOC = 4.27 + 1.32 crop share + 0.93 per 100 mm precipitation + -0.39 per degree C; R2 0.84
Moran's I of the residuals 0.61 (p_sim 0.001)




Code
fig, ax = plt.subplots(1, 2, figsize=(15, 5.6))  # two panels
colors = {"HH": "#d7191c", "LL": "#2c7bb6", "LH": "#abd9e9", "HL": "#fdae61", "ns": "#eeeeee"}  # quadrant colours
counties.plot(color=counties.lisa_q.map(colors), ax=ax[0], edgecolor="grey", linewidth=0.2)  # LISA map
for k, v in colors.items():  # legend entries
    ax[0].scatter([], [], color=v, label=f"{k} ({(counties.lisa_q == k).sum()})", marker="s")  # proxy artists
ax[0].legend(fontsize=8, loc="lower left"); ax[0].set_title("LISA clusters of county mean SOC (p_sim < 0.05)"); ax[0].set_axis_off()  # labels
sc = ax[1].scatter(counties.crop_share, counties.soc_mean, c=counties.preci_mean, cmap="viridis", s=18)  # SOC against cropland
plt.colorbar(sc, ax=ax[1], label="mean annual precipitation (mm)")  # colour scale
ax[1].set_xlabel("cropland share"); ax[1].set_ylabel("mean predicted SOC (kg m-2)"); ax[1].set_title("County SOC, cropland and rainfall")  # labels
plt.tight_layout(); plt.show()  # draw









County SOC is strongly clustered (Moran’s I about 0.8): a high-high cluster in the wetter east of Kansas and another in the Colorado mountains, low-low clusters across New Mexico and the dry plains of south-eastern Colorado. Precipitation and temperature explain most of the county differences. The regression gives cropland share a positive coefficient, which seems to contradict the expectation that cultivation lowers SOC. It does not: in the Great Plains, cropland is concentrated on the deeper, wetter soils of central and eastern Kansas, and the regression picks up where crops are grown, not what cultivation does to a given soil. The scatter shows it: at the same rainfall, cropland and SOC are hardly related. A county regression cannot separate the two; answering the causal question needs paired comparisons of cultivated and uncultivated soils, or the causal methods of chapter 03. The residuals are still clustered, so a spatial regression model (chapter 05) would be the next step.

title: Capstone: Soil Carbon and Cropland of Every Great Plains County
text:
Summary and exercises

One pipeline joined every part of the chapter: an out-of-core pass over 21 billion CDL pixels, aligned covariate stacks, a spatially validated model, a 262 million pixel prediction, zonal statistics on CPU and GPU, and spatial statistics of the county table.
Reading and decompressing the 10 m CDL dominated the time budget; that stage is I/O-bound and stays on the CPU, while the GPU took over the prediction and the zonal partial sums.
County SOC was strongly clustered: high in the wetter east and the mountains, low on the warm, dry southern plains. A regression on cropland share, precipitation and temperature explained most of it (R2 about 0.8). Its positive cropland coefficient reflects where crops are grown, not an effect of cultivation, and its residuals remained clustered, so a spatial model (chapter 05) would be the next step.
The results are analysis-ready: a county GeoParquet file and a COG of the SOC map.

Exercises

Run the whole notebook with gpu = "cpu" and compare the time budget stage by stage.
Replace cropland share with wheat share and corn share in the regression. Which crop is associated with lower SOC after accounting for climate?
Add the prediction uncertainty: fit 10 models on bootstrap samples, predict the map with each, and compute the county mean of the standard deviation.
Extend the cropland stage to the whole of Nebraska and South Dakota (the CDL is national) and compare their cropland shares with Kansas.


Option B for further work
The outline of this chapter also proposed a Bangladesh flood exposure capstone: Microsoft building footprints of Bangladesh (from the same Planetary Computer collection as the Kansas buildings), the Sentinel-1 char land flood maps of the remote sensing capstone, a partitioned spatial join of buildings to flooded areas, zonal counts per upazila, HDBSCAN settlement clusters and network distance to the nearest road. Every step uses functions shown in notebooks 02 to 07.

title: Spatial SQL on Spark with Apache Sedona
text: Banner

title: Spatial SQL on Spark with Apache Sedona
text:
Overview

Spark’s model







Part
Role




Driver
the program you write; plans the job


Executors
JVM processes (on this machine: threads of one JVM in local[*] mode) that run tasks


Partitions
slices of a DataFrame; one task per partition per stage


Shuffle
moves rows between partitions between stages (joins, group-bys)


Lazy plans
transformations build a plan; actions (count, collect, write) run it, after the Catalyst optimizer has rewritten it





What Sedona adds

A geometry type and about 200 ST_ functions (ST_Contains, ST_Intersects, ST_DWithin, ST_Buffer, ST_Area, ST_Transform, …), callable from SQL and the DataFrame API.
Spatial joins: when a join condition is a spatial predicate, Sedona partitions both sides spatially (KDB-tree or quadtree grids), builds an index per partition and tests only matching partitions. A small side can instead be broadcast to every executor.
GeoParquet and shapefile readers and writers, and raster functions.



Spark or Dask?







Situation
Better fit




data already in a Spark lake, SQL users, a Databricks or EMR cluster
Spark with Sedona


both sides of a join have hundreds of millions of rows
Spark with Sedona (spatial partitioning of both sides)


one side is small (zones, counties, facilities)
either; Dask sends the small side to every task


rasters, NumPy and GPU work, Python-first workflows
Dask (and GeoLattice)



Moving data between Python and the JVM is not free: GeoPandas frames are serialized (with Arrow) on the way in and out. A fair comparison counts that cost.

title: Spatial SQL on Spark with Apache Sedona
text:
Sedona with GeoLattice







Function
Does




pdist.sedona.spark(master=, config=)
starts (or reuses) a Sedona-enabled Spark session; the Sedona JARs matching the installed versions are fetched from Maven on first use


pdist.sedona.to_spark(gdf), to_geopandas(sdf)
GeoDataFrame to Spark DataFrame and back (GeoArrow when available)


pdist.sedona.sjoin(left, right, predicate=)
spatial join as Spark SQL; GeoPandas in gives GeoPandas out with geopandas.sjoin’s columns, Spark in gives a lazy Spark DataFrame


pdist.vector.sjoin(..., engine="sedona")
the same, from the Dask API; engine="auto" picks Sedona when an input is a Spark DataFrame


pdist.sedona.is_spark(obj), stop()
type check; shut the session down



Installation: pip install "geolattice[distributed-spark]" (PySpark and apache-sedona) and a Java 17 or newer runtime.

Learning objectives

Describe Spark’s driver, executors, partitions and shuffles, and what Sedona adds.
Start a Sedona session and move GeoDataFrames into and out of Spark.
Run the same spatial join with Sedona and with Dask, check that the results agree, and compare the costs.
Write spatial SQL with ST_ functions on zones and trips.
Read and write GeoParquet from Spark.



Data







Dataset
Content




Kansas building footprints and counties
1.6 million polygons; 105 county polygons (EPSG:5070)

title: Spatial SQL on Spark with Apache Sedona
section: Buildings by county: Sedona and Dask
text:
Buildings by county: Sedona and Dask
The join from notebook 04, now with three engines: GeoPandas on one core, GeoLattice’s partitioned Dask join, and Sedona. With GeoPandas input, pdist.sedona.sjoin sends the geometries to Spark, joins there and builds the result with GeoPandas’ own join code, so the columns match geopandas.sjoin exactly.


Code
bld = pdist.vector.to_crs(dd.kansas_buildings(), 5070)  # 1.6 million buildings in metres
ks = dd.gp_counties().query("state == 'KS'")[["FIPS", "county", "geometry"]].reset_index(drop=True)  # 105 counties
t = {}  # timings
t["GeoPandas, one core"], j_gpd = timed(lambda: gpd.sjoin(bld, ks, predicate="intersects"))  # reference
t["GeoLattice Dask, 24 threads"], j_dask = timed(lambda: pdist.vector.sjoin(bld, ks, predicate="intersects"))  # partitioned
t["Sedona, GeoPandas in and out"], j_sed = timed(lambda: pdist.vector.sjoin(bld, ks, predicate="intersects", engine="sedona"))  # Spark
key = lambda j: sorted(zip(j.index, j.index_right))  # the joined pairs
print("same pairs: Dask", key(j_dask) == key(j_gpd), "| Sedona", key(j_sed) == key(j_gpd), "| same columns:", list(j_sed.columns) == list(j_gpd.columns))  # checks
pd.Series(t, name="seconds").round(2).to_frame()  # table


same pairs: Dask True | Sedona True | same columns: True









seconds




GeoPandas, one core
2.02


GeoLattice Dask, 24 threads
1.05


Sedona, GeoPandas in and out
2.48







All three engines return the same 1.6 million pairs and the same columns. On one machine with a small right side, the Dask join is the fastest: it ships the 105 counties to every task and never leaves Python. Sedona pays to move 1.6 million geometries from Python into the JVM and the pairs back. That overhead is fixed by the data size, not the cluster size; on a cluster with the data already in Spark it disappears, and Sedona’s spatial partitioning then scales across machines.

title: Spatial SQL on Spark with Apache Sedona
text:
Joining two Spark DataFrames
When the data start in Spark, nothing crosses the Python boundary until the result is small. The buildings are written once as GeoParquet; Spark reads them directly, and pdist.vector.sjoin with Spark DataFrames on both sides returns a lazy Spark DataFrame (engine="auto" detects Spark). Spark plans the join as a spatial join, visible in the physical plan.


Code
bld[["geometry"]].to_parquet(SP / "buildings_5070.parquet")  # GeoParquet for Spark
s_bld = spark.read.format("geoparquet").load(str(SP / "buildings_5070.parquet"))  # lazy Spark DataFrame
s_ks = pdist.sedona.to_spark(ks)  # 105 counties into Spark
print("Spark inputs:", pdist.sedona.is_spark(s_bld), pdist.sedona.is_spark(s_ks), "| partitions:", s_bld.rdd.getNumPartitions())  # types
joined = pdist.vector.sjoin(s_bld, s_ks, predicate="intersects")  # engine="auto" picks Sedona: lazy result
plan = joined._jdf.queryExecution().executedPlan().toString()  # the physical plan
print([line.strip()[:90] for line in plan.splitlines() if "Join" in line or "Range" in line][:3])  # the join operator
t0 = time.perf_counter()  # start
per_county = joined.groupBy("FIPS", "county").count().toPandas()  # run: only 105 rows come back
print(f"join and count in Spark: {time.perf_counter() - t0:.1f} s; {int(per_county['count'].sum()):,} pairs")  # time
per_county.sort_values("count", ascending=False).head(5)  # largest counties

title: Spatial SQL on Spark with Apache Sedona
text:
Summary and exercises

Spark runs lazy, optimized plans over partitions with executors; Sedona adds geometry types, ST_ functions, spatial partitioning and spatial joins.
pdist.sedona.spark starts a session with the matching Sedona JARs; to_spark and to_geopandas move data across the Python and JVM boundary.
The county join gave identical pairs with GeoPandas, Dask and Sedona. With GeoPandas input on one machine, Dask was fastest, because Sedona paid to move the geometries into the JVM; with both inputs read by Spark, the join and aggregation ran inside Spark and only 105 rows came back, in about the same time.
Spatial SQL combined ST_Area, ST_DWithin, ST_Distance and ST_Contains with ordinary aggregation of 38 million trips, and Spark wrote GeoParquet that GeoPandas read directly.

Exercises

Repeat the Spark-only join with spark.sql.shuffle.partitions set to 8 and to 200. How does the time change?
Use ST_Buffer to find the taxi zones within 1 mile of Central Park and count their pickups.
Join the buildings with themselves in Sedona (ST_DWithin with 20 m) to count each building’s close neighbours; why would this be hard with the Dask engine?
Read the GeoParquet written by Spark with DuckDB’s spatial extension and repeat one query.

title: Flow Direction and Accumulation on Large DEMs
text:
Overview

The D8 model
Each cell drains to the steepest downhill of its 8 neighbours (flow direction). Following those pointers from cell to cell traces flow paths; counting how many cells’ paths pass through a cell gives its flow accumulation (contributing area). Cells whose accumulation exceeds a threshold form the stream network, and the cells that drain to a chosen outlet form its catchment.


Local and global steps








Step
Information needed
Chunking




Flow direction
the 8 neighbours
local: chunks plus a 1 pixel halo, exact


Depression filling
the lowest outlet of every depression, possibly far away
global: a depression can span many chunks


Flow accumulation
every cell upstream
global: one cell’s answer depends on cells across the DEM


Streams, catchments
accumulation and flow paths
global



Real DEMs contain depressions (pits) with no downhill neighbour: real closed basins, errors, and places where a road embankment hides a culvert. Water would stop there, so depressions are filled (raised to their spill level; priority-flood, Barnes et al. 2014) or breached (a channel is cut through the barrier) before accumulation.


Strategies for DEMs that are too large

In memory, when it fits: simplest and exact.
Tile by watershed: cut the DEM along drainage divides (from a coarse DEM or a basin dataset such as HydroBASINS), so no flow crosses a tile edge, and process each basin alone.
Coarsen: run on a 270 m or 1 km DEM when the analysis allows.
Specialised out-of-core tools: WhiteboxTools (multithreaded Rust), TauDEM (MPI), RichDEM, or parallel priority-flood algorithms that exchange information between tiles (Barnes 2016).

title: Flow Direction and Accumulation on Large DEMs
section: D8 flow direction, chunked, on CPU and GPU
text:
D8 flow direction, chunked, on CPU and GPU
Flow direction needs only each cell’s 8 neighbours, so it runs chunk by chunk with a 1 pixel halo. Outside the DEM (and in no-data holes) the halo holds NaN, so no cell drains off the edge by accident.


Code
dem = dd.gp_raster("elev").compute()  # 262 million pixels in memory
t = {}  # timings
for c in (["cpu", "gpu"] if caps["gpus"] else ["cpu"]):  # both targets
    pdist.hydrology.flow_direction(dem, compute=c); sync()  # warm-up
    t0 = time.perf_counter(); fd = pdist.hydrology.flow_direction(dem, compute=c); sync(); t[f"chunked, {c}"] = time.perf_counter() - t0  # time
t0 = time.perf_counter(); fd_ref = tr.flow_direction(dem); t["whole array, NumPy, one core"] = time.perf_counter() - t0  # reference
print(pd.Series(t, name="seconds").round(2).to_string())  # timings
print("chunked equals whole-array result:", bool((fd.values == np.asarray(fd_ref)).all()))  # exact match
codes = pd.Series(fd.values.ravel()).value_counts().sort_index()  # cells per direction
names = {-1: "none (pit, flat or no data)", 0: "N", 1: "NE", 2: "E", 3: "SE", 4: "S", 5: "SW", 6: "W", 7: "NW"}  # code names
valid = int(np.isfinite(dem.values).sum())  # cells with data
pits = int(((fd.values == -1) & np.isfinite(dem.values)).sum())  # cells with data and no lower neighbour
print(f"cells with data: {valid:,}; with no lower neighbour: {pits:,} ({pits / valid:.1%})")  # depressions and flats
codes.rename(index=names).to_frame("cells")  # table

title: Flow Direction and Accumulation on Large DEMs
section: How far does in-memory filling and accumulation scale?
text:
How far does in-memory filling and accumulation scale?
Filling and accumulation are global. GeoLattice computes them in memory: priority-flood filling (a heap-based loop, one cell at a time in Python) and accumulation as a topological sweep down the flow paths. (An earlier version solved accumulation as one sparse linear system with SciPy’s general LU solver; while this notebook was written it ran out of memory on the 4096 x 4096 basin below, so it was replaced by the sweep, which gives identical results with memory that grows linearly.) The cells below time both on square windows of growing size in central Kansas and record the peak memory, then fit power laws and extrapolate to the full DEM.


Code
r0, c0 = 8000, 9000  # top-left corner of the windows, central Kansas
rows = []  # one row per window size
for n in [256, 512, 1024, 2048]:  # window sides (4096 follows in the basin section)
    w = dem[r0:r0 + n, c0:c0 + n].rio.interpolate_na()  # fill the scattered no-data holes from their neighbours
    with dd.PeakMemory(0.02) as pm:  # watch memory
        t0 = time.perf_counter(); filled = pdist.hydrology.fill_depressions(w); t_fill = time.perf_counter() - t0  # priority flood
        t0 = time.perf_counter(); acc = pdist.hydrology.flow_accumulation(filled, filled=True); t_acc = time.perf_counter() - t0  # sparse solve
    rows.append({"cells": n * n, "fill (s)": t_fill, "accumulate (s)": t_acc, "extra memory (GB)": pm.peak_gb - pm.start_gb})  # row
scal = pd.DataFrame(rows).set_index("cells")  # table

    fits[col] = {"exponent": b, "full DEM (extrapolated)": power(N, a, b)}  # extrapolate
fits = pd.DataFrame(fits).T  # table
per_cell = scal["extra memory (GB)"].iloc[-1] * 1e9 / scal.index[-1]  # bytes per cell at the largest window
print(f"full DEM: {N / 1e6:.0f} million cells, {dd.gb(dem.nbytes)} as float32; memory grows linearly, "  # size
      f"about {per_cell:.0f} bytes per cell, so roughly {per_cell * N / 1e9:.0f} GB for the full DEM")  # memory estimate
fits.round(2)  # show

Both run times grow close to linearly with the number of cells, and so does memory, at a few tens of bytes per cell. Extrapolated to all 262 million cells, accumulation would take a few minutes and the memory would fit this machine easily; filling is the slow part, at more than twenty minutes, because the priority-flood loop visits one cell at a time in Python. The full Great Plains DEM is therefore within reach of the in-memory route on this machine, but slowly, and a DEM ten times larger would not fit. For the whole region, a compiled tool is the better choice.

title: Flow Direction and Accumulation on Large DEMs
text:
The full DEM with WhiteboxTools
WhiteboxTools is a compiled, multithreaded program; geolattice.whitebox runs it on files. The full DEM is written to a GeoTIFF, filled (Wang and Liu’s fast priority-flood variant), and accumulated with D8 (output in cells).


Code
wbt = whitebox.WhiteboxTools(); wbt.set_verbose_mode(False)  # quiet runs
src = HY / "elev.tif"  # input
dem.rio.to_raster(src, tiled=True, compress="DEFLATE")  # write the in-memory DEM
steps = {}  # timings
t0 = time.perf_counter(); wbt.fill_depressions_wang_and_liu(str(src), str(HY / "filled.tif")); steps["fill depressions"] = time.perf_counter() - t0  # fill
t0 = time.perf_counter(); wbt.d8_flow_accumulation(str(HY / "filled.tif"), str(HY / "acc.tif"), out_type="cells"); steps["D8 flow accumulation"] = time.perf_counter() - t0  # accumulate
print(pd.Series(steps, name="seconds").round(1).to_string())  # timings
acc_full = pdist.read_raster(HY / "acc.tif", chunks={"y": 2048, "x": 2048})  # lazy result
print(f"largest accumulation: {float(acc_full.max()):,.0f} cells = {float(acc_full.max()) * 0.0081:,.0f} km2")  # biggest basin


fill depressions        50.1
D8 flow accumulation    10.5
largest accumulation: 12,717,194 cells = 103,009 km2




Code
streams = (acc_full >= 10_000)  # cells draining at least 81 km2
q = streams[::4, ::4].compute()  # every 4th cell for plotting
fig, ax = plt.subplots(figsize=(8, 8))  # one map
ax.imshow(dd.quicklook(dd.gp_raster("elev"), 4), cmap="Greys", extent=dd.extent(q), alpha=0.5)  # elevation backdrop
ax.imshow(np.where(q, 1.0, np.nan), cmap="Blues_r", extent=dd.extent(q), interpolation="nearest")  # streams

ax.set_title("Streams draining more than 81 km2 (WhiteboxTools, full 90 m DEM)"); ax.set_axis_off(); plt.tight_layout(); plt.show()  # draw









WhiteboxTools processed all 262 million cells in about a minute: the out-of-core and multithreaded route for DEMs too large for the in-memory functions. The stream network shows the Platte, Arkansas, Smoky Hill, Republican and Kansas rivers and the Rio Grande. Breaks in some rivers come from the DEM’s no-data holes, where the filling treats every hole as an outlet.

title: Flow Direction and Accumulation on Large DEMs
section: Streams and catchments of a Kansas basin
text:
Streams and catchments of a Kansas basin
GeoLattice’s in-memory functions handle a 4096 x 4096 window (369 x 369 km) of central Kansas in about a minute and a half, and the results can be compared with WhiteboxTools on the same window. Every cell then gets the outlet its flow path ends at (by pointer jumping along the D8 receivers), and the cells sharing the outlet with the largest accumulation form the window’s largest catchment.


Code
w = dem[r0:r0 + 4096, c0:c0 + 4096].rio.interpolate_na()  # the window, holes filled
t0 = time.perf_counter()  # start
zf = pdist.hydrology.fill_depressions(w)  # fill
fdw = pdist.hydrology.flow_direction(zf, compute="cpu")  # flow direction of the filled DEM
acc = pdist.hydrology.flow_accumulation(zf, filled=True)  # accumulation
print(f"GeoLattice, 17 million cells in memory: {time.perf_counter() - t0:.0f} s")  # time
w.rio.to_raster(HY / "win.tif")  # the same window for WhiteboxTools
wbt.fill_depressions_wang_and_liu(str(HY / "win.tif"), str(HY / "win_f.tif"))  # fill
wbt.d8_flow_accumulation(str(HY / "win_f.tif"), str(HY / "win_acc.tif"), out_type="cells")  # accumulate
acc_wb = pdist.read_raster(HY / "win_acc.tif").compute()  # Whitebox result
s_gl, s_wb = np.asarray(acc) >= 1000, acc_wb.values >= 1000  # streams draining 8.1 km2
agree = (s_gl & s_wb).sum() / (s_gl | s_wb).sum()  # overlap of the two stream networks
print(f"stream cells: GeoLattice {s_gl.sum():,}, WhiteboxTools {s_wb.sum():,}; overlap (intersection / union) {agree:.1%}")  # comparison


GeoLattice, 17 million cells in memory: 90 s
stream cells: GeoLattice 680,482, WhiteboxTools 680,894; overlap (intersection / union) 98.9%




Code
rec = _receivers(np.asarray(fdw.values))  # receiver of every cell (-1 at outlets)
idx = np.arange(rec.size)  # cell numbers
tgt = np.where(rec < 0, idx, rec)  # one step downstream (outlets point to themselves)
for _ in range(64):  # pointer jumping: each round doubles the distance followed
    nxt = tgt[tgt]  # two steps
    if np.array_equal(nxt, tgt):  # every cell has reached its outlet
        break
    tgt = nxt  # continue
acc_v = np.asarray(acc).ravel()  # accumulation as a vector
main = tgt[np.argmax(acc_v)]  # outlet of the cell with the largest accumulation
catch = (tgt == main).reshape(acc.shape)  # its catchment
print(f"largest catchment in the window: {catch.sum():,} cells = {catch.sum() * 0.0081:,.0f} km2")  # area
fig, ax = plt.subplots(1, 2, figsize=(15, 7))  # two maps
ext = dd.extent(w)  # extent
ax[0].imshow(w, cmap="terrain", extent=ext)  # elevation
ax[0].imshow(np.where(np.asarray(acc) >= 1000, np.log10(np.asarray(acc)), np.nan), cmap="Blues", extent=ext, interpolation="nearest")  # streams
ax[0].set_title("Elevation and streams draining more than 8 km2 (GeoLattice)")  # title
ax[1].imshow(np.where(catch, 1, np.nan), cmap="Oranges", vmin=0, vmax=1.5, extent=ext, interpolation="nearest")  # catchment
ax[1].imshow(np.where(s_gl, 1, np.nan), cmap="Blues_r", extent=ext, interpolation="nearest")  # streams on top
ax[1].set_title("The window's largest catchment"); [a.set_axis_off() for a in ax]  # labels
plt.tight_layout(); plt.show()  # draw


largest catchment in the window: 5,471,197 cells = 44,317 km2











Code
shutil.rmtree(HY)  # remove the scratch files


GeoLattice and WhiteboxTools give nearly the same stream network on the window. The remaining differences come from flats: the two programs give filled flats slightly different gradients (GeoLattice an epsilon of 10^-4 m per step, Wang and Liu’s method none), so flow across large flat areas can take different routes. The largest catchment in the window ends where its river leaves the window. That is the practical lesson of the section: a catchment cut by a tile edge is incomplete, which is why large DEMs are tiled along drainage divides, not along rows and columns.

title: Flow Direction and Accumulation on Large DEMs
text:
Summary and exercises

Flow direction is local and was computed for 262 million cells chunk by chunk, identical to the whole-array result, on CPU and GPU.
Depression filling and flow accumulation are global. GeoLattice’s in-memory versions grew close to linearly in time and memory; the full DEM would fit in memory but filling would take more than twenty minutes. Accumulation, rewritten as a topological sweep while this notebook was written, no longer runs out of memory.
WhiteboxTools filled and accumulated the full DEM in about a minute, out of process and multithreaded.
On a 4096 x 4096 basin window the stream networks of GeoLattice and WhiteboxTools overlapped by 99 %; the differences come from the gradient given to filled flats.
Catchments cut by tile edges are incomplete: tile large DEMs by watershed.

Exercises

Repeat the stream comparison with thresholds of 100, 1,000 and 10,000 cells. Where do the two programs differ most?
Coarsen the DEM to 270 m (dem.coarsen(x=3, y=3).mean()) and run the in-memory functions on all of Kansas. Compare the stream network with the 90 m WhiteboxTools result.
Use geolattice.rsense.lidar.terrain.hand on the basin window to compute the height above nearest drainage, and map the cells less than 2 m above a stream.
Use WhiteboxTools’ breach_depressions_least_cost instead of filling and compare the stream networks. Which handles road embankments better?

title: Spatial Weights, Autocorrelation, Hot Spots and Clustering for Large Data
text: Banner

title: Spatial Weights, Autocorrelation, Hot Spots and Clustering for Large Data
text:
Overview

Why spatial statistics get expensive








Step
Naive cost
What makes it tractable




Spatial weights
compare every pair: n^2
k-nearest neighbours with a KD-tree, contiguity with a spatial join: about n log n


Global statistic (Moran’s I)
one sparse product z' W z
cheap: proportional to the number of neighbour pairs


999 permutations of a global statistic
999 sparse products
batch the permutations as columns of one matrix: a few sparse matrix products


Local statistics (LISA, G*) with permutations
999 permutations for each of n observations
conditional permutation with shared random draws, computed in blocks





Spatial weights
A weights matrix W lists, for each observation, its neighbours: polygons that share an edge (rook) or a point (queen), the k nearest points (knn), or all points within a distance (distance band, binary or inverse distance). It is stored sparse: a million observations with 8 neighbours each need 8 million entries, not 10^12. Row standardisation divides each row by its sum, so the spatial lag W y is the mean of the neighbours.


Global and local statistics

Moran’s I: I = (n / S0) (z' W z) / (z' z), with z the deviations from the mean. Positive when similar values cluster.
Geary’s C: based on squared differences between neighbours; below 1 means positive autocorrelation.
Local Moran’s I (LISA): I_i = z_i (W z)_i / m2, one value per observation, with quadrants HH (high among high), LL, HL and LH.
Getis-Ord G*: the share of the total in each neighbourhood (including the observation itself), as a z-score: positive for hot spots, negative for cold spots.

Inference compares the observed statistic with its distribution under random permutations of the values (the pseudo p-value p_sim), or with a normal approximation.


Clustering points

DBSCAN groups points that have at least min_samples neighbours within eps; the rest is noise. One distance scale for all clusters.
HDBSCAN builds DBSCAN for every eps at once and keeps the most stable clusters; it finds dense and sparse clusters together.
k-means splits points into k groups around centres; every point belongs to a group.
Kernel density estimation (KDE) spreads each point over a smooth kernel and sums them on a grid.

title: Spatial Weights, Autocorrelation, Hot Spots and Clustering for Large Data
text:
Weights for counties
Queen and rook contiguity for the 225 Great Plains counties come from a partitioned spatial join with the touches predicate (rook keeps pairs that share a boundary segment, not just a point). libpysal computes the same from the polygons’ shared vertices.


Code
counties = dd.gp_counties()  # 225 counties, EPSG:5070
wq = pdist.analysis.weights(counties, "queen")  # queen contiguity, row-standardised
wr = pdist.analysis.weights(counties, "rook")  # rook contiguity
wk = pdist.analysis.weights(counties, "knn", k=6)  # 6 nearest centroids
lq = libpysal.weights.Queen.from_dataframe(counties, use_index=False)  # the reference
lr = libpysal.weights.Rook.from_dataframe(counties, use_index=False)  # the reference
same = lambda w, l: (w.binary().sparse != l.sparse).nnz == 0  # identical neighbour sets?
print(f"queen: mean {wq.cardinalities.mean():.2f} neighbours, islands {len(wq.islands)}, same as libpysal: {same(wq, lq)}")  # queen
print(f"rook:  mean {wr.cardinalities.mean():.2f} neighbours, same as libpysal: {same(wr, lr)}")  # rook
print(f"knn:   {wk.cardinalities.min()} to {wk.cardinalities.max()} neighbours, {wk.sparse.nnz} entries")  # knn


queen: mean 5.39 neighbours, islands 0, same as libpysal: True
rook:  mean 5.19 neighbours, same as libpysal: True
knn:   6 to 6 neighbours, 1350 entries


GeoLattice and libpysal find the same neighbours. Queen counties have one more neighbour on average than rook counties: the corner contacts of the township and range grid, where four counties meet at a point.

The local values equal esda’s; the counts of significant counties differ slightly because the permutations use different random draws. Eastern Kansas forms a high-high cluster and hot spot of vegetation, joined by a small high-high cluster of forested counties in the Colorado mountains. New Mexico, most of Wyoming and the dry plains of south-eastern Colorado form low-low clusters and cold spots.

section: From a thousand to a million observations
text:
From a thousand to a million observations
The same statistics on Kansas buildings: the variable is the logarithm of footprint area, the weights are the 8 nearest neighbours of each building’s representative point. Samples of 10^3 to 10^6 buildings show how each step scales on the CPU and the GPU, with esda for comparison where it finishes in reasonable time.


Code
bld = pdist.vector.to_crs(dd.kansas_buildings(), 5070)  # 1.6 million buildings in metres
bld["log_area"] = np.log(pdist.vector.area(bld))  # log footprint area
pts = bld.set_geometry(bld.geometry.representative_point())  # one point per building
rows = []  # timings
for n in [1_000, 10_000, 100_000, 1_000_000]:  # sample sizes
    s = pts.sample(n, random_state=0)  # random sample
    y = s.log_area.values  # the variable
    r = {"n": n}  # one row
    r["weights knn CPU"], w = timed(lambda: pdist.analysis.weights(s, "knn", k=8, compute="cpu"))  # KD-tree
    if caps["gpus"] and n <= 100_000:  # GPU knn is brute force: n x n distances, so only up to 10^5
        r["weights knn GPU"], _ = timed(lambda: pdist.analysis.weights(s, "knn", k=8, compute="gpu"))  # brute force
    r["Moran 999 CPU"], m_c = timed(lambda: pdist.analysis.morans_i(y, w, permutations=999, seed=0, compute="cpu"))  # batched permutations
    if caps["gpus"]:  # GPU Moran
        r["Moran 999 GPU"], m_g = timed(lambda: pdist.analysis.morans_i(y, w, permutations=999, seed=0, compute="gpu"))  # on the GPU
    r["LISA 999 CPU"], _ = timed(lambda: pdist.analysis.local_morans(y, w, permutations=999, seed=0, compute="cpu"))  # local
    if caps["gpus"]:  # GPU LISA
        r["LISA 999 GPU"], _ = timed(lambda: pdist.analysis.local_morans(y, w, permutations=999, seed=0, compute="gpu"))  # local on GPU
    if n <= 100_000:  # esda for the smaller samples
        wl = w.to_libpysal(); wl.transform = "r"  # same weights
        r["esda Moran 999"], e = timed(lambda: esda.Moran(y, wl, permutations=999))  # reference
        r["esda LISA 999"], _ = timed(lambda: esda.Moran_Local(y, wl, permutations=999, n_jobs=-1, seed=0))  # reference
        r["I equals esda"] = bool(np.isclose(m_c.statistic, e.I))  # check
    r["Moran I"] = m_c.statistic  # the statistic
    rows.append(r)  # keep
scale = pd.DataFrame(rows).set_index("n")  # table
scale.round(3)  # show

for col, style in [("weights knn CPU", "o-"), ("weights knn GPU", "o--"), ("Moran 999 CPU", "s-"), ("Moran 999 GPU", "s--"), ("LISA 999 CPU", "^-"),  # series
                   ("LISA 999 GPU", "^--"), ("esda Moran 999", "x:"), ("esda LISA 999", "+:")]:  # esda
    if col in scale:  # present on this machine
        ax.loglog(scale.index, scale[col], style, label=col)  # time against n
ax.set_xlabel("observations"); ax.set_ylabel("seconds"); ax.legend(fontsize=8, ncol=2)  # labels
ax.set_title("Cost of spatial statistics as n grows (k = 8 neighbours, 999 permutations)"); plt.tight_layout(); plt.show()  # draw









All costs grow roughly linearly with n, which is what sparse weights and batched permutations buy. The exception is the GPU’s brute-force nearest-neighbour search, which compares every pair and grows with n^2; it was run only up to 10^5 points, and the KD-tree is the right tool beyond that. On the CPU, GeoLattice’s batched permutations were somewhat slower than esda, whose permutation loops are compiled with numba (esda’s very first LISA call, at 10^3, includes about half a minute of that compilation). On the GPU the same batched algorithm was about ten times faster than the CPU for Moran’s I and about five times faster for LISA, and it finished the million-building case (999 permutations, 8 neighbours each) in seconds. The statistic itself agreed with esda at every size where esda was run. Building sizes are positively but weakly autocorrelated (I of 0.1 to 0.25, higher in the denser samples): neighbouring buildings tend to be of similar size, as in subdivisions, farmsteads and industrial parks.

title: Spatial Weights, Autocorrelation, Hot Spots and Clustering for Large Data
text:
Settlements from building centroids
Clusters of buildings are settlements. DBSCAN with eps = 100 m and 20 buildings finds compact built-up areas; HDBSCAN adapts to varying density. The 270,000 buildings of the Wichita area are clustered on the CPU (scikit-learn) and on the GPU (cuML), and the two labelings compared with the adjusted Rand index (1 = identical partitions).


Code
x0, y0 = gpd.GeoSeries.from_xy([-97.34], [37.69], crs=4326).to_crs(5070).iloc[0].coords[0]  # central Wichita
area = pts.cx[x0 - 40_000:x0 + 40_000, y0 - 40_000:y0 + 40_000]  # 80 x 80 km
print(f"{len(area):,} buildings")  # size

res["DBSCAN CPU"], db_c = timed(lambda: pdist.analysis.dbscan(area, eps=100, min_samples=20, compute="cpu"))  # scikit-learn

    print("DBSCAN CPU vs GPU adjusted Rand index:", round(adjusted_rand_score(db_c, db_g), 4))  # agreement
res["HDBSCAN CPU"], hd_c = timed(lambda: pdist.analysis.hdbscan(area, min_cluster_size=50, compute="cpu"))  # scikit-learn
if caps["gpus"]:  # cuML
    res["HDBSCAN GPU"], hd_g = timed(lambda: pdist.analysis.hdbscan(area, min_cluster_size=50, compute="gpu"))  # cuML
    print("HDBSCAN CPU vs GPU adjusted Rand index:", round(adjusted_rand_score(hd_c, hd_g), 4))  # agreement
res["k-means CPU"], (km_c, cen) = timed(lambda: pdist.analysis.kmeans(area, 12, compute="cpu"))  # 12 groups

DBSCAN separates Wichita and its suburbs from the surrounding small towns and farmsteads (grey noise). HDBSCAN finds many more, smaller clusters, down to individual subdivisions and villages, because it does not fix one density threshold. k-means is the odd one out: it must put every building in one of 12 groups, so it cuts the city into slices instead of finding settlements.
The two engines behave very differently here, and the reasons matter.

DBSCAN: the CPU and GPU labelings agree, but scikit-learn’s KD-tree beats cuML’s brute-force neighbour search on two-dimensional points by a wide margin. GeoLattice therefore keeps DBSCAN on the CPU unless compute="gpu" is asked for.
HDBSCAN: cuML was about twenty times faster, but its partition differs from scikit-learn’s (an adjusted Rand index of about 0.7 above). Two things were found while writing this notebook. First, on raw EPSG:5070 coordinates (values in the millions of metres) cuML lost precision and agreed with scikit-learn at an index near 0; GeoLattice now subtracts the mean of the coordinates before clustering, which changes nothing mathematically. Second, even on centred coordinates cuML builds its cluster hierarchy differently (it found fewer, larger clusters), while scikit-learn’s result was stable to a 1 cm jitter of the points. cuML’s HDBSCAN is therefore opt-in: use it when speed matters more than matching the reference implementation, and check its clusters.
k-means gave the same groups on both, at similar speed.

title: Spatial Weights, Autocorrelation, Hot Spots and Clustering for Large Data
text:
Building density surface
pdist.analysis.kde computes a kernel density surface on the grid of a template raster. Each chunk receives only the points within the kernel’s reach, so 1.6 million points and a statewide grid stay manageable. Here a quartic kernel with a 3 km bandwidth on a 1 km grid covering Kansas.


Code
xmin, ymin, xmax, ymax = pts.total_bounds  # Kansas extent
xs = np.arange(xmin, xmax, 1000) + 500; ys = np.arange(ymax, ymin, -1000) - 500  # 1 km pixel centres
grid = xr.DataArray(np.zeros((len(ys), len(xs)), np.float32), dims=("y", "x"), coords={"y": ys, "x": xs}).rio.write_crs(5070)  # template
res = {}  # timings
for c in (["cpu", "gpu"] if caps["gpus"] else ["cpu"]):  # both targets
    res[c], dens = timed(lambda: pdist.analysis.kde(pts, grid, bandwidth=3000, kernel="quartic", compute=c, chunks=(64, 64)))  # density
    print(f"compute={c}: {res[c]:.1f} s for {len(pts):,} points on a {grid.shape[0]} x {grid.shape[1]} grid")  # time
dens_km2 = dens * 1e6  # buildings per km2
print(f"integral {float(dens.sum()) * 1e6:,.0f} (should be close to {len(pts):,})")  # check: density integrates to the count
fig, ax = plt.subplots(figsize=(12, 5.5))  # one map
im = ax.imshow(np.log10(dens_km2 + 0.1), extent=dd.extent(dens), cmap="magma")  # log density
plt.colorbar(im, ax=ax, shrink=0.7, label="log10 buildings per km2")  # scale
ax.set_title("Kernel density of 1.6 million Kansas buildings (quartic, 3 km)"); ax.set_axis_off(); plt.tight_layout(); plt.show()  # draw


compute=cpu: 23.8 s for 1,605,334 points on a 353 x 652 grid
compute=gpu: 3.2 s for 1,605,334 points on a 353 x 652 grid
integral 1,604,789 (should be close to 1,605,334)









The density integrates to the number of buildings (up to the kernels that spill over the state border), a quick check that the surface is a proper density. The towns along the highways and rivers, Wichita, Topeka, Lawrence and the Kansas City suburbs stand out against the sparse west.

title: Spatial Weights, Autocorrelation, Hot Spots and Clustering for Large Data
text:
Summary and exercises

Sparse weights, batched global permutations and blocked conditional permutations keep spatial statistics close to linear in the number of observations.
GeoLattice’s contiguity weights matched libpysal’s, and Moran’s I, Geary’s C, LISA and G* matched esda; permutation p-values agree in distribution.
From 10^3 to 10^6 buildings the cost grew roughly linearly. On the CPU esda was somewhat faster; the GPU was five to ten times faster than both and handled a million buildings in seconds.
DBSCAN, HDBSCAN and k-means answer different questions about building clusters. cuML’s HDBSCAN was much faster than scikit-learn’s but found a different partition, so it is opt-in; for 2-D DBSCAN the CPU KD-tree is faster.
A kernel density surface of 1.6 million points was computed chunk by chunk and integrates to the number of points.

Exercises

Repeat the county analysis with rook and knn (k = 4) weights. How much do Moran’s I and the LISA map change?
Compute G* hot spots of building size for the 100,000 building sample and map them for Wichita.
Run DBSCAN with eps of 50, 100 and 200 m. How do the number of settlements and the noise share change?
Compute the KDE with a Gaussian kernel and a 1 km bandwidth on a 250 m grid for Sedgwick County. How do CPU and GPU times change with the bandwidth?

title: Geometry Operations, Clipping, Spatial Joins and Nearest Neighbours on Millions of Features
text: Banner

title: Geometry Operations, Clipping, Spatial Joins and Nearest Neighbours on Millions of Features
text:
Overview

Two kinds of vector work








Kind
Examples
Parallel pattern




Per feature
area, length, bounds, centroid, buffer, simplify, reproject, repair
split rows into partitions; no communication


Between features
spatial join, clip, overlay, nearest neighbour, weights
find candidate pairs first, then test them exactly





Finding candidate pairs
Testing whether two polygons intersect is expensive; testing whether their bounding boxes intersect is four comparisons. Every efficient spatial join therefore works in two steps:

Filter: a spatial index (an R-tree such as GEOS’s STRtree) returns the pairs whose boxes overlap.
Refine: the exact geometric predicate (intersects, within, …) runs only on those candidates.

When the data are split into partitions, the same idea works one level up: a partition of left features needs only the right features whose boxes touch the partition’s bounding box. This partition pruning is effective only when partitions are spatially compact, which is why GeoLattice sorts features along a Hilbert curve first (notebook 00).


Shuffles
When both tables are large and partitioned differently, a distributed join must move rows so that features that might match end up in the same partition: a shuffle, the most expensive step in distributed vector work. GeoLattice avoids it when one side is small enough to send to every task (counties, zones, facilities), and partitions only the large side. Spark (notebook 10) and dask-geopandas shuffle both sides when neither is small.


Points in polygons on a GPU
The most common big join is points in polygons (GPS fixes, building centroids, sensor locations). Its refine step is the crossing-number test: count how often a ray from the point crosses the polygon’s edges. Every candidate pair is independent, which suits a GPU.

import numpy as np  # arrays
import pandas as pd  # tables
import geopandas as gpd  # vector data
import xarray as xr  # labelled rasters

import geolattice  # GeoLattice
import geolattice.distributed as pdist  # distributed and GPU spatial computing
import dist_data as dd  # chapter helper: paths, cached downloads, timers

plt.rcParams.update({"figure.dpi": 110})  # figure resolution
pd.set_option("display.width", 140)  # wider printed tables
OUT = Path("outputs")  # results and scratch files written by this chapter
OUT.mkdir(exist_ok=True)  # create it if needed
caps = pdist.capabilities()  # engines and GPUs on this machine
print("GeoLattice", geolattice.__version__, "|", os.cpu_count(), "CPU cores |", caps["gpus"], "GPU(s)",  # versions
      f"({caps.get('gpu_memory_total', 0) / 1e9:.0f} GB)" if caps["gpus"] else "")  # GPU memory

import dask  # Dask configuration


def sync():  # wait for queued GPU work so timings are real
    if caps["gpus"]:  # only with a GPU
        import cupy as cp  # GPU arrays
        cp.cuda.Device().synchronize()  # block until done


def timed(fn, n=2):  # best wall time of n runs after a warm-up, and the last result
    out = fn(); sync()  # warm-up
    best = np.inf  # best time
    for _ in range(n):  # timed runs
        t = time.perf_counter(); out = fn(); sync(); best = min(best, time.perf_counter() - t)  # one run
    return best, out  # time and result

title: Geometry Operations, Clipping, Spatial Joins and Nearest Neighbours on Millions of Features
text:
Reprojecting 1.6 million buildings
The footprints come in longitude and latitude (EPSG:4326). Areas and distances need metres, so the first step reprojects them to the Albers equal-area grid (EPSG:5070) of the Great Plains rasters. pdist.vector.to_crs reprojects partitions in parallel.


Code
b4326 = dd.kansas_buildings()  # 1.6 million polygons, EPSG:4326
print(f"{len(b4326):,} buildings, {int(b4326.geometry.count_coordinates().sum()):,} vertices")  # size
t_gpd, _ = timed(lambda: b4326.to_crs(5070), n=1)  # GeoPandas, one call
t_pd, bld = timed(lambda: pdist.vector.to_crs(b4326, 5070), n=1)  # 24 partitions on 24 threads
print(f"GeoPandas to_crs {t_gpd:.2f} s | pdist.vector.to_crs {t_pd:.2f} s | same result:",  # timings
      bool(bld.geometry.geom_equals_exact(b4326.to_crs(5070).geometry, 1e-6).all()))  # check

section: Per-feature measures on CPU and GPU
text:
Per-feature measures on CPU and GPU
Area, perimeter and bounding boxes need only each polygon’s own vertices. On the CPU, GEOS computes them partition by partition on all cores; on the GPU, GeoLattice packs all vertices into flat CuPy arrays (a “ragged” layout with offsets per polygon) and computes every polygon in one kernel launch.


Code
rows = []  # timings
for name, fn in [("area", pdist.vector.area), ("length", pdist.vector.length), ("bounds", pdist.vector.bounds)]:  # measures
    t_g, _ = timed(lambda: getattr(bld.geometry, name if name != "bounds" else "bounds"), n=1)  # plain GeoPandas, one core
    t_c, r_c = timed(lambda: fn(bld, compute="cpu"))  # all cores
    t_u, r_u = timed(lambda: fn(bld, compute="gpu")) if caps["gpus"] else (np.nan, r_c)  # GPU
    diff = float(np.nanmax(np.abs(np.asarray(r_u, float) - np.asarray(r_c, float))))  # largest difference
    rows.append({"measure": name, "GeoPandas (s)": t_g, "pdist CPU (s)": t_c, "pdist GPU (s)": t_u, "largest |GPU - CPU|": diff})  # row

Each measure is a few additions per vertex, while packing 1.6 million Shapely polygons into flat coordinate and offset arrays happens in Python on the CPU and copying them to the device follows; the kernel itself is a small part of the time. Half of Kansas’s buildings have less than about 150 m2 of footprint; the largest are warehouses, factories and grain elevators.

title: Geometry Operations, Clipping, Spatial Joins and Nearest Neighbours on Millions of Features
text:
Clipping to a county
pdist.vector.clip partitions the buildings along a Hilbert curve and drops every partition whose bounding box misses the mask before any clipping is done. Sedgwick County (Wichita) is small compared with Kansas, so most partitions are dropped.


Code
counties = dd.gp_counties()  # Great Plains counties, EPSG:5070
ks = counties[counties.state == "KS"].reset_index(drop=True)  # the 105 Kansas counties
sedgwick = ks[ks.county.str.startswith("Sedgwick")]  # Sedgwick County
parts = pdist.spatial_partition(bld, 24)  # the partitions clip will use
box = pdist.partition_bounds(parts)  # their bounding boxes
x0, y0, x1, y1 = sedgwick.total_bounds  # the mask's box
kept = int(np.sum(~((box[:, 2] < x0) | (box[:, 0] > x1) | (box[:, 3] < y0) | (box[:, 1] > y1))))  # partitions that touch it
t_g, c_g = timed(lambda: gpd.clip(bld, sedgwick), n=1)  # GeoPandas
t_p, c_p = timed(lambda: pdist.vector.clip(bld, sedgwick), n=1)  # GeoLattice
print(f"partitions touching Sedgwick County: {kept} of 24")  # pruning
print(f"GeoPandas clip {t_g:.2f} s, pdist.vector.clip {t_p:.2f} s; {len(c_p):,} buildings in both: {len(c_g) == len(c_p)}")  # result

section: Buildings by county: a partitioned spatial join
text:
Buildings by county: a partitioned spatial join
Which county is each building in? pdist.vector.sjoin cuts the 1.6 million buildings into Hilbert-ordered partitions; for each partition, the county polygons whose boxes touch the partition’s box are the only ones sent to its task. The result has the same rows and columns as geopandas.sjoin.

t_p, j_p = timed(lambda: pdist.vector.sjoin(bld, ks_c, predicate="intersects"), n=1)  # partitioned, 24 threads
same = set(zip(j_g.index, j_g.index_right)) == set(zip(j_p.index, j_p.index_right))  # same building-county pairs
print(f"GeoPandas {t_g:.2f} s | pdist {t_p:.2f} s | {len(j_p):,} building-county pairs | identical: {bool(same)}")  # result
print(f"buildings in two counties (on a boundary): {int(j_p.index.duplicated().sum()):,}")  # boundary cases

section: Points in polygons on the GPU
text:
Points in polygons on the GPU
Joining building centroids instead of polygons turns the question into a point-in-polygon join, which GeoLattice runs on the GPU: the STRtree supplies candidate pairs and a CUDA kernel runs the crossing-number test for all of them at once.


Code
pts = bld.set_geometry(bld.geometry.representative_point())  # one point inside each building
rows = {}  # timings
rows["GeoPandas, one core"], r_g = timed(lambda: gpd.sjoin(pts, ks_c, predicate="within"), n=1)  # reference
rows["pdist CPU, 24 threads"], r_c = timed(lambda: pdist.vector.sjoin(pts, ks_c, predicate="within", compute="cpu"))  # CPU
if caps["gpus"]:  # GPU kernel
    rows["pdist GPU"], r_u = timed(lambda: pdist.vector.sjoin(pts, ks_c, predicate="within", compute="gpu"))  # GPU
    print("GPU pairs equal CPU pairs:", bool((r_u.index_right.values == r_c.index_right.values).all() and r_u.index.equals(r_c.index)))  # check
print(f"{len(r_c):,} points matched; unmatched (outside every county): {len(pts) - len(r_c):,}")  # coverage
pd.Series(rows, name="seconds").round(3).to_frame()  # table


GPU pairs equal CPU pairs: True
1,605,334 points matched; unmatched (outside every county): 0









seconds




GeoPandas, one core
0.288


pdist CPU, 24 threads
1.121


pdist GPU
0.746







A point lies in exactly one county, so the 1.6 million points give 1.6 million pairs, identical on CPU and GPU. The timings hold a surprise: plain GeoPandas on one core was the fastest. Its bulk STRtree.query with a predicate runs entirely in GEOS’s C code, and with only 105 polygons the refine step is cheap. The partitioned join spends more on its own bookkeeping (Hilbert sorting 1.6 million points, 24 tasks, concatenating and restoring the row order) than it saves; the GPU refine step makes it faster than the partitioned CPU path, but not than GeoPandas. Partitioning pays off when the refine step is expensive (the polygon join above was more than twice as fast), when the data do not fit one process, or on a cluster. Measure before assuming that parallel is faster.

title: Geometry Operations, Clipping, Spatial Joins and Nearest Neighbours on Millions of Features
text:
Nearest neighbours
pdist.vector.knn finds the k nearest points: a multi-threaded KD-tree on the CPU, an exact brute-force search in float64 on the GPU (which pays off when the target set is small to moderate). Two questions for Wichita:

Which school is nearest to each of its buildings, and how far is it (straight line)?
How far apart are buildings: the distance from each building to its 5 nearest neighbours.



Code
fac = dd.wichita_facilities()  # schools and hospitals, EPSG:5070
schools = fac[fac.amenity == "school"].reset_index(drop=True)  # 171 schools
wich = pts.cx[schools.total_bounds[0] - 2000:schools.total_bounds[2] + 2000,  # buildings around Wichita
              schools.total_bounds[1] - 2000:schools.total_bounds[3] + 2000]  # 2 km margin
print(f"{len(wich):,} buildings and {len(schools)} schools")  # sizes
t_c, nn_c = timed(lambda: pdist.vector.knn(wich, schools, k=1, compute="cpu"))  # KD-tree
t_u, nn_u = timed(lambda: pdist.vector.knn(wich, schools, k=1, compute="gpu")) if caps["gpus"] else (np.nan, nn_c)  # GPU
print(f"nearest school: CPU {t_c:.3f} s, GPU {t_u:.3f} s, same answer: {bool(np.allclose(nn_c.distance, nn_u.distance))}")  # check
print((nn_c.distance / 1000).describe(percentiles=[0.5, 0.9, 0.99]).round(2).to_string())  # km to the nearest school


183,800 buildings and 171 schools
nearest school: CPU 0.017 s, GPU 0.038 s, same answer: True
count    183800.00
mean          1.22
std           1.21
min           0.00
50%           0.78
90%           2.70
99%           6.36
max          10.60




Code
t_c, self_c = timed(lambda: pdist.vector.knn(wich, k=5, compute="cpu"))  # 5 nearest other buildings
t_u, self_u = timed(lambda: pdist.vector.knn(wich, k=5, compute="gpu")) if caps["gpus"] else (np.nan, self_c)  # GPU
print(f"5 nearest neighbours of {len(wich):,} buildings: CPU {t_c:.2f} s, GPU {t_u:.2f} s,",  # timings
      "same distances:", bool(np.allclose(self_c.distance.values, self_u.distance.values)))  # check
fig, ax = plt.subplots(1, 2, figsize=(13, 5))  # two panels
d1 = nn_c.distance / 1000  # km
sc = ax[0].scatter(wich.geometry.x, wich.geometry.y, c=d1.values, s=0.3, cmap="viridis_r", vmax=3)  # buildings coloured by distance
schools.plot(ax=ax[0], color="r", markersize=8, marker="^")  # schools
plt.colorbar(sc, ax=ax[0], label="km to nearest school"); ax[0].set_aspect("equal"); ax[0].set_axis_off()  # labels
ax[0].set_title("Straight-line distance to the nearest school")  # title
ax[1].hist(self_c[self_c.k == 5].distance, bins=np.linspace(0, 200, 81), color="#4575b4")  # distance to the 5th neighbour
ax[1].set_xlabel("distance to the 5th nearest building (m)"); ax[1].set_ylabel("buildings")  # axes
plt.tight_layout(); plt.show()  # draw


5 nearest neighbours of 183,800 buildings: CPU 0.10 s, GPU 21.10 s, same distances: True









With 171 schools as targets both searches take a few hundredths of a second. With 184,000 targets (the self search) the GPU’s brute force compares every pair, about 3 x 10^10 distances, and took around 200 times longer than the KD-tree, whose search grows only with the logarithm of the number of targets. GPU knn is therefore opt-in as well. Straight-line distances underestimate travel distance; notebook 07 measures the same accessibility along the road network.

title: Geometry Operations, Clipping, Spatial Joins and Nearest Neighbours on Millions of Features
text:
38 million taxi trips by zone
The 2023 taxi records carry the pickup and drop-off zone ID rather than coordinates, so the spatial step is an attribute join between trip counts and the 263 zone polygons. The counting is the heavy part: 38 million rows. It runs once with Dask on the CPU (one partition per Parquet row group) and once with cuDF on the GPU.


Code
cols = ["PULocationID", "DOLocationID", "total_amount"]  # the columns needed
trips = dd.taxi_trips(columns=cols)  # lazy Dask DataFrame
t_cpu, pu = timed(lambda: trips.groupby("PULocationID").total_amount.agg(["count", "mean"]).compute(), n=1)  # Dask on CPU
print(f"Dask on CPU: {t_cpu:.2f} s for {int(pu['count'].sum()):,} trips")  # time
if caps["gpus"]:  # GPU dataframe
    from geolattice.distributed._backend import rapids  # imports cuDF without changing CuPy's allocator
    cudf = rapids("cudf")  # GPU DataFrames
    t_read, g = timed(lambda: cudf.read_parquet(dd.TAXI, columns=cols), n=1)  # read straight into GPU memory
    t_gpu, pu_g = timed(lambda: g.groupby("PULocationID").total_amount.agg(["count", "mean"]))  # group on the GPU
    print(f"cuDF: read {t_read:.2f} s, group by zone {t_gpu:.3f} s; same counts:",  # time
          bool((pu_g.to_pandas().sort_index()["count"] == pu.sort_index()["count"]).all()))  # check
    del g  # free GPU memory


Dask on CPU: 0.28 s for 38,310,226 trips
cuDF: read 0.10 s, group by zone 0.025 s; same counts: True




Code
zones = dd.taxi_zones()  # 263 zone polygons
zmap = zones.merge(pu.rename(columns={"count": "pickups", "mean": "mean_fare"}), left_on="LocationID", right_index=True, how="left")  # attribute join
flows = trips.groupby(["PULocationID", "DOLocationID"]).size().compute()  # trips between every pair of zones
boro = zones.set_index("LocationID").borough  # zone -> borough
f = flows.rename("trips").reset_index()  # as a table
f["from"] = f.PULocationID.map(boro); f["to"] = f.DOLocationID.map(boro)  # boroughs
od = f.pivot_table(index="from", columns="to", values="trips", aggfunc="sum").fillna(0) / 1e6  # millions of trips
fig, ax = plt.subplots(1, 2, figsize=(14, 6), gridspec_kw={"width_ratios": [1.1, 1]})  # map and matrix
zmap.plot("pickups", ax=ax[0], cmap="inferno_r", legend=True, scheme="quantiles", k=7,  # pickups per zone
          legend_kwds={"title": "pickups in 2023", "fontsize": 7, "loc": "upper left"}, missing_kwds={"color": "lightgrey"})  # legend
ax[0].set_title("Yellow taxi pickups by zone, 2023"); ax[0].set_axis_off()  # title
im = ax[1].imshow(np.log10(od.values * 1e6 + 1), cmap="viridis")  # log scale
ax[1].set_xticks(range(len(od.columns))); ax[1].set_xticklabels(od.columns, rotation=45, ha="right")  # labels
ax[1].set_yticks(range(len(od.index))); ax[1].set_yticklabels(od.index)  # labels
for (i, j), v in np.ndenumerate(od.values):  # annotate
    ax[1].text(j, i, f"{v:.2f}" if v >= 0.01 else "", ha="center", va="center", color="w", fontsize=7)  # millions
ax[1].set_title("Trips between boroughs (millions; colour: log10 trips)"); ax[1].set_xlabel("drop-off"); ax[1].set_ylabel("pickup")  # labels
plt.tight_layout(); plt.show()  # draw









Yellow taxis are a Manhattan service: most trips start and end there, with the airports (JFK and LaGuardia, in Queens) the main exceptions. Reading the Parquet file straight into GPU memory and grouping there took about half the Dask time, and the group-by itself only a few hundredths of a second. For tabular aggregations that fit in GPU memory, cuDF is the quickest tool on this machine; Dask DataFrames take over when the table does not fit.

title: Geometry Operations, Clipping, Spatial Joins and Nearest Neighbours on Millions of Features
text:
Summary and exercises

Per-feature operations split over partitions: buffering 1.6 million buildings ran almost eight times faster on 24 threads than in plain GeoPandas, simplifying four times; cheap operations such as centroids gained little.
Area, length and bounds also run as CuPy kernels; the GPU matched the CPU to rounding but was about forty times slower, because packing the geometries dominates. These GPU versions are opt-in.
Spatial joins filter with bounding boxes and refine exactly. Partition pruning sent each Hilbert-ordered partition only the counties near it, and the result equalled geopandas.sjoin; it halved the time of the polygon join, but plain GeoPandas won the cheap point-in-polygon join.
The GPU point-in-polygon join and the GPU k-nearest-neighbour search gave the same answers as the CPU. Brute-force GPU knn was far slower than the KD-tree for large target sets.
38 million taxi trips were grouped by zone with Dask and with cuDF; cuDF took about half the time, almost all of it reading the file.

Exercises

Repeat the county join with npartitions=6, 24 and 96. How does the time change, and why?
Find the nearest hospital for each Wichita building with k=3, and the share of buildings more than 5 km from any hospital.
Buffer each school by 800 m and count the buildings within walking distance with pdist.vector.sjoin(..., predicate="dwithin", distance=800) on the school points instead. Are the two approaches equivalent?
Group the taxi trips by hour of day and pickup borough with cuDF, and plot the daily cycle.

title: Reading and Writing Big Spatial Data in Parallel
text:
Overview

Raster layouts









Format
Layout
Good for
Watch out for




GeoTIFF, striped
rows stored one after another
reading whole rows or the whole file
a small window still reads full rows


GeoTIFF, tiled
square blocks (here 128 x 128) stored independently
windows, parallel reads of blocks
chunks should be multiples of the block size


Cloud-Optimized GeoTIFF (COG)
tiled, plus internal overviews, with the header first
HTTP range requests from object storage, quick previews
written once; updating is awkward


Zarr
one compressed file (object) per chunk, plus JSON metadata
parallel reads and writes, cloud storage, n-dimensional cubes
many small objects if chunks are tiny



A Dask chunk that covers parts of several file blocks forces each task to read and decode blocks that other tasks also read. Chunks aligned to the storage blocks (equal to them or a whole multiple) avoid the duplicate work.


Vector layouts








Format
Parallel read
Spatial filter without reading everything




Shapefile, GeoPackage, FlatGeobuf (OGR)
by row ranges (each worker skips to its rows)
spatial index inside the file (GeoPackage, FlatGeobuf)


GeoParquet
one task per file or row group
per-file and per-row-group bounding box statistics (the bbox covering column, GeoParquet 1.1)


Partitioned GeoParquet
one task per file, files written in parallel
whole files skipped when their bounding box misses the query



Columnar storage also lets a reader take only the columns it needs. And when rows are written in Hilbert order, each file covers a compact area, so a bounding-box query touches few files.


STAC
A SpatioTemporal Asset Catalog lists satellite scenes and the URLs of their COG bands. A lazy reader (here odc-stac) turns a search result into an xarray cube whose chunks are read only when computed, directly from object storage.

title: Reading and Writing Big Spatial Data in Parallel
text:
Lazy rasters and block-aligned chunks
The Great Plains GeoTIFFs store 128 x 128 pixel blocks. pdist.read_raster with chunks="auto" asks pdist.plan_chunks for about 128 MB chunks; explicit chunks of 2048 are a multiple of the block, and 2000 are not.


Code
src = dd.GP_RASTERS / "elev.tif"  # the DEM
auto = pdist.read_raster(src)  # chunks="auto"
print("auto chunks:", auto.data.chunksize, "|", auto.data.npartitions, "chunks | lazy:", pdist.is_lazy(auto))  # plan
rows = []  # timings
cases = [("DEM, uncompressed, 128 x 128 blocks", src, None, [((2048, 2048), True), ((2000, 2000), False)]),  # file, window, chunkings
         ("CDL, PackBits, 512 x 576 blocks", dd.CDL, (slice(128000, 160768), slice(144000, 180864)),
          [((4096, 4608), True), ((4000, 4500), False)])]
for name, path, window, chunkings in cases:  # both files
    for ch, aligned in chunkings:  # aligned first, then misaligned
        r = pdist.read_raster(path, masked=window is None, chunks={"y": ch[0], "x": ch[1]})  # lazy raster
        r = r if window is None else r[window]  # a 33,000 x 37,000 pixel window of the CDL
        float(r.mean())  # warm the page cache
        t = time.perf_counter(); float(r.mean()); sec = time.perf_counter() - t  # read and reduce
        rows.append({"file": name, "chunks": f"{ch[0]} x {ch[1]}", "aligned": aligned,  # description
                     "tasks": r.data.npartitions, "seconds": round(sec, 2)})  # time
pd.DataFrame(rows)  # table

Alignment made no measurable difference here, for either file (in repeated runs the CDL times varied by up to a fifth in both directions). With misaligned chunks the blocks on chunk edges are read by two tasks, but GDAL keeps recently decoded blocks in its block cache, which all threads of this process share, so the second read is mostly a memory copy. The penalty appears where that cache does not help: with several worker processes (each has its own cache, and neighbouring chunks often go to different workers), and with COGs on object storage, where every misaligned edge block is an extra HTTP range request. Aligning chunks to blocks costs nothing, so it remains the safe default.

A window of the 152 billion pixel CDL

title: Reading and Writing Big Spatial Data in Parallel
text:
GeoTIFF, COG and Zarr compared
The DEM is rewritten four ways: a striped GeoTIFF (gdal_translate -co TILED=NO), a tiled DEFLATE GeoTIFF (format="gtiff"), a COG with overviews (format="cog") and a Zstandard compressed Zarr store (format="zarr"). Then each is read whole, and 200 random 256 x 256 windows are read from each.


Code
dem = pdist.read_raster(src, chunks={"y": 2048, "x": 2048})  # lazy DEM
paths = {"GeoTIFF tiled, uncompressed (original)": src}  # name -> path
paths["GeoTIFF striped"] = IO / "elev_striped.tif"  # rows, no tiles
subprocess.run(["gdal_translate", "-q", "-co", "TILED=NO", str(src), str(paths["GeoTIFF striped"])], check=True)  # write it
w = {}  # write times
with dd.timer("write tiled DEFLATE GeoTIFF", w):  # chunk by chunk
    paths["GeoTIFF tiled, DEFLATE"] = Path(pdist.write_raster(dem, IO / "elev_deflate.tif", format="gtiff"))  # write
with dd.timer("write COG", w):  # tiled, then converted with overviews
    paths["COG, DEFLATE"] = Path(pdist.write_raster(dem, IO / "elev_cog.tif", format="cog"))  # write
with dd.timer("write Zarr", w):  # chunks written in parallel
    paths["Zarr, Zstandard"] = Path(pdist.write_raster(dem.rename("elev"), IO / "elev.zarr"))  # write


write tiled DEFLATE GeoTIFF: 14.11 s
write COG: 17.92 s
write Zarr: 1.03 s




Code
import rasterio  # direct windowed reads of GeoTIFFs
import zarr  # direct reads of Zarr chunks
from rasterio.windows import Window  # a rectangle of rows and columns

rng = np.random.default_rng(0)  # random windows
wins = [(int(r), int(c)) for r, c in zip(rng.integers(0, dem.shape[0] - 256, 200), rng.integers(0, dem.shape[1] - 256, 200))]  # corners


def open_any(p):  # lazy DataArray for any of the formats
    if p.suffix == ".zarr":  # Zarr store
        return pdist.read_zarr(p)["elev"]  # its variable
    return pdist.read_raster(p, chunks={"y": 2048, "x": 2048})  # GeoTIFF or COG


def read_windows(p):  # 200 windows read straight from the file, without Dask
    if p.suffix == ".zarr":  # Zarr: slicing reads only the chunks that overlap
        arr = zarr.open(str(p), mode="r")["elev"]  # the array
        for r, c in wins:  # each window
            arr[r:r + 256, c:c + 256]  # read it
    else:  # GeoTIFF or COG through GDAL
        with rasterio.open(p) as f:  # one open file handle
            for r, c in wins:  # each window
                f.read(1, window=Window(c, r, 256, 256))  # read it


rows = []  # one row per format
for name, p in paths.items():  # each format

Compression shrank the DEM about eightfold (half the pixels are NaN and elevations vary smoothly), yet whole-file reads were no slower, because 24 threads decompress in parallel. Small windows tell the formats apart. The original tiled GeoTIFF read a 256 x 256 window in about a tenth of a millisecond, touching only the few 128 x 128 blocks under it. The striped copy took about six times longer, because every window reads 256 complete rows of 15,245 pixels. The compressed tiled files pay for decompressing their blocks (the COG’s larger 512 x 512 blocks cost more per window). The Zarr store was slowest by far for windows: its chunks are 2048 x 2048, so every small window decompresses a whole 16 MB chunk. The writes differ too: GeoTIFF and COG were written chunk by chunk under a lock, Zarr’s independent chunk files in parallel. Zarr suits the intermediate results of a Dask pipeline (use chunks near the size of the windows you will read); COG is the format to publish, since any HTTP client can read its windows and overviews.
