title: Reading and Writing Big Spatial Data in Parallel
text:
Partitioned GeoParquet
The Kansas buildings were written by pdist.write_vector as 24 Hilbert-sorted GeoParquet files, each with a bbox covering column. pdist.read_vector reads a folder with one task per file; with bbox= each file’s statistics decide whether it is opened at all.


Code
files = sorted(dd.BUILDINGS.glob("*.parquet"))  # the partition files
print(len(files), "files,", f"{folder_gb(dd.BUILDINGS):.2f} GB")  # dataset size
t = {}  # timings
with dd.timer("read all 24 files in parallel", t):  # one task per file
    bld = pdist.read_vector(dd.BUILDINGS)  # GeoDataFrame
with dask.config.set(scheduler="synchronous"):  # one file at a time
    with dd.timer("read all 24 files one after another", t):  # for comparison
        pdist.read_vector(dd.BUILDINGS)  # same result
with dd.timer("read only buildings in a Wichita bounding box", t):  # filtered read
    wich = pdist.read_vector(dd.BUILDINGS, bbox=bbox)  # row groups outside the box are skipped
print(f"{len(bld):,} buildings in all; {len(wich):,} in the Wichita box")  # sizes


24 files, 0.19 GB
read all 24 files in parallel: 2.28 s
read all 24 files one after another: 2.07 s
read only buildings in a Wichita bounding box: 0.88 s
1,605,334 buildings in all; 159,731 in the Wichita box


Reading the 24 files on 24 threads was no faster than reading them one after another. Most of the time goes into turning the stored WKB bytes into Shapely geometry objects, and that step holds the GIL, so the threads take turns. (Worker processes would decode in parallel, but then pay to send 1.6 million geometries back to this process.) What does help is reading less: the bounding-box read decoded only the buildings near Wichita and was faster. To see why the Hilbert order matters, the next cell writes the same buildings in two ways (Hilbert-sorted and in random order) and repeats the bounding-box query on both.


Code
shuffled = bld.sample(frac=1, random_state=0)  # rows in random order
pdist.write_vector(bld, IO / "bld_hilbert", npartitions=48)  # 48 Hilbert-sorted files
pdist.write_vector(shuffled, IO / "bld_random", npartitions=48, spatial=False)  # 48 files in random order
import pyarrow.parquet as pq  # Parquet metadata
for name in ["bld_hilbert", "bld_random"]:  # both layouts
    fs = sorted((IO / name).glob("*.parquet"))  # its files
    hit = 0  # files whose bbox statistics overlap the query box
    for f in fs:  # each file
        st = pq.ParquetFile(f).metadata.row_group(0)  # first row group statistics
        cols = {st.column(i).path_in_schema: st.column(i).statistics for i in range(st.num_columns)}  # by column
        x0, y0 = cols["bbox.xmin"].min, cols["bbox.ymin"].min  # lower left of the file
        x1, y1 = cols["bbox.xmax"].max, cols["bbox.ymax"].max  # upper right
        hit += not (x1 < bbox[0] or x0 > bbox[2] or y1 < bbox[1] or y0 > bbox[3])  # overlaps the query?
    t0 = time.perf_counter(); n = len(pdist.read_vector(IO / name, bbox=bbox)); s = time.perf_counter() - t0  # the query
    print(f"{name:12s} files read for the Wichita box: {hit:2d} of {len(fs)} | {n:,} buildings in {s:.2f} s")  # result


bld_hilbert  files read for the Wichita box: 10 of 48 | 159,731 buildings in 1.74 s
bld_random   files read for the Wichita box: 48 of 48 | 159,731 buildings in 1.64 s


Both layouts return the same buildings. In random order every file spans the whole state, so all 48 files must be opened and filtered; Hilbert-sorted, only 10 files overlap Wichita. Locally both queries took the same time, because the files sit in the page cache and decoding the 160,000 matching geometries dominates. On object storage (S3, Azure Blob) every file is a separate download, and reading 10 files instead of 48 is what makes a query fast.

title: Reading and Writing Big Spatial Data in Parallel
text:
Summary and exercises

Lazy readers open the header only; a window of the 152 billion pixel CDL was read in a fraction of a second because only its blocks were decoded.
Chunks should be multiples of the file’s blocks. Here GDAL’s block cache hid the cost of misaligned chunks; with worker processes or object storage it does not.
The 15 Great Plains rasters lie on four slightly different grids; layers must be snapped to one grid before they are combined.
Striped GeoTIFFs suit whole-file reads, tiled GeoTIFFs and COGs suit windows, and Zarr suits parallel writes and reads of intermediate results and multi-layer cubes.
pdist.read_stac builds a lazy cube from catalogue metadata and downloads only what a computation needs.
Partitioned, Hilbert-sorted GeoParquet with a bbox column lets bounding-box queries skip most files. Decoding geometries holds the GIL, so reading fewer of them beats reading them on more threads. GeoParquet was the smallest format and the fastest to read.
A Parquet table of 38 million rows is a lazy Dask DataFrame with one partition per row group.

Exercises

Write the DEM to Zarr with 512, 2048 and 8192 pixel chunks. How do the number of files, the write time and the time to read 200 random windows change?
Read the CDL window around Wichita with chunks={"y": 576, "x": 512} (the file’s blocks) and with {"y": 600, "x": 600}. Compare the times.
Repeat the Sentinel-2 search for winter 2024-25 and map the difference in median NDVI.
Write the buildings with partition_on set to a column of your choice (for example a size class from pdist.vector.area) and inspect the folder structure that results.

title: Why Spatial Data Outgrow One Core, and What to Do About It
text: Banner

title: Why Spatial Data Outgrow One Core, and What to Do About It
text:
Overview

Two reasons to leave one core

Too large. The data do not fit in memory (the 10 m CDL is 152 GB as bytes), or they fit but leave no room for the intermediate arrays an analysis creates. A slope calculation on a 1 GB DEM allocates several more gigabytes of temporaries.
Too slow. The data fit, but one core takes too long, or the analysis must be repeated many times (999 permutations of a spatial statistic, a model fitted for every fold of a cross-validation, a prediction for every pixel).



Three ways out, and what each costs








Route
What it gives
What it costs




All cores of one machine
8 to 128 workers that share memory
memory bandwidth is shared too; Python’s GIL blocks pure Python threads


Many machines (a cluster)
memory and cores without a fixed limit
data travel over the network; a scheduler and serialization add overhead


A GPU
thousands of simple cores and very fast memory
data must be copied to the device and back over PCIe; device memory is small (8 to 80 GB)





Embarrassingly parallel and communication-heavy work
Some spatial operations split cleanly: NDVI, a reclassification or a slope calculation needs only each pixel (and for slope, its 8 neighbours), so each piece of the raster can be processed alone. Others need information from far away: flow accumulation depends on every cell upstream, a spatial join must find every polygon that touches every point, and a weights matrix links each observation to its neighbours wherever they fall. The first kind scales almost linearly with workers; the second needs data exchange, and the exchange often limits the speed-up.


Amdahl’s law
If a fraction p of the work can run in parallel and the rest is serial, the speed-up on n workers is
S(n) = 1 / ((1 - p) + p / n)
With p = 0.9 the speed-up can never exceed 10, however many cores are added. In geospatial work the serial part is often reading and decoding files, moving data between host and GPU, or assembling the result. Measuring where the time goes (notebook 11) matters more than adding hardware.


The ideas behind parallel spatial computing








Idea
Meaning
Spatial example




Chunk (raster) or partition (table)
a piece of the data that one task processes
a 2048 x 2048 block of the DEM; 1/24 of the buildings


Halo (overlap, ghost cells)
extra border pixels a chunk borrows from its neighbours
slope needs 1 pixel, a 9 x 9 mean 4 pixels


Shuffle
moving rows between partitions so that matching keys meet
taxi trips regrouped by zone; a join of two tables partitioned differently


Lazy task graph
a recipe of tasks recorded first and run only when a result is asked for
Dask arrays and dask-geopandas frames


Host and device memory
RAM used by the CPU, and separate memory on the GPU
copying a 1 GB DEM to the GPU takes about 0.15 s over PCIe


Spatial ordering
sorting features so that neighbours share a partition
a Hilbert curve through building centroids





Rasters and vectors differ
A raster is a regular grid: any rectangle of rows and columns is a valid chunk, its neighbours are known from its position, and a halo of h pixels makes a moving window exact. Vector features have irregular shapes and sizes and no implied neighbours. A partition of polygons can overlap any other partition, so a spatial join must test pairs of partitions; ordering features along a space-filling curve keeps each partition compact, and a quick test of partition bounding boxes (partition pruning) rules out most pairs before any geometry is compared.

title: Why Spatial Data Outgrow One Core, and What to Do About It
text:
Distributed Spatial Computing with GeoLattice
geolattice.distributed, imported as pdist, gives one API for these routes. Three rules hold for every function:

compute="auto" | "cpu" | "gpu". "auto" uses the GPU when a CUDA device and a GPU implementation exist, otherwise the CPU; asking for "gpu" on a machine without one falls back to the CPU with a single warning, so notebooks run anywhere.
Same type and memory space out as in. NumPy in gives NumPy out, a GeoDataFrame gives a GeoDataFrame, a CuPy array stays on the GPU, and a lazy Dask input stays lazy.
Local threads unless a session is started. Without a cluster, Dask’s threaded scheduler uses every core. pdist.start("local"), pdist.start("cuda"), pdist.start("slurm") and friends move the same code onto a cluster (notebook 01).

Learning objectives

import xarray as xr  # labelled rasters

import geolattice  # GeoLattice
import geolattice.distributed as pdist  # distributed and GPU spatial computing
import dist_data as dd  # chapter helper: paths, cached downloads, timers

section: A raster larger than it looks
text:
A raster larger than it looks
pdist.read_raster opens the DEM lazily: it reads the header, not the pixels, and returns an xarray DataArray backed by a Dask array cut into chunks.


Code
dem = dd.gp_raster("elev")  # lazy DataArray, 2048 x 2048 chunks

print(f"chunks {dem.data.chunksize}, {dem.data.npartitions} chunks, is lazy: {pdist.is_lazy(dem)}")  # how it is cut
print("CRS", dem.rio.crs.to_epsg(), "| resolution", dem.rio.resolution())  # georeferencing

fig, ax = plt.subplots(figsize=(7.5, 7.5))  # one map

Each square is one chunk, the unit of work Dask hands to a worker. About half the pixels lie outside the four states and are NaN, and small no-data holes are scattered inside them. A whole chunk of NaN still costs a read and a task, which is one reason cropped or masked data are cheaper than their rectangle suggests.

title: Why Spatial Data Outgrow One Core, and What to Do About It
text:
Lazy task graphs
Calling a function on a lazy input records tasks instead of computing. The slope below is returned almost instantly, as a recipe of read, overlap and slope tasks per chunk; it runs when .compute() (or plotting, or writing) asks for numbers.


Code
t = time.perf_counter()  # start the clock
s_lazy = pdist.raster.slope(dem, compute="cpu")  # lazy: records tasks, computes nothing
print(f"built in {time.perf_counter() - t:.3f} s | lazy: {pdist.is_lazy(s_lazy)} | "  # nearly free
      f"{len(s_lazy.data.__dask_graph__())} tasks for {s_lazy.data.npartitions} output chunks")  # graph size
layers = s_lazy.data.__dask_graph__().layers  # the high-level graph, one layer per step
print([k.split("-")[0] for k in layers])  # the steps in order


built in 0.005 s | lazy: True | 1631 tasks for 72 output chunks
['concatenate', 'concatenate', 'original', 'open_rasterio', 'getitem', 'rechunk', 'getitem', 'getitem', 'getitem', 'getitem', 'overlap', 'getitem', 'lambda', '_trim']




Code
with dd.timer("slope of the lazy DEM, read from disk and computed on all cores"):  # time the whole chain
    s_all = s_lazy.compute()  # run the graph
print(type(s_all.data).__name__, f"{dd.gb(s_all.nbytes)}, mean slope {float(s_all.mean()):.2f} degrees")  # in memory now


slope of the lazy DEM, read from disk and computed on all cores: 2.35 s
ndarray 1.05 GB, mean slope 4.48 degrees


The graph has a few tasks per chunk: one to read it, a few to share edge pixels with its neighbours (the halo, next section), and one to compute slope. Dask runs them on all cores as soon as their inputs are ready, reading one chunk while computing another.

title: Why Spatial Data Outgrow One Core, and What to Do About It
text:
Chunks need halos
Slope at a pixel uses its 8 neighbours, and a 9 x 9 moving mean uses 80. A chunk processed on its own lacks the neighbours that lie in the next chunk, so its edge pixels come out wrong. The fix is a halo: each chunk borrows h rows and columns from its neighbours, computes, and trims them again. pdist.raster adds the halo every moving-window operation needs. The cell below compares three 9 x 9 means on a 4096 x 4096 window: the whole array at once (the reference), chunks without a halo, and pdist.raster.focal.


Code
win = dem[6000:10096, 6000:10096].compute()  # a 4096 x 4096 window in memory
win = win.fillna(float(win.mean()))  # fill the scattered no-data holes (same input for every method)
ref = ndi.uniform_filter(win.values, 9, mode="nearest")  # whole-array 9 x 9 mean: the reference
naive = da.from_array(win.values, chunks=1024).map_blocks(  # 16 chunks, each filtered alone
    lambda b: ndi.uniform_filter(b, 9, mode="nearest")).compute()  # no halo
halo = pdist.raster.focal(win, "mean", size=9, chunks=(1024, 1024))  # GeoLattice adds a 4 pixel halo
for name, r in [("chunks without a halo", naive), ("pdist.raster.focal", halo.values)]:  # compare both
    bad = np.abs(r - ref) > 1e-3  # pixels that differ from the reference
    print(f"{name:24s} wrong pixels: {bad.sum():7d} ({bad.mean():.2%}), largest error {np.abs(r - ref).max():.2f} m")  # error


chunks without a halo    wrong pixels:  165261 (0.99%), largest error 208.12 m
pdist.raster.focal       wrong pixels:       0 (0.00%), largest error 0.00 m




Code
z = (slice(2048 - 48, 2048 + 48), slice(2048 - 48, 2048 + 48))  # 96 x 96 pixels around a seam crossing
fig, ax = plt.subplots(1, 3, figsize=(15, 4.6))  # three panels
im = ax[0].imshow(np.abs(naive - ref) > 1e-3, cmap="Greys", interpolation="nearest")  # where the no-halo result is wrong
ax[0].set_title("wrong pixels without a halo (whole window)")  # whole window
ax[0].set_xticks(np.arange(0, 4097, 1024)); ax[0].set_yticks(np.arange(0, 4097, 1024))  # chunk seams as ticks
for a, r, t in [(ax[1], naive, "chunks without a halo"), (ax[2], halo.values, "pdist.raster.focal (4 pixel halo)")]:  # zoomed errors
    im = a.imshow(np.abs(r - ref)[z], cmap="magma", vmin=0, vmax=10, interpolation="nearest",  # error in metres
                  extent=[2000, 2096, 2096, 2000])  # pixel coordinates
    a.set_title(f"|{t} - whole array| (m)", fontsize=10); plt.colorbar(im, ax=a, shrink=0.8)  # labels
plt.tight_layout(); plt.show()  # draw









Without a halo the errors form a grid of lines along the chunk seams wherever the terrain is not flat, four pixels wide on each side of every seam (the zoom shows the crossing at pixel 2048, 2048); with the halo the chunked result equals the whole-array result everywhere, edges included. The halo is not free: it adds reads and data copies proportional to the chunk perimeter, so the library keeps chunks at least eight halo widths wide (pdist.plan_chunks).

title: Why Spatial Data Outgrow One Core, and What to Do About It
text:
Slope four ways
Now the same slope on the whole in-memory DEM, computed four ways:

one core: Dask’s synchronous scheduler runs the chunks one after another;
all cores: the default threaded scheduler (NumPy and SciPy release the GIL, so threads run in parallel);
GPU from host: compute="gpu" copies each chunk to the GPU, computes there and copies the result back, because a host input must give a host output;
GPU resident: the DEM is moved to the GPU once with pdist.to_gpu, and the result stays there.



Code
d = dem.compute()  # the DEM in host memory (1 GB)
d_gpu = pdist.to_gpu(d) if caps["gpus"] else None  # a copy in GPU memory, if there is a GPU


def sync():  # wait until the GPU has finished, so timings are real
    if caps["gpus"]:  # only with a GPU
        import cupy as cp  # GPU arrays
        cp.cuda.Device().synchronize()  # block until queued kernels finish


def best_of(fn, n=3):  # best wall time of n runs after one warm-up run
    fn(); sync()  # warm-up: compile kernels, fill caches
    times = []  # timings
    for _ in range(n):  # timed runs
        t = time.perf_counter(); fn(); sync(); times.append(time.perf_counter() - t)  # one run
    return min(times)  # best run


runs = {}  # seconds per way
with dask.config.set(scheduler="synchronous"):  # one task at a time
    runs["one core"] = best_of(lambda: pdist.raster.slope(d, compute="cpu"))  # NumPy, one core
runs[f"all {os.cpu_count()} cores"] = best_of(lambda: pdist.raster.slope(d, compute="cpu"))  # NumPy, threads
if caps["gpus"]:  # GPU timings only where a GPU exists
    runs["GPU from host"] = best_of(lambda: pdist.raster.slope(d, compute="gpu"))  # copies in and out
    runs["GPU resident"] = best_of(lambda: pdist.raster.slope(d_gpu, compute="gpu"))  # stays on the device
t4 = pd.Series(runs, name="seconds").to_frame()  # table
t4["speed-up vs one core"] = t4.seconds.iloc[0] / t4.seconds  # relative speed
t4["Mpixels per s"] = d.size / 1e6 / t4.seconds  # throughput
t4.round(2)  # show

All cores were only about twice as fast as one core here: slope does little arithmetic per byte, so the cores spend most of their time waiting for memory, and every core shares the same memory bus. The GPU has its own, much faster memory, and with the DEM already on the device it was about an order of magnitude faster than all CPU cores. Copying a gigabyte in and a gigabyte back costs more than the computation, so “GPU from host” lands between the two. The lesson recurs in every notebook: keep data on the GPU across several operations, and move it only at the start and the end.
pdist.check_equivalence runs a function on each target and compares the results; the CPU and GPU slopes agree to float32 rounding.


Code
rep = pdist.check_equivalence(pdist.raster.slope, d, rtol=1e-4, atol=1e-3)  # CPU vs GPU on the full DEM
print("equivalent:", rep.ok, "| largest difference", f"{rep.max_abs:.2e} degrees")  # verdict
print(*rep.details, sep="\n")  # what was compared

title: Why Spatial Data Outgrow One Core, and What to Do About It
text:
Where the GPU time goes
Splitting the “GPU from host” run into its three parts shows why transfers matter.


Code
if caps["gpus"]:  # needs a GPU
    import cupy as cp  # GPU arrays
    parts = {}  # seconds per step
    t = time.perf_counter(); g = cp.asarray(d.values); sync(); parts["copy to GPU"] = time.perf_counter() - t  # host to device
    gda = d.copy(data=g)  # the same DataArray around GPU data
    pdist.raster.slope(gda, compute="gpu"); sync()  # warm-up
    t = time.perf_counter(); r = pdist.raster.slope(gda, compute="gpu"); sync(); parts["slope on GPU"] = time.perf_counter() - t  # compute
    t = time.perf_counter(); h = r.data.get(); parts["copy to host"] = time.perf_counter() - t  # device to host
    parts = pd.Series(parts, name="seconds")  # table
    print(parts.round(3).to_string()); print(f"PCIe throughput about {d.nbytes / parts['copy to GPU'] / 1e9:.1f} GB/s")  # transfer speed
    del g, gda, r, h  # free GPU memory


copy to GPU     0.137
slope on GPU    0.173
copy to host    0.166
PCIe throughput about 7.7 GB/s

title: Why Spatial Data Outgrow One Core, and What to Do About It
text:
Amdahl’s law in practice
The threaded run can be repeated with 1, 2, 4, … workers. Fitting Amdahl’s law to the measured speed-ups estimates the parallel fraction p of this workload on this machine.


Code
from scipy.optimize import curve_fit  # least-squares fit

workers = [1, 2, 4, 8, 12, 16, os.cpu_count()]  # thread counts to try
secs = []  # best time per count
for n in workers:  # each thread count
    with dask.config.set(scheduler="threads", num_workers=n):  # n threads
        secs.append(best_of(lambda: pdist.raster.slope(d, compute="cpu", chunks=(1024, 1024)), n=2))  # time it
speed = secs[0] / np.array(secs)  # measured speed-up
amdahl = lambda n, p: 1 / ((1 - p) + p / n)  # the law
p_fit, _ = curve_fit(amdahl, np.array(workers, float), speed, p0=[0.9], bounds=(0, 1))  # fitted parallel fraction
print("seconds:", dict(zip(workers, np.round(secs, 2))), f"| fitted p = {p_fit[0]:.2f}")  # results


seconds: {1: np.float64(3.77), 2: np.float64(2.27), 4: np.float64(1.62), 8: np.float64(1.7), 12: np.float64(1.85), 16: np.float64(1.98), 24: np.float64(1.95)} | fitted p = 0.57




Code
fig, ax = plt.subplots(figsize=(7, 4.2))  # one panel
nn = np.linspace(1, max(workers), 100)  # smooth curve
ax.plot(workers, speed, "o-", label="measured slope (threads)")  # data
ax.plot(nn, amdahl(nn, p_fit[0]), "--", label=f"Amdahl, p = {p_fit[0]:.2f}")  # fitted law
ax.plot(nn, nn, ":", color="grey", label="perfect scaling")  # ideal
ax.set_ylim(0, max(4, speed.max() * 1.5)); ax.set_xlabel("threads"); ax.set_ylabel("speed-up")  # axes
ax.legend(); ax.set_title("Strong scaling of slope on 262 million pixels"); plt.tight_layout(); plt.show()  # draw









The curve peaks at about four threads and then falls slightly. Amdahl’s law fits it with a parallel fraction near 0.6, as if 40 % of the work were serial. Little of slope is really serial; the limit is memory bandwidth. Slope does a few additions per pixel, so a handful of cores already saturate the memory bus, and more threads only add contention. A compute-heavy operation (a 9 x 9 median, a model prediction) scales much better, as notebooks 03 and 09 show. Either way, measure before buying hardware.

title: Why Spatial Data Outgrow One Core, and What to Do About It
text:
Vector partitions need spatial order
For vectors the unit of work is a partition: a slice of the rows. pdist.spatial_partition cuts a GeoDataFrame into partitions; with method="none" the rows keep their current order, with method="hilbert" they are first sorted along a Hilbert curve, which visits nearby places consecutively. pdist.partition_bounds returns each partition’s bounding box. The building cache was written Hilbert-sorted already (pdist.write_vector does that by default), so the cell below draws a random sample, whose rows are in arbitrary order, as rows sorted by an attribute or an ID would be.


Code
bld = dd.kansas_buildings()  # 1.6 million building polygons (downloads once)
pts = bld.set_geometry(bld.geometry.representative_point()).to_crs(5070).sample(200_000, random_state=0)  # a sample of points inside them
print(f"{len(bld):,} buildings; using {len(pts):,} sample points")  # sizes
parts = {m: pdist.spatial_partition(pts, 24, method=m) for m in ["none", "hilbert"]}  # 24 partitions each way
for m, p in parts.items():  # both methods
    b = pdist.partition_bounds(p)  # (24, 4) bounding boxes
    area = ((b[:, 2] - b[:, 0]) * (b[:, 3] - b[:, 1])).sum() / 1e6  # summed bounding-box area, km2
    print(f"{m:8s} sum of partition bounding boxes {area:12,.0f} km2 ({area / 213_100:.1f} x the area of Kansas)")  # compactness


1,605,334 buildings; using 200,000 sample points
none     sum of partition bounding boxes    5,380,857 km2 (25.3 x the area of Kansas)
hilbert  sum of partition bounding boxes      300,673 km2 (1.4 x the area of Kansas)




Code
from matplotlib.patches import Rectangle  # boxes

fig, axs = plt.subplots(1, 2, figsize=(14, 4.6))  # two maps
cmap = plt.get_cmap("tab20", 24)  # one colour per partition
for ax, (m, p) in zip(axs, parts.items()):  # both methods
    for i, part in enumerate(p):  # each partition
        ax.scatter(part.geometry.x, part.geometry.y, s=0.2, color=cmap(i))  # its points
        x0, y0, x1, y1 = part.total_bounds  # its bounding box
        ax.add_patch(Rectangle((x0, y0), x1 - x0, y1 - y0, fill=False, lw=0.6, color=cmap(i)))  # draw it
    ax.set_title(f"method='{m}': 24 partitions and their bounding boxes"); ax.set_aspect("equal"); ax.set_axis_off()  # title
plt.tight_layout(); plt.show()  # draw









In arbitrary order every partition holds points from the whole state, so all 24 bounding boxes cover Kansas and each overlaps all the others. After Hilbert sorting each partition covers a compact patch, and the summed bounding-box area falls from 25 times to 1.4 times the area of the state. That is what makes a partitioned spatial join fast (notebook 04): a partition of points needs only the polygons whose boxes touch its own box.

title: Why Spatial Data Outgrow One Core, and What to Do About It
text:
Summary and exercises

Data outgrow one core when they do not fit in memory or one core is too slow; the routes out are all cores, a cluster and a GPU, each with its own costs (shared memory bandwidth, network and serialization, PCIe transfers and small device memory).
Rasters split into chunks; moving windows need a halo, without which errors line every chunk seam. Vector partitions need spatial ordering so that bounding boxes stay compact.
Lazy task graphs record work and run it on demand; building the slope graph of 72 chunks took a fraction of a millisecond per task.
On this machine slope of 262 million pixels took a few seconds on one core, about half that on all cores, and a fraction of a second on the GPU when the data stayed there. Copies to and from the GPU cost more than the computation.
pdist.capabilities, pdist.list_ops, pdist.explain and pdist.check_equivalence show what will run where and confirm that CPU and GPU agree.

Exercises

Repeat the slope timing with chunks=(512, 512) and chunks=(8192, 8192). Which is fastest on all cores, and why are both extremes slower?
Time pdist.raster.focal(d, "median", size=9) on all cores and on the GPU. Is the speed-up larger or smaller than for slope? Fit Amdahl’s law to its thread scaling.
Use the halo experiment with pdist.raster.tpi(win, window=21). How wide is the band of wrong pixels without a halo?
Partition the building sample into 6, 24 and 96 partitions with both methods and plot the summed bounding-box area against the number of partitions.

title: GeoLattice: Distributed Spatial Computing
text:
Spatial data outgrow one core quickly. A 90 m raster of the Great Plains has 262 million pixels per layer, a national crop map at 10 m has 152 billion, and a year of taxi trips has tens of millions of rows. Distributed computing splits that work into chunks and partitions, runs them on every core, on a cluster or on a GPU, and handles what makes spatial data different: moving windows that need a halo of neighbouring cells, and joins that only work if nearby features share a partition.
These 13 notebooks are chapter 08 of the GeoLattice tutorials. They start with sessions, clusters and parallel I/O, scale up raster, vector, statistics, network, hydrology and machine learning work, run spatial SQL on Spark with Apache Sedona, measure and tune the result, and finish with soil carbon and cropland for every Great Plains county, using geolattice.distributed.

title: GeoLattice: Distributed Spatial Computing
text:
GeoLattice
GeoLattice is a Python library for geospatial analysis that brings vector and raster processing, spatial analysis, spatial statistics, geostatistics, spatial databases, web and cloud GIS and remote sensing together under one import. It is built on GDAL, NumPy, pandas, GeoPandas, Shapely and xarray, so its functions take and return objects these libraries already use: GeoDataFrames, xarray DataArrays, NumPy arrays and GDAL-readable files.



Package
geolattice


Repository
github.com/zia207/GeoLattice


Python
3.10 or newer


License
MIT


Author
Zia Ahmed, Upatta Analytics



GDAL and PROJ must be installed first, with Python GDAL bindings that match the GDAL library (conda or your system package manager). Then install the distributed option; GPUs, HPC schedulers and Spark each have their own extra:
python3 -m pip install "geolattice[distributed]"
python3 -m pip install "geolattice[distributed-gpu]"     # CuPy and dask-cuda (cuDF, cuML, cuGraph from the RAPIDS index)
python3 -m pip install "geolattice[distributed-hpc]"     # SLURM, PBS and Kubernetes clusters
python3 -m pip install "geolattice[distributed-spark]"   # Apache Sedona, needs Java 17 or newer

import geopandas as gpd
import geolattice.distributed as pdist

    print(pdist.capabilities())                                    # engines and GPUs on this machine
    with pdist.start("local", n_workers=2):                        # a local Dask cluster
        dem = pdist.read_raster("Data/03_spatial_analysis/MCSM_data/dem_texas_utm.tif")  # lazy, chunked
        slope = pdist.raster.slope(dem, compute="auto")            # halo-aware, CPU or GPU
        pdist.write_raster(slope, "slope.zarr")                    # Zarr; format="cog" for a COG
        print(pdist.explain("raster.slope", compute="auto"))       # which implementation, and why

        counties = gpd.read_file("Data/00_shared/vector_data/USA/US_COUNTY.shp")
        points = counties.representative_point().to_frame("geometry")
        hits = pdist.vector.sjoin(points, counties, predicate="within")  # partition-pruned join

title: From a Laptop to a Cluster: Sessions, Workers and the Dashboard
text:
Overview

The parts of a Dask cluster







Part
Role




Client
your Python session; builds task graphs and submits them


Scheduler
one process that tracks every task and decides which worker runs it, preferring the worker that already holds its inputs


Workers
processes that run tasks with a pool of threads, hold results in memory and send them to each other when needed


Nanny
a small process per worker that restarts it if it dies or exceeds its memory limit



With no cluster, Dask’s threaded scheduler runs the graph with a thread pool inside your own process: no scheduler, no copies, no network, but also no isolation and only one machine.


Threads or processes
Python’s global interpreter lock (GIL) lets only one thread run Python bytecode at a time. Compiled libraries (NumPy, SciPy, GDAL, Shapely 2, CuPy) release it during their inner loops, so threads run them in parallel. Code that loops in Python (a for loop over features, a function applied row by row) does not, and only separate processes run it in parallel. Processes pay for that: data crossing between them are serialized and copied.







Work
Best choice




NumPy, SciPy, GDAL and rasterio, Shapely 2 vectorized operations
threads (or few processes with many threads)


pure Python loops, GeoPandas apply, many small objects
processes with one or two threads each


GPU work
one worker process per GPU (dask-cuda)


more memory or cores than one machine has
a cluster on several machines (HPC or cloud)





Memory limits and spilling
Each worker has a memory limit. Above 60 % of it the worker writes (spills) results to disk, above 80 % it pauses, and at 95 % the nanny restarts it. Spilling keeps large jobs alive but slow; a job that spills constantly needs smaller chunks, more workers or persist used more carefully.


Chunk size
Every chunk is at least one task, and every task costs the scheduler roughly a millisecond of overhead plus a little memory. Tiny chunks drown the work in overhead; huge chunks leave cores idle and risk running out of memory. Dask’s guidance is chunks of about 100 MB; for moving windows the chunk must also be much wider than the halo.

title: From a Laptop to a Cluster: Sessions, Workers and the Dashboard
section: The default: threads in this process
text:
The default: threads in this process
Without a session, pdist.status() reports Dask’s threaded scheduler: one “worker” (this process) with one thread per core.
This machine has a GPU, so compute="auto" would put the slope chunks on it. The comparisons of threads, processes and chunk sizes below pass compute="cpu" so that they measure the CPU; the GPU worker gets its own section.


Code
print(pdist.status())  # no session yet
dem = dd.gp_raster("elev")  # lazy DEM, 2048 x 2048 chunks
with dd.timer("mean slope, threaded scheduler"):  # time it
    print(f"mean slope {float(pdist.raster.slope(dem, compute='cpu').mean()):.3f} degrees")  # read, slope, reduce


{'kind': 'threads', 'workers': 1, 'threads': 24, 'dashboard': None}

mean slope, threaded scheduler: 2.30 s

title: From a Laptop to a Cluster: Sessions, Workers and the Dashboard
text:
A local cluster
pdist.start("local") starts a scheduler and worker processes on this machine. Here 4 workers with 6 threads each use the 24 cores, each limited to 24 GB of memory.


Code
s = pdist.start("local", n_workers=4, threads_per_worker=6, memory_limit="24GB")  # start the cluster
print(s)  # session and dashboard
st = s.status()  # workers, threads, memory
print({k: (dd.gb(v) if k == "memory_limit" else v) for k, v in st.items()})  # readable
print("active session:", pdist.get_session() is s)  # every lazy operation now runs here


<Session kind='local' dashboard='http://127.0.0.1:8787/status'>
{'kind': 'local', 'workers': 4, 'threads': 24, 'memory_limit': '96.00 GB', 'dashboard': 'http://127.0.0.1:8787/status'}
active session: True




Code
with dd.timer("mean slope, local cluster (4 processes x 6 threads)"):  # same computation on the cluster
    print(f"mean slope {float(pdist.raster.slope(dem, compute='cpu').mean()):.3f} degrees")  # identical result


mean slope 4.484 degrees
mean slope, local cluster (4 processes x 6 threads): 3.90 s


The result is identical, but the cluster was slower than plain threads. This workload is NumPy, which already ran in parallel on threads inside one process; on the cluster, the halo strips that neighbouring chunks exchange travel between processes, and every task goes through the scheduler. For NumPy and GDAL work on one machine the threaded scheduler is usually the fastest choice; the cluster pays off with code that holds the GIL (next section), with several machines, and when isolation and the dashboard matter. The dashboard link above opens a live view of the task stream, worker memory and progress bars; on a remote machine forward port 8787 with ssh -L 8787:localhost:8787 host.

title: From a Laptop to a Cluster: Sessions, Workers and the Dashboard
text:
Threads or processes
The difference appears with pure Python code. The function below computes building areas with a Python loop over the vertices (the shoelace formula), as hand-written per-feature code often does. It runs on 24 partitions of 400,000 buildings three ways: the threaded scheduler, the local cluster’s processes, and, for comparison, the vectorized pdist.vector.area (Shapely releases the GIL).


Code
def shoelace_area(part):  # pure Python: one loop per building, one per vertex
    out = []  # areas
    for g in part.geometry:  # each polygon
        xy = list(g.exterior.coords)  # its vertices as Python tuples
        a = 0.0  # running sum
        for (x0, y0), (x1, y1) in zip(xy[:-1], xy[1:]):  # each edge
            a += x0 * y1 - x1 * y0  # shoelace term
        out.append(abs(a) / 2)  # polygon area
    return pd.Series(out, index=part.index)  # aligned to the input


bld = dd.kansas_buildings().iloc[:400_000].to_crs(5070)  # 400,000 buildings in metres
parts = pdist.spatial_partition(bld, 24, method="none")  # 24 slices of rows
tasks = [dask.delayed(shoelace_area)(p) for p in parts]  # one task per slice
res = {}  # seconds per way
with dask.config.set(scheduler="threads"):  # ignore the cluster: threads in this process
    with dd.timer("pure Python, 24 threads (GIL)", res):  # time it
        a_thr = pd.concat(dask.compute(*tasks))  # run
with dd.timer("pure Python, 4 processes x 6 threads", res):  # the cluster
    a_proc = pd.concat(dask.compute(*tasks))  # run on workers


pure Python, 24 threads (GIL): 3.81 s
pure Python, 4 processes x 6 threads: 2.32 s




Code
s.close()  # close the 4 x 6 cluster
s = pdist.start("local", n_workers=24, threads_per_worker=1, memory_limit="4GB")  # one thread per process
s.client.wait_for_workers(24)  # wait until all have started
with dd.timer("pure Python, 24 processes x 1 thread", res):  # one Python interpreter per core
    a_p24 = pd.concat(dask.compute(*tasks))  # run
with dask.config.set(scheduler="threads"):  # back to threads for the vectorized version
    with dd.timer("Shapely vectorized, 24 threads", res):  # compiled code releases the GIL
        a_vec = pdist.vector.area(bld)  # GEOS area
print("largest difference between methods:", float((a_p24 - a_vec).abs().max()), "m2")  # same answer
pd.Series(res, name="seconds").round(2).to_frame()  # table


pure Python, 24 processes x 1 thread: 2.02 s
Shapely vectorized, 24 threads: 0.08 s
largest difference between methods: 0.0003866876122629037 m2









seconds




pure Python, 24 threads (GIL)
3.81


pure Python, 4 processes x 6 threads
2.32


pure Python, 24 processes x 1 thread
2.02


Shapely vectorized, 24 threads
0.08







On threads the Python loop gains little from 24 cores, because the GIL lets one thread run Python at a time. Four processes with six threads each were nearly twice as fast, and 24 single-threaded processes a little faster again, because each process has its own interpreter and its own GIL. The gain is far below 24-fold: every partition of polygons has to be pickled, sent to a worker process and unpickled there, and the areas sent back. The real lesson is in the last row: the vectorized Shapely call, which runs in C and releases the GIL, was about twenty-five times faster than the best of them. Vectorize first; reach for processes only for code that cannot be vectorized.

title: From a Laptop to a Cluster: Sessions, Workers and the Dashboard
text:
Scaling a cluster
scale(n) sets a fixed number of workers; adapt(minimum, maximum) adds workers while tasks are waiting and retires idle ones, which on a shared HPC system releases nodes as soon as they are not needed.


Code
s.scale(8); s.client.wait_for_workers(8); time.sleep(2)  # shrink to 8 workers
print("after scale(8):", s.status()["workers"], "workers")  # check
s.adapt(minimum=2, maximum=12)  # let load decide between 2 and 12
print("adaptive between 2 and 12 workers; now", s.status()["workers"])  # adaptive mode
s.close()  # shut down
print("after close:", pdist.status()["kind"])  # back to threads


after scale(8): 8 workers
adaptive between 2 and 12 workers; now 8
after close: threads

title: From a Laptop to a Cluster: Sessions, Workers and the Dashboard
text:
One worker per GPU
pdist.start("cuda") uses dask-cuda’s LocalCUDACluster: one worker process per visible GPU, each pinned to its device. Arguments such as rmm_pool_size="8GB" give each worker an RMM memory pool, and device_memory_limit makes the worker spill GPU data to host memory before the device fills up. Inside the session, compute="gpu" operations run on the GPU worker.


Code
if caps["gpus"]:  # needs a GPU and dask-cuda
    with pdist.start("cuda") as g:  # one worker per GPU, closed at the end of the block
        print(g, g.status()["workers"], "worker(s), GPU session:", g.is_gpu)  # one worker here
        with dd.timer("mean slope on the GPU worker (read on the worker, slope on its GPU)"):  # time it
            v = float(pdist.raster.slope(dem, compute="gpu").mean())  # chunks become CuPy on the worker
        print(f"mean slope {v:.3f} degrees")  # same answer
else:  # without a GPU
    print("no GPU: pdist.start('auto') would start a CPU cluster instead")  # fallback


<Session kind='cuda' dashboard='http://127.0.0.1:8787/status'> 1 worker(s), GPU session: True
mean slope on the GPU worker (read on the worker, slope on its GPU): 5.61 s
mean slope 4.484 degrees


With one GPU the GPU worker has one thread, so it reads and decodes the GeoTIFF chunks one after another; the CPU sessions read them on 24 threads. That is why the whole chain (read, copy to the GPU, slope, reduce) was several times slower here than on the CPU, even though slope itself is much faster on the GPU (notebook 00). For a GPU pipeline the reading has to keep up: data already in GPU memory, a faster format (notebook 02) or several CPU threads feeding the device. On a machine with several GPUs pdist.start("cuda") starts one worker per device and the chunks are shared between them; here, with one, the same code runs on one.

title: From a Laptop to a Cluster: Sessions, Workers and the Dashboard
text:
HPC and cloud clusters
On an HPC system the workers run inside batch jobs. pdist.start("slurm", ...) creates a dask_jobqueue.SLURMCluster: the scheduler runs where you are (a login node or a small job), and each worker is an sbatch job. Starting the session without n_workers submits nothing, so the job script it would submit can be read on any machine. The scheduler address is replaced by <scheduler> in the printout.


Code
hpc = pdist.start("slurm", cores=24, processes=4, memory="96GB", walltime="02:00:00",  # one job = 4 workers x 6 threads
                  queue="normal", account="my_project",  # partition and allocation
                  job_extra_directives=["--constraint=intel"])  # any extra #SBATCH line
print(re.sub(r"tcp://\S+", "tcp://<scheduler>", hpc.cluster.job_script()))  # the script sbatch would receive
print("workers now:", hpc.status()["workers"], "(nothing submitted)")  # no job until scale()
hpc.close()  # stop the local scheduler


#!/usr/bin/env bash

#SBATCH -J dask-worker
#SBATCH -p normal
#SBATCH -A my_project
#SBATCH -n 1
#SBATCH --cpus-per-task=24
#SBATCH --mem=90G
#SBATCH -t 02:00:00
#SBATCH --constraint=intel

/home/zia207/.pyenv/versions/3.11.16/bin/python3 -m distributed.cli.dask_worker tcp://<scheduler> --name dummy-name --nthreads 6 --memory-limit 22.35GiB --nworkers 4 --nanny --death-timeout 60

workers now: 0 (nothing submitted)


On a real cluster, hpc.scale(jobs=10) (or pdist.start("slurm", n_workers=10, ...)) would submit ten such jobs and hpc.adapt(maximum_jobs=50) would let the load decide. kind="pbs" writes the same with #PBS directives. Two practical rules: keep cores and memory equal to what one job really gets, and use processes= to split a job into several workers when the work holds the GIL.
On Kubernetes, pdist.start("kubernetes", image="ghcr.io/dask/dask:latest", n_workers=10, resources={"requests": {"memory": "8Gi"}}) asks the dask-kubernetes operator for a scheduler pod and ten worker pods. The image must contain the same Python packages (GeoLattice included) as the client. This cannot run on the build machine, which has no Kubernetes cluster, so the call is shown, not executed.

title: From a Laptop to a Cluster: Sessions, Workers and the Dashboard
text:
Connecting to a running scheduler
A scheduler can also be started outside Python (dask scheduler and dask worker on the command line, a Helm chart, a cloud service). pdist.start("address", address=...) connects to it. Here a small cluster stands in for such a service.


Code
from dask.distributed import LocalCluster  # stand-in for a cluster started elsewhere

service = LocalCluster(n_workers=2, threads_per_worker=2, dashboard_address=None)  # "someone else's" cluster
s = pdist.start("address", address=service.scheduler_address)  # connect by address
print(s.kind, s.status()["workers"], "workers,", s.status()["threads"], "threads")  # what we joined
try:  # a session by address does not own the cluster
    s.scale(4)  # not allowed
except RuntimeError as e:  # expected
    print("scale():", e)  # message
s.close(); service.close()  # disconnect, then stop the stand-in


address 2 workers, 4 threads
scale(): Cannot scale a cluster this session did not create

title: From a Laptop to a Cluster: Sessions, Workers and the Dashboard
text:
Choosing a chunk size
pdist.plan_chunks(shape, dtype) proposes square chunks of about 128 MB for the CPU, or about 5 % of free GPU memory for the GPU, and keeps them at least eight halo widths wide. The cell below measures slope with the DEM read in chunks from 256 to 8192 pixels on a side.


Code
print("CPU plan:", pdist.plan_chunks(dem.shape, "float32"),  # suggested chunks
      "| GPU plan:", pdist.plan_chunks(dem.shape, "float32", compute="gpu"),  # GPU suggestion
      "| 3 layers:", pdist.plan_chunks((3,) + dem.shape, "float32", n_layers=3))  # stacks get smaller chunks
rows = []  # one row per chunk size
for c in [256, 512, 1024, 2048, 4096, 8192]:  # chunk sides
    d_c = dd.gp_raster("elev", chunks={"y": c, "x": c})  # reopen with this chunking
    sl = pdist.raster.slope(d_c, compute="cpu")  # lazy slope
    t = time.perf_counter(); float(sl.mean()); sec = time.perf_counter() - t  # read, slope, reduce
    rows.append({"chunk": c, "chunk MB": c * c * 4 / 1e6, "chunks": d_c.data.npartitions,  # sizes
                 "tasks": len(sl.mean().data.__dask_graph__()), "seconds": sec})  # graph size and time
chunks = pd.DataFrame(rows).set_index("chunk")  # table
chunks.round(2)  # show

ax.plot(chunks.index, chunks.seconds, "o-")  # time against chunk side
for c, r in chunks.iterrows():  # label each point
    ax.annotate(f"{r.tasks:,.0f} tasks", (c, r.seconds), textcoords="offset points", xytext=(4, 6), fontsize=8)  # task count

The 256 pixel chunks (0.26 MB each) created 77,000 tasks and took about nine times longer than the best setting. In this run 2048 pixel chunks (17 MB) were fastest, with 4096 (67 MB) close behind, and 8192 pixel chunks slowed down again because six chunks cannot keep 24 threads busy. The best size is somewhat below the 100 MB rule of thumb here because slope does little work per pixel and smaller chunks stay in the CPU caches; for heavier work per pixel the optimum moves up. Measuring a few sizes, as here, takes a minute and is worth it for any job that will run for hours.

title: From a Laptop to a Cluster: Sessions, Workers and the Dashboard
text:
Persist, compute and pulling results

.compute() (or pdist.compute) runs the graph and returns the result to the client.
pdist.persist(x) runs the graph and keeps the result in worker memory, returning a lazy handle to it. Later computations start from there instead of re-reading the files.
.values and np.asarray on a lazy array compute it and copy everything to the client: fine for a summary, costly for a gigabyte.



Code
s = pdist.start("local", n_workers=4, threads_per_worker=6, memory_limit="24GB")  # a fresh cluster
t = {}  # seconds per step
with dd.timer("slope and aspect from the files (two reads)", t):  # without persist
    float(pdist.raster.slope(dem, compute="cpu").mean()); float(pdist.raster.aspect(dem, compute="cpu").mean())  # each reads the DEM
with dd.timer("persist the DEM in worker memory", t):  # keep it on the workers
    dem_p = pdist.persist(dem); from dask.distributed import wait; wait(dem_p.data)  # wait until loaded
with dd.timer("slope and aspect from the persisted DEM", t):  # reuse
    float(pdist.raster.slope(dem_p, compute="cpu").mean()); float(pdist.raster.aspect(dem_p, compute="cpu").mean())  # no file reads
with dd.timer("pull the full slope raster to the client (.values)", t):  # a gigabyte over the network
    arr = pdist.raster.slope(dem_p, compute="cpu").values  # computed and copied
print(f"pulled {dd.gb(arr.nbytes)}; client process now uses {dd.rss_gb():.1f} GB")  # what it cost
print(pdist.memory_report()["workers"])  # memory on each worker

{'tcp://127.0.0.1:38505': {'memory_gb': 1.751, 'limit_gb': 24.0}, 'tcp://127.0.0.1:40075': {'memory_gb': 1.503, 'limit_gb': 24.0}, 'tcp://127.0.0.1:42751': {'memory_gb': 1.339, 'limit_gb': 24.0}, 'tcp://127.0.0.1:44949': {'memory_gb': 1.262, 'limit_gb': 24.0}}


Persisting paid off as soon as the DEM was reused: the second pair of operations skipped the GeoTIFF reads and decoding and ran about a third faster. Pulling the whole slope raster to the client took 2.7 s, more than half the time of computing slope and aspect on the persisted DEM, and all of it went into serializing every chunk and sending it from the worker processes to this one. Keep large results on the workers and bring back summaries, or write them to disk from the workers with pdist.write_raster (notebook 02).


Code

s.close()  # shut down

title: From a Laptop to a Cluster: Sessions, Workers and the Dashboard
text:
A cluster script
Worker processes start by importing the main module. In a script, code at the top level would run again in every worker, so cluster code must sit under if __name__ == "__main__":. (Notebooks do not need the guard: their main module is the kernel.) The cell below writes such a script to scripts/slope_on_cluster.py and runs it.


Code
script = Path("scripts/slope_on_cluster.py")  # where the script goes
script.parent.mkdir(exist_ok=True)  # create the folder
script.write_text("""\
\"\"\"Slope of the Great Plains DEM on a local Dask cluster, written to Zarr.\"\"\"

import time
from pathlib import Path

import geolattice.distributed as pdist

ROOT = Path(__file__).resolve().parents[4]
DEM = ROOT / "Data" / "03_spatial_analysis" / "Great_plain" / "Raster" / "elev.tif"
OUT = Path(__file__).resolve().parents[1] / "outputs" / "gp_slope.zarr"


def main():
    with pdist.start("local", n_workers=4, threads_per_worker=6) as session:
        print("workers:", session.status()["workers"])
        t = time.perf_counter()
        dem = pdist.read_raster(DEM, chunks={"y": 2048, "x": 2048})
        slope = pdist.raster.slope(dem, compute="cpu")
        pdist.write_raster(slope, OUT)  # each worker writes its own chunks
        print(f"wrote {OUT.name} in {time.perf_counter() - t:.1f} s")


if __name__ == "__main__":  # worker processes import this file; only the parent runs main()
    main()
""")  # script text
r = subprocess.run([sys.executable, str(script)], capture_output=True, text=True)  # run it
print(r.stdout or r.stderr[-1500:])  # its output
z = pdist.read_zarr(OUT / "gp_slope.zarr")  # open the result lazily
print(z, "\nchunks:", z.slope.data.chunksize)  # same grid, written chunk by chunk

title: From a Laptop to a Cluster: Sessions, Workers and the Dashboard
text:
Summary and exercises

A Dask cluster has a client, a scheduler, workers and nannies; without one, Dask’s threaded scheduler runs everything in this process on all cores.
NumPy, GDAL and vectorized Shapely run in parallel on threads; pure Python loops need processes. Here 24 single-threaded processes ran a Python loop twice as fast as 24 threads, and a vectorized Shapely call was about twenty-five times faster again.
For NumPy work on one machine the threaded scheduler beat the local cluster, which pays for moving halo strips between processes.
pdist.start starts local, GPU, SLURM, PBS and Kubernetes clusters or joins a running one; the Session scales, adapts, reports status and closes, also as a context manager.
Chunk size matters: tiny chunks drown in task overhead and huge ones leave cores idle; measure a few sizes for long jobs.
persist keeps reused data in worker memory; .values copies everything to the client.
Cluster scripts need the if __name__ == "__main__": guard.

Exercises

Repeat the threads and processes comparison with pdist.vector.buffer(bld, 10). Which setup wins, and why?
Start a cluster with memory_limit="1GB" per worker and persist the DEM. Watch what the workers do (the dashboard, or pdist.memory_report()), and explain.
Write the PBS version of the SLURM job script with pdist.start("pbs", ...) and compare the two.
Add a --workers argument to scripts/slope_on_cluster.py and plot the run time for 1, 2, 4 and 8 workers.

title: Map Algebra, Focal Operations and Terrain on Chunked and GPU Rasters
text:
Overview

Local, focal and zonal









Kind
Output pixel depends on
Examples
Parallel pattern




Local
the same pixel of each input
arithmetic, NDVI, reclassification, masks
any chunking; no communication


Focal
a window of k x k pixels around it
moving mean or median, convolution, slope, curvature
chunks plus a halo of k // 2 pixels


Zonal
every pixel of its zone
mean NDVI by county
partial sums per chunk, combined at the end


Global
possibly every pixel
flow accumulation, cost distance, viewshed
hard to chunk (notebook 08)





Edges
A moving window at the edge of the raster reaches outside it. GeoLattice repeats the nearest edge value there (mode="nearest"), the same rule SciPy uses, so a chunked result and a whole-array result agree everywhere, including the raster border. NaN propagates: any window containing a NaN gives NaN for means and convolutions, so fill gaps first if that matters.


Arithmetic intensity
What a GPU or more cores can gain depends on how much arithmetic an operation does per byte it reads. Slope does a few operations per pixel and is limited by memory bandwidth; a 9 x 9 median sorts 81 values per pixel and is limited by arithmetic. Reading a compressed file is limited by decompression on the CPU. The timings below show all three regimes.


Terrain derivatives
GeoLattice computes them from the 3 x 3 neighbourhood with Horn’s (1981) finite differences:








Function
Quantity
Units




slope
steepest gradient
degrees, radians or percent


aspect
direction of steepest descent, clockwise from north
degrees


hillshade
illumination from a light source (azimuth 315, altitude 45 by default)
0 to 255


curvature
Laplacian (total) curvature: negative on ridges, positive in hollows
1/m


tpi
elevation minus the mean of a window x window neighbourhood
m


tri
terrain ruggedness index (Riley et al. 1999)
m


roughness
largest minus smallest elevation in the 3 x 3 window
m

title: Map Algebra, Focal Operations and Terrain on Chunked and GPU Rasters
text:
Setup


Code
import warnings  # warning control
warnings.filterwarnings("ignore")  # hide routine library warnings
import os  # environment and CPU count
import time  # wall-clock timing
from pathlib import Path  # file paths

import matplotlib.pyplot as plt  # figures
import numpy as np  # arrays
import pandas as pd  # tables
import geopandas as gpd  # vector data
import xarray as xr  # labelled rasters

import geolattice  # GeoLattice
import geolattice.distributed as pdist  # distributed and GPU spatial computing
import dist_data as dd  # chapter helper: paths, cached downloads, timers

plt.rcParams.update({"figure.dpi": 110})  # figure resolution
pd.set_option("display.width", 140)  # wider printed tables
OUT = Path("outputs")  # results and scratch files written by this chapter
OUT.mkdir(exist_ok=True)  # create it if needed
caps = pdist.capabilities()  # engines and GPUs on this machine
print("GeoLattice", geolattice.__version__, "|", os.cpu_count(), "CPU cores |", caps["gpus"], "GPU(s)",  # versions
      f"({caps.get('gpu_memory_total', 0) / 1e9:.0f} GB)" if caps["gpus"] else "")  # GPU memory

import dask  # Dask configuration
import dask.array as da  # chunked arrays
import scipy.ndimage as ndi  # whole-array filters for checks


def sync():  # wait for queued GPU work so timings are real
    if caps["gpus"]:  # only with a GPU
        import cupy as cp  # GPU arrays
        cp.cuda.Device().synchronize()  # block until done


def best_of(fn, n=2):  # best wall time of n runs after a warm-up run
    fn(); sync()  # warm-up
    times = []  # timings
    for _ in range(n):  # timed runs
        t = time.perf_counter(); fn(); sync(); times.append(time.perf_counter() - t)  # one run
    return min(times)  # best


GeoLattice 0.3.49 | 24 CPU cores | 1 GPU(s) (17 GB)

title: Map Algebra, Focal Operations and Terrain on Chunked and GPU Rasters
text:
Map algebra on the covariates
pdist.raster.calc evaluates an expression over named layers. As an example, a relative erosion potential combines soil erodibility (K factor), slope length and the sine of the slope, the three terrain and soil terms of the Universal Soil Loss Equation (without rainfall and cover). The layers stay lazy, so nothing is read until the result is used.


Code
lay = {n: dd.gp_raster(n) for n in ["kfactor", "slopeleng", "slope"]}  # three lazy covariates
erosion = pdist.raster.calc("kfactor * sqrt(slopeleng) * sin(slope * pi / 180)", **lay)  # expression over layers
print("lazy:", pdist.is_lazy(erosion), "| chunks:", erosion.data.npartitions, "| dtype:", erosion.dtype)  # still a recipe
q = np.nanpercentile(erosion[::10, ::10].values, [50, 75, 90, 97.5])  # class breaks from every 100th pixel
print("class breaks (median, 75th, 90th, 97.5th percentile):", np.round(q, 4))  # breaks
classes = pdist.raster.reclassify(erosion, bins=list(q), values=[1, 2, 3, 4, 5])  # five classes
steep = pdist.raster.where(lay["slope"] > 15, classes, 0)  # keep classes only on slopes above 15 degrees
with dd.timer("erosion potential, five classes and the steep-land mask for 262 million pixels"):  # run the chain
    cls_small, steep_share = dask.compute(classes[::10, ::10], (steep > 0).mean())  # a preview and one statistic
print(f"share of the Great Plains rectangle that is steep (above 15 degrees): {float(steep_share):.2%}")  # result

class breaks (median, 75th, 90th, 97.5th percentile): [0.0013 0.0242 0.118  0.4143]

fig, ax = plt.subplots(figsize=(7.5, 7))  # one map
cm = plt.get_cmap("YlOrBr", 5)  # five colours
im = ax.imshow(cls_small, cmap=cm, vmin=0.5, vmax=5.5, extent=dd.extent(cls_small), interpolation="nearest")  # classes
cb = plt.colorbar(im, ax=ax, shrink=0.7, ticks=[1, 2, 3, 4, 5]); cb.ax.set_yticklabels(["< 50 %", "50 to 75", "75 to 90", "90 to 97.5", "> 97.5 %"])  # legend
dd.gp_states().boundary.plot(ax=ax, color="k", lw=0.6)  # states
ax.set_title("Relative erosion potential (K x slope length x sin slope), percentile classes"); ax.set_axis_off()  # title

The highest classes follow the Rocky Mountain front and the dissected terrain of Wyoming and New Mexico, where steep slopes meet long slope lengths; most of Kansas falls in the lowest classes. The whole chain (three reads, an expression, a reclassification, a mask and two reductions) ran as one task graph in a few seconds.

title: Map Algebra, Focal Operations and Terrain on Chunked and GPU Rasters
text:
Focal statistics and convolution
pdist.raster.focal computes moving-window statistics with the halo each window size needs. The check below compares the chunked 9 x 9 median, standard deviation and a custom 5 x 5 convolution with SciPy on the whole window at once, including the pixels along chunk seams.


Code
w = dd.gp_raster("elev")[7000:11096, 3000:7096].compute()  # 4096 x 4096 window in the Colorado mountains
w = w.fillna(float(w.mean()))  # fill the few no-data holes
laplace = np.array([[0, 0, 1, 0, 0], [0, 1, 2, 1, 0], [1, 2, -16, 2, 1], [0, 1, 2, 1, 0], [0, 0, 1, 0, 0]], float)  # 5 x 5 edge kernel
checks = {  # GeoLattice (1024 pixel chunks) and SciPy on the whole window
    "median 9 x 9": (pdist.raster.focal(w, "median", size=9, chunks=(1024, 1024)), ndi.median_filter(w.values, 9, mode="nearest")),
    "std 9 x 9": (pdist.raster.focal(w, "std", size=9, chunks=(1024, 1024)),  # reference in float64 (see below)
                  np.sqrt(np.maximum(ndi.uniform_filter(w.values.astype(float) ** 2, 9, mode="nearest") - ndi.uniform_filter(w.values.astype(float), 9, mode="nearest") ** 2, 0))),
    "convolve 5 x 5": (pdist.raster.convolve(w, laplace, chunks=(1024, 1024)), ndi.convolve(w.values, laplace, mode="nearest")),
}
for name, (mine, ref) in checks.items():  # compare each pair
    print(f"{name:15s} largest difference {np.abs(np.asarray(mine) - ref).max():.2e}")  # agreement


median 9 x 9    largest difference 0.00e+00
std 9 x 9       largest difference 3.66e-04
convolve 5 x 5  largest difference 5.86e-03




Code
fig, ax = plt.subplots(1, 3, figsize=(15, 4.8))  # three panels
for a, (name, arr, cmap) in zip(ax, [("elevation (m)", w.values, "terrain"), ("9 x 9 standard deviation (m)", checks["std 9 x 9"][0], "magma"),  # panels
                                      ("5 x 5 Laplacian convolution", checks["convolve 5 x 5"][0], "RdBu")]):  # third
    v = np.nanpercentile(arr, [2, 98])  # robust colour range
    im = a.imshow(arr, cmap=cmap, vmin=-max(abs(v)) if cmap == "RdBu" else v[0], vmax=max(abs(v)) if cmap == "RdBu" else v[1])  # draw
    a.set_title(name); a.set_axis_off(); plt.colorbar(im, ax=a, shrink=0.75)  # labels
plt.suptitle("Focal operations on a 4096 x 4096 window (368 x 368 km) of the Colorado Rockies"); plt.tight_layout(); plt.show()  # draw









The chunked results equal SciPy’s whole-array results to float32 rounding, seams included. The standard deviation needed care: computed as E[x^2] - E[x]^2 in float32, elevations of 3,000 m that vary by a few metres lose most of their significant digits (an earlier version of the function was off by up to 1.7 m here). GeoLattice therefore subtracts each chunk’s mean and works in float64 inside the chunk, and the reference is computed in float64 too. The 9 x 9 standard deviation is a simple measure of local relief: high along the mountain fronts and canyon walls, low on the plains. The Laplacian kernel highlights ridges (negative) and valley bottoms (positive).

title: Map Algebra, Focal Operations and Terrain on Chunked and GPU Rasters
section: Terrain derivatives of the Great Plains
text:
Terrain derivatives of the Great Plains
All seven terrain functions run on the full DEM. Because NaN propagates into every window that touches it, the scattered no-data holes would spread: a 21 x 21 TPI window almost always contains one. The holes are therefore filled with their nearest valid neighbour first (scipy.ndimage.distance_transform_edt returns that neighbour’s index for every pixel), and masked again afterwards. Slope is also published with the dataset (slope.tif), which allows a check against an independent implementation.


Code
dem = dd.gp_raster("elev").compute()  # 262 million pixels in memory
holes = dem.isnull()  # no-data pixels: outside the states and scattered holes inside
near = ndi.distance_transform_edt(holes.values, return_distances=False, return_indices=True)  # nearest valid pixel of every pixel
dem_f = dem.copy(data=dem.values[tuple(near)])  # holes filled by their nearest valid neighbour
del near  # free 4 GB of indices
terrain = {}  # results
with dd.timer("slope, aspect, hillshade, curvature, TPI, TRI and roughness on all CPU cores"):  # seven passes
    for name, fn in [("slope", pdist.raster.slope), ("aspect", pdist.raster.aspect), ("hillshade", pdist.raster.hillshade),  # functions
                     ("curvature", pdist.raster.curvature), ("tpi", lambda d, **k: pdist.raster.tpi(d, window=21, **k)),  # TPI over 21 x 21 (1.9 km)
                     ("tri", pdist.raster.tri), ("roughness", pdist.raster.roughness)]:  # the rest
        terrain[name] = fn(dem_f, compute="cpu").where(~holes)  # on the filled DEM, holes masked again
published = dd.gp_raster("slope").compute()  # the slope layer shipped with the data
diff = (terrain["slope"] - published).values  # difference in degrees
ok = np.isfinite(diff)  # pixels where both exist
print(f"slope vs published: mean difference {np.mean(diff[ok]):.3f}, mean absolute {np.mean(np.abs(diff[ok])):.3f} degrees,",  # bias and error
      f"correlation {np.corrcoef(terrain['slope'].values[ok], published.values[ok])[0, 1]:.4f}")  # agreement


slope, aspect, hillshade, curvature, TPI, TRI and roughness on all CPU cores: 16.57 s
slope vs published: mean difference -0.784, mean absolute 0.915 degrees, correlation 0.9877




Code
z = (slice(6000, 6800), slice(3700, 4500))  # 72 x 72 km of the Colorado Front Range
fig, ax = plt.subplots(2, 3, figsize=(15, 9.5))  # six panels
panels = [("hillshade", "Greys_r", None), ("slope", "viridis", (0, 30)), ("aspect", "twilight", (0, 360)),  # name, colours, range
          ("curvature", "RdBu", "auto"), ("tpi", "RdBu_r", (-60, 60)), ("roughness", "magma", (0, 60))]  # second row
for a, (name, cmap, rng) in zip(ax.ravel(), panels):  # each panel
    arr = terrain[name].values[z]  # the zoom
    if rng == "auto":  # symmetric range from the data
        v = np.nanpercentile(np.abs(arr), 95); rng = (-v, v)  # 95th percentile of the magnitude
    im = a.imshow(arr, cmap=cmap, vmin=rng[0] if rng else None, vmax=rng[1] if rng else None)  # map
    a.set_title(f"{name} ({terrain[name].attrs.get('units', '')})"); a.set_axis_off(); plt.colorbar(im, ax=a, shrink=0.75)  # labels
plt.suptitle("Terrain derivatives of the 90 m DEM: Colorado Front Range"); plt.tight_layout(); plt.show()  # draw









The computed slope correlates closely with the published layer (0.99), but is on average about 0.8 degrees lower. The published layer was evidently made with a different method or from a finer DEM; slope depends on the resolution it is computed at, and steeper values from a finer grid are the usual result. Curvature, TPI and roughness each pick out ridges, valleys and rough ground in their own way; notebook 09 uses such layers as predictors. The slope and roughness maps also show a faint grid of straight lines. They are striping in the source DEM, left over from how it was assembled, and derivatives amplify such artefacts. Curvature, a second derivative, amplifies them most: at 90 m it is dominated by the striping, while TPI, which averages over 21 x 21 pixels, shows the ridges and valleys clearly. Check derivative maps for artefacts before using them as predictors, and smooth the DEM first (pdist.raster.focal(dem, "mean", size=5)) when they appear.

title: Map Algebra, Focal Operations and Terrain on Chunked and GPU Rasters
section: CPU and GPU, operation by operation
text:
CPU and GPU, operation by operation
Each operation runs on the full in-memory DEM on all CPU cores and on the GPU with the DEM already in device memory, so the GPU time is compute only.


Code
dem_gpu = pdist.to_gpu(dem) if caps["gpus"] else None  # one copy on the device
ops = {"slope": lambda d, c: pdist.raster.slope(d, compute=c),  # the operations to time
       "hillshade": lambda d, c: pdist.raster.hillshade(d, compute=c),
       "curvature": lambda d, c: pdist.raster.curvature(d, compute=c),
       "TPI 21 x 21": lambda d, c: pdist.raster.tpi(d, window=21, compute=c),
       "roughness": lambda d, c: pdist.raster.roughness(d, compute=c),
       "focal mean 9 x 9": lambda d, c: pdist.raster.focal(d, "mean", size=9, compute=c),
       "focal std 9 x 9": lambda d, c: pdist.raster.focal(d, "std", size=9, compute=c),
       "convolve 5 x 5": lambda d, c: pdist.raster.convolve(d, laplace, compute=c),
       "focal median 9 x 9": lambda d, c: pdist.raster.focal(d, "median", size=9, compute=c)}
rows = []  # timings
for name, op in ops.items():  # each operation
    n = 1 if "median" in name else 2  # the CPU median is slow: one timed run
    cpu = best_of(lambda: op(dem, "cpu"), n=n)  # all CPU cores, NumPy chunks
    gpu = best_of(lambda: op(dem_gpu, "gpu")) if caps["gpus"] else np.nan  # GPU, data resident
    rows.append({"operation": name, "CPU all cores (s)": cpu, "GPU resident (s)": gpu, "GPU speed-up": cpu / gpu})  # row

b = bench.sort_values("GPU speed-up")  # order by speed-up

The memory-bound operations (slope, hillshade, curvature, roughness, the moving mean, the convolution) gain roughly an order of magnitude: the GPU’s memory is that much faster than the CPU’s. The standard deviation gains less, because it now computes in float64, which this laptop GPU executes at a small fraction of its float32 speed. The 9 x 9 median, which sorts 81 values for every pixel, is compute-bound and gains the most: the 24 CPU cores needed tens of seconds, the GPU a fraction of a second. When choosing what to move to a GPU, start with the heavy per-pixel operations.

title: Map Algebra, Focal Operations and Terrain on Chunked and GPU Rasters
section: Every pixel of the 10 m CDL, out of core
text:
Every pixel of the 10 m CDL, out of core
The 2025 CDL has 152 billion pixels, 152 GB as bytes. The task: count every pixel in the United States by land cover group. The pipeline is lazy from end to end:

dd.cdl() opens the file with 8192 x 8192 chunks (67 MB of uint8 each, 2,301 chunks).
pdist.raster.map_tiles reclassifies each chunk with a 256-entry lookup table, which keeps the result uint8. (pdist.raster.reclassify(mapping=...) would also work but loops over the codes and returns float32; for categorical rasters a lookup table is the efficient way.)
A per-chunk bincount gives 12 numbers per chunk, summed over all chunks.

At no time does more than a few chunks per thread exist in memory; dd.PeakMemory samples this process’s memory while the job runs.


Code
import gc  # free memory before measuring
del dem, dem_f, holes, dem_gpu, terrain, published, diff, w, checks  # drop the DEM work of the previous sections
gc.collect()  # return the memory
cdl = dd.cdl()  # lazy, 8192 x 8192 chunks
lut = dd.cdl_lookup()  # CDL code -> group number (0 = no data or outside the US)
groups = pdist.raster.map_tiles(cdl, lambda b, xp: xp.asarray(lut)[b], dtype="uint8", compute="cpu")  # reclassify each chunk
k = len(dd.CDL_GROUPS) + 1  # group numbers 0..11
hist = groups.data.map_blocks(lambda b: np.bincount(b.ravel(), minlength=k)[None, None, :],  # 12 counts per chunk
                              new_axis=2, chunks=(1, 1, k), dtype=np.int64).sum(axis=(0, 1))  # summed over chunks
print(f"{cdl.size / 1e9:.0f} billion pixels in {cdl.data.npartitions:,} chunks; graph of {len(hist.__dask_graph__()):,} tasks")  # size
with dd.PeakMemory() as pm:  # watch memory
    t0 = time.perf_counter()  # start
    counts = hist.compute()  # read, reclassify and count every pixel
    secs = time.perf_counter() - t0  # elapsed
print(f"{secs / 60:.1f} minutes, {cdl.size / secs / 1e6:,.0f} million pixels per second;",  # throughput
      f"process memory {pm.start_gb:.1f} GB before, peak {pm.peak_gb:.1f} GB, an increase of {pm.peak_gb - pm.start_gb:.1f} GB (data: {dd.gb(cdl.nbytes)})")  # memory


152 billion pixels in 2,301 chunks; graph of 18,978 tasks
3.5 minutes, 726 million pixels per second; process memory 11.3 GB before, peak 33.1 GB, an increase of 21.7 GB (data: 151.98 GB)

The mapped total matches the area of the conterminous United States, and the group areas are plausible: grassland and shrubland dominate, and corn, soybeans and wheat together cover about a ninth of the land in 2025. title: Map Algebra, Focal Operations and Terrain on Chunked and GPU Rasters
section: From 10 m crop codes to a 300 m crop fraction
text:
From 10 m crop codes to a 300 m crop fraction
A common next step is to aggregate a fine categorical raster to a coarser grid: here the fraction of each 300 m cell (30 x 30 pixels) that is cropland, for the Great Plains rectangle (21 billion pixels). The chunks are set to multiples of 30 so that coarsen never straddles a chunk edge, and the same pipeline runs once with compute="cpu" and once with compute="gpu".


Code
gp = dd.gp_states().total_bounds  # Great Plains extent in EPSG:5070
crop_lut = np.zeros(256, np.float32)  # 1 for crop codes, 0 for other land
for g in dd.CROP_GROUPS:  # crop groups
    crop_lut[dd.CDL_GROUPS[g]] = 1.0  # their codes
crop_lut[0] = np.nan  # no data stays NaN


def crop_fraction(compute):  # 300 m crop fraction of the Great Plains rectangle
    c = dd.cdl(chunks={"y": 7680, "x": 7680}).sel(x=slice(gp[0], gp[2]), y=slice(gp[3], gp[1]))  # lazy window
    c = c.chunk({"y": 7680, "x": 7680})  # chunks that are multiples of 30
    is_crop = pdist.raster.map_tiles(c, lambda b, xp: xp.asarray(crop_lut)[b], dtype="float32", compute=compute)  # 0, 1 or NaN
    return is_crop.coarsen(y=30, x=30, boundary="trim").mean()  # NaN-aware mean of 900 pixels


rows = {}  # timings
for c in ["cpu", "gpu"] if caps["gpus"] else ["cpu"]:  # both targets
    with dd.PeakMemory() as pm:  # watch memory
        t0 = time.perf_counter(); frac = crop_fraction(c).compute(); rows[c] = time.perf_counter() - t0  # run
    print(f"compute={c}: {rows[c]:.0f} s for {frac.size * 900 / 1e9:.1f} billion pixels, peak memory {pm.peak_gb:.1f} GB")  # result
print("output grid", frac.shape, "| mean crop fraction", round(float(frac.mean()), 3))  # small result


compute=cpu: 29 s for 21.2 billion pixels, peak memory 30.3 GB
compute=gpu: 34 s for 21.2 billion pixels, peak memory 24.6 GB
output grid (5159, 4573) | mean crop fraction 0.188




Code
fig, ax = plt.subplots(figsize=(8, 7))  # one map
im = ax.imshow(frac, cmap="YlGn", vmin=0, vmax=1, extent=dd.extent(frac))  # fraction
plt.colorbar(im, ax=ax, shrink=0.7, label="cropland fraction of each 300 m cell")  # scale
dd.gp_states().boundary.plot(ax=ax, color="k", lw=0.6)  # states
ax.set_title("Cropland in 2025 from 21 billion 10 m CDL pixels"); ax.set_axis_off(); plt.tight_layout(); plt.show()  # draw









Cropland covers most of central and western Kansas, eastern Colorado and the irrigated valleys, and almost none of the mountains and the New Mexico rangeland. The CPU and GPU runs took about the same time: both spend nearly all of it reading and decompressing the file on the CPU. That is the I/O-bound regime of the Overview: a GPU helps only once the data are in memory and the arithmetic is heavy.

title: Map Algebra, Focal Operations and Terrain on Chunked and GPU Rasters
text:
Summary and exercises

Local operations need no communication; focal operations need a halo of half the window; zonal and global operations need combining steps (notebooks 05 and 08).
calc, where and reclassify chain into one lazy graph; a lookup table in map_tiles is the efficient way to reclassify categorical rasters.
Chunked focal statistics, convolutions and terrain derivatives equal whole-array results, seams and borders included. Computed slope agreed closely with the published layer.
GPU speed-ups followed arithmetic intensity: about an order of magnitude for memory-bound operations and about forty times for the 9 x 9 median.
A moving standard deviation in float32 loses precision on large values; computing it in float64 inside each chunk fixed that.
All 152 billion pixels of the 10 m CDL were counted by land cover group in minutes, with peak memory a small fraction of the data size; a 300 m crop fraction of the Great Plains came from 21 billion pixels. Both are limited by reading and decompression, so the GPU did not help.

Exercises

Add pdist.raster.focal(dem, "max", size=21) and pdist.raster.tpi(dem, window=51) to the benchmark. How do the GPU speed-ups change with window size?
Write the erosion classes to a COG with pdist.write_raster(..., format="cog") and open it in a GIS.
Count the CDL groups for Kansas only (select the Kansas bounding box first) and compare with the USDA’s published Kansas acreages for 2025.
Change the crop fraction to a 1 km grid. Which chunk size must you use, and why?

title: Rasterize, Zonal Statistics, Point Extraction and Polygonize at Scale
text: Banner

title: Rasterize, Zonal Statistics, Point Extraction and Polygonize at Scale
text:
Overview

Four bridges between vectors and rasters








Direction
Operation
Question it answers




vector to raster
rasterize
which zone (or how much of a feature) is in each pixel?


raster to vector, by zone
zonal statistics
what is the mean, sum or range of a raster inside each polygon?


raster to vector, by point
point extraction
what are the raster values at these locations?


raster to vector, by region
polygonize
which connected regions of equal value does the raster contain?





How each one is split into chunks

Rasterize: each raster chunk needs only the features whose bounding boxes touch it (a spatial index query per chunk); chunks are burned independently.
Zonal statistics is a reduction. Each chunk computes per-zone partial results (count, sum, sum of squares, minimum, maximum) for the zones it contains; adding the partials gives exact totals, means and standard deviations, however many chunks a zone spans.
Point extraction reads only the chunks that hold points, and for bilinear interpolation the four neighbouring pixels (which may lie in a neighbouring chunk).
Polygonize traces each chunk separately; regions cut by chunk seams are then merged with their same-valued neighbours across the seam.



Pixel-centre rule
A pixel belongs to a polygon when its centre falls inside it (GDAL’s default). Small or thin polygons can therefore get no pixels at all; all_touched=True instead takes every pixel the polygon touches, which overcounts along edges. For zonal statistics over counties (thousands of pixels each) the choice hardly matters; for building footprints on a 10 m grid it matters a lot.

title: Rasterize, Zonal Statistics, Point Extraction and Polygonize at Scale

Raster and Vector Bridges with GeoLattice

All four accept lazy rasters and work chunk by chunk. pdist.explain("bridge.rasterize") shows that compute="auto" keeps rasterize on the CPU: GDAL’s scanline fill was faster than the GPU kernel on typical inputs.

title: Rasterize, Zonal Statistics, Point Extraction and Polygonize at Scale
section: Cropland of every county from 21 billion pixels
text:
Cropland of every county from 21 billion pixels
The same function works on the 10 m CDL. A lazy three-band raster flags, for every pixel, all cropland, wheat and corn (1 or 0, NaN where there is no data); the sum statistic of each band is then a pixel count per county, and 100 m2 per pixel turns it into area. Nothing larger than a few chunks per thread is ever in memory, which makes the chunk size the memory control: each task holds the uint8 codes, three float32 flag bands and the zone labels of one chunk, about a gigabyte for 4096 x 4096 pixels. With 8192 pixel chunks the same job needed four times that per task, and with 24 threads it exhausted this machine’s 123 GB of memory while the notebook was written.


Code
gp = counties.total_bounds  # extent of the counties
cdl = dd.cdl(chunks={"y": 4096, "x": 4096}).sel(x=slice(gp[0], gp[2]), y=slice(gp[3], gp[1]))  # lazy 10 m window, 4096 pixel chunks
print(f"{cdl.shape[0]:,} x {cdl.shape[1]:,} = {cdl.size / 1e9:.1f} billion pixels, {cdl.data.npartitions} chunks")  # size
luts = {}  # one lookup table per band
for band, groups in [("crop", dd.CROP_GROUPS), ("wheat", ["Wheat"]), ("corn", ["Corn"])]:  # three flags
    lut = np.zeros(256, np.float32)  # 0 for everything else
    for g in groups:  # the groups in this band
        lut[dd.CDL_GROUPS[g]] = 1.0  # 1 for their codes
    lut[0] = np.nan  # no data
    luts[band] = lut  # keep it
flags = xr.concat([pdist.raster.map_tiles(cdl, lambda b, xp, l=l: xp.asarray(l)[b], dtype="float32", compute="cpu")  # one band per flag
                   for l in luts.values()], dim="band").assign_coords(band=list(luts))  # (3, y, x)
with dd.PeakMemory() as pm:  # watch memory
    t0 = time.perf_counter()  # start
    crops = pdist.zonal_stats(counties, flags, stats=["count", "sum"], compute="cpu")  # one pass over 21 billion pixels
    secs = time.perf_counter() - t0  # elapsed
print(f"{secs / 60:.1f} minutes; peak process memory {pm.peak_gb:.1f} GB")  # cost
for band in luts:  # areas
    crops[f"{band}_km2"] = crops[f"sum_{band}"] * 100 / 1e6  # pixels to km2
