title: Rasterize, Zonal Statistics, Point Extraction and Polygonize at Scale
text:
Rasterizing counties and buildings
pdist.rasterize burns features onto the grid of a template raster. Counties onto the 90 m grid give a zone raster (one number per county). Here the opt-in GPU kernel is timed against the default GDAL scanline fill.


Code
like = dd.gp_raster("elev")  # template grid, lazy
print(pdist.explain("bridge.rasterize")["reason"])  # why auto stays on the CPU
r = {}  # timings
for c in (["cpu", "gpu"] if caps["gpus"] else ["cpu"]):  # both targets
    t0 = time.perf_counter(); zone = pdist.rasterize(counties, like, values=np.arange(1, len(counties) + 1), dtype="int32", compute=c).compute(); sync()  # burn
    r[c] = time.perf_counter() - t0  # elapsed
    print(f"compute={c}: {r[c]:.2f} s, {int((zone > 0).sum()):,} pixels inside a county")  # result


GPU version is opt-in (slower on typical inputs); pass compute='gpu'
compute=cpu: 0.60 s, 129,746,588 pixels inside a county
compute=gpu: 0.63 s, 129,746,588 pixels inside a county


On this grid GDAL’s scanline fill and the GPU kernel are close. GDAL fills each polygon row by row, visiting only pixels inside it; the GPU kernel tests every pixel of a chunk against every candidate polygon, which pays off only for many small polygons on fine grids.
Buildings are the opposite case: small polygons on a fine grid. Burned onto a 10 m grid of central Wichita, the pixel-centre rule and all_touched give very different building areas.


Code
bld = dd.kansas_buildings()  # buildings, EPSG:4326
box = gpd.GeoSeries.from_xy([-97.34], [37.69], crs=4326).to_crs(5070).iloc[0]  # central Wichita
x0, y0 = box.x - 2500, box.y - 2500  # 5 x 5 km window
tmpl = xr.DataArray(np.zeros((500, 500), np.float32), dims=("y", "x"),  # a 10 m template grid
                    coords={"y": y0 + 5000 - 5 - 10 * np.arange(500), "x": x0 + 5 + 10 * np.arange(500)}).rio.write_crs(5070)  # pixel centres
win = pdist.vector.to_crs(bld, 5070).cx[x0:x0 + 5000, y0:y0 + 5000]  # buildings in the window
true_area = float(pdist.vector.clip(win, (x0, y0, x0 + 5000, y0 + 5000)).area.sum())  # footprint area inside
centre = pdist.rasterize(win, tmpl, dtype="uint8")  # pixel-centre rule
touched = pdist.rasterize(win, tmpl, all_touched=True, dtype="uint8")  # every touched pixel
print(f"{len(win):,} buildings; footprint area {true_area / 1e6:.2f} km2;",  # truth
      f"pixel centre {float(centre.sum()) * 100 / 1e6:.2f} km2; all touched {float(touched.sum()) * 100 / 1e6:.2f} km2")  # estimates
fig, ax = plt.subplots(1, 2, figsize=(12, 5.5))  # two panels
for a, arr, t in [(ax[0], centre, "pixel centre rule"), (ax[1], touched, "all_touched=True")]:  # both rules
    a.imshow(arr[150:300, 150:300], cmap="Greys", interpolation="nearest", extent=[x0 + 1500, x0 + 3000, y0 + 3500, y0 + 2000])  # 1.5 km zoom
    win.cx[x0 + 1500:x0 + 3000, y0 + 2000:y0 + 3500].boundary.plot(ax=a, color="r", lw=0.5)  # outlines
    a.set_xlim(x0 + 1500, x0 + 3000); a.set_ylim(y0 + 2000, y0 + 3500); a.set_title(t); a.set_axis_off()  # zoom
plt.tight_layout(); plt.show()  # draw


13,645 buildings; footprint area 3.65 km2; pixel centre 3.67 km2; all touched 8.11 km2









In total the pixel-centre rule came remarkably close to the true footprint area, while all_touched more than doubled it. The total hides the errors of individual buildings: the zoom shows small houses that got no pixel at all, and others that got a whole 10 x 10 m pixel for a corner. The errors cancel over thousands of buildings but not for any single one. For building or road coverage per pixel, compute the area fraction instead (for example by rasterizing onto a grid ten times finer and coarsening), and never use all_touched for areas.

title: Rasterize, Zonal Statistics, Point Extraction and Polygonize at Scale
text:
Polygonizing crop fields
pdist.polygonize traces regions of equal value chunk by chunk and merges regions cut by chunk seams. Polygonizing a 6 x 6 km CDL window south of Wichita with one chunk and with 16 chunks of 150 x 150 pixels should give the same polygons.


Code
c = dd.cdl().sel(x=slice(box.x - 3000, box.x + 3000), y=slice(box.y - 9000, box.y - 15000)).compute()  # 600 x 600 pixels, 10 m
c = c.where(c > 0)  # no data as NaN
t0 = time.perf_counter(); one = pdist.polygonize(c, chunks=(600, 600)); t1 = time.perf_counter() - t0  # one chunk
t0 = time.perf_counter(); many = pdist.polygonize(c, chunks=(150, 150)); t16 = time.perf_counter() - t0  # 16 chunks with seams
print(f"one chunk: {len(one)} polygons ({t1:.2f} s) | 16 chunks: {len(many)} polygons ({t16:.2f} s)")  # counts
print(f"total area {one.area.sum() / 1e6:.3f} vs {many.area.sum() / 1e6:.3f} km2;",  # areas
      "same region areas:", bool(np.allclose(np.sort(one.area.values), np.sort(many.area.values))))  # identical regions


one chunk: 5281 polygons (0.12 s) | 16 chunks: 5281 polygons (0.28 s)
total area 36.000 vs 36.000 km2; same region areas: True




Code
fields = many[many.value.isin(sum((dd.CDL_GROUPS[g] for g in dd.CROP_GROUPS), []))]  # crop regions only
fields = fields[fields.area > 2e4]  # larger than 2 ha
fig, ax = plt.subplots(figsize=(7, 7))  # one map
fields.plot(ax=ax, column="value", categorical=True, cmap="tab20", edgecolor="k", linewidth=0.3, legend=False)  # fields by crop code
for x in np.arange(1, 4) * 1500:  # chunk seams
    ax.axvline(box.x - 3000 + x, color="b", lw=0.6, ls="--"); ax.axhline(box.y - 15000 + x, color="b", lw=0.6, ls="--")  # dashed lines
ax.set_title(f"{len(fields)} crop regions larger than 2 ha (dashed: chunk seams)"); ax.set_axis_off(); plt.tight_layout(); plt.show()  # draw









The 16-chunk result contains the same regions as the single-chunk result: fields cut by the dashed seams were stitched back together. CDL regions are not field boundaries in a cadastral sense (neighbouring fields with the same crop merge, and classification noise creates small fragments), but they are a useful first approximation, and the chunked algorithm makes it possible to polygonize a whole state.

title: Rasterize, Zonal Statistics, Point Extraction and Polygonize at Scale
text:
Summary and exercises

Rasterize, zonal statistics, point extraction and polygonize each split cleanly into chunks: per-chunk feature queries, per-chunk partial statistics, per-chunk gathers, and per-chunk tracing with seam merging.
County statistics of three 262 million pixel covariates agreed with a direct clip-and-average, and the GPU matched the CPU.
Counting cropland, wheat and corn in 225 counties from 21 billion 10 m pixels took about six minutes with less than 30 GB of memory; the chunk size controls that memory.
The pixel-centre rule matched the total building area, though not single buildings; all_touched doubled it. For coverage fractions, rasterize finer and aggregate.
Twelve covariates were extracted at 570 scattered points in seconds, and polygonizing with 16 chunks gave the same regions as one chunk.

Exercises

Add "std" to the CDL zonal statistics. What does the standard deviation of a 0 or 1 flag mean?
Rasterize the Wichita buildings onto a 1 m grid and coarsen to 10 m to get a building fraction per pixel; compare its total with the true footprint area.
Extract the covariates with method="linear" and fit a linear model of log SOC on them. Does bilinear extraction improve the fit compared with nearest?
Polygonize the whole of Sedgwick County from the CDL with 2048 pixel chunks and count the corn and soybean fields.

title: Shortest Paths, Centrality and Accessibility on Large Road Networks
text: Banner

title: Shortest Paths, Centrality and Accessibility on Large Road Networks
text:
Overview

From lines to a graph
A road network is a graph: nodes are junctions and dead ends, edges are the road segments between them, each with a weight (length, or travel time). Turning lines into a graph needs the lines to be noded: two roads are connected only where they share an end point. OSMnx delivers noded, simplified networks; raw line data (a shapefile of roads) often needs noding and snapping of end points that almost meet.


The costs of the common questions








Question
Algorithm
Cost for n nodes and m edges




Shortest path from one source
Dijkstra
about m log n


Distances from many sources (accessibility)
multi-source Dijkstra, or one Dijkstra per source
sources x m log n


Connected parts of the network
breadth-first search
n + m


PageRank
power iteration
iterations x m


Betweenness centrality
Brandes: shortest paths from every node
n x m, quadratic and more



Betweenness counts, for each node, the share of all shortest paths that pass through it: the junctions and bridges that carry through traffic. Exact betweenness of a 16,000 node network needs 16,000 shortest-path trees. Sampling k source nodes gives an unbiased approximation at k / n of the cost.


Graphs on GPUs
cuGraph runs breadth-first search, single-source shortest paths, PageRank and betweenness on the GPU. Road networks are a hard case for GPUs: they are sparse, nearly planar and have long shortest paths, so each step of a search touches few nodes and the GPU’s thousands of cores have little to do at once. GPUs shine on large graphs with short paths (social and web graphs). A second limit is numerical: Brandes’ algorithm counts the shortest paths between nodes, and on grid-like networks those counts grow exponentially with distance; cuGraph stores them as 64-bit integers, which overflow on large lattices.

Most nodes are three- and four-way junctions; nodes of degree 1 are dead ends (cul-de-sacs, the edge of the city limits). OSMnx removes most nodes of degree 2 (mere bends); the few hundred left mark places where a road’s attributes, such as its name or class, change.

title: Shortest Paths, Centrality and Accessibility on Large Road Networks
section: Travel time weights and one route
text:
Travel time weights and one route
Length is not what drivers minimize. Each segment gets a speed from its OSM maxspeed tag, or a typical speed for its road class when the tag is missing, and its travel time in minutes becomes the edge weight.


Code
default_kmh = {"motorway": 105, "motorway_link": 60, "trunk": 90, "primary": 70, "secondary": 60,  # typical speeds by class
               "tertiary": 50, "unclassified": 45, "residential": 40, "living_street": 20}  # km/h
first = lambda h: h.strip("[]").replace("'", "").split(",")[0].strip()  # first class of multi-class segments
mph = pd.to_numeric(roads.maxspeed.str.extract(r"(\d+)")[0], errors="coerce")  # posted speed in mph
roads["kmh"] = (mph * 1.609).fillna(roads.highway.map(first).map(default_kmh)).fillna(40)  # km/h
roads["minutes"] = roads.length / 1000 / roads.kmh * 60  # travel time per segment
gt = pdist.network.graph_from_lines(roads, weight="minutes")  # same nodes, time weights
print(f"posted speed on {mph.notna().mean():.0%} of segments; total driving time over all roads {roads.minutes.sum() / 60:.0f} h")  # coverage


posted speed on 8% of segments; total driving time over all roads 76 h




Code
fac = dd.wichita_facilities()  # schools and hospitals
hosp = fac[fac.amenity == "hospital"].reset_index(drop=True)  # 12 hospitals
nodes = gt.nodes_gdf()  # nodes as points
src = int(pdist.network.nearest_nodes(gt, gpd.GeoDataFrame(geometry=[shapely.Point(nodes.total_bounds[[0, 1]] + 3000)], crs=5070))[0])  # a node near the south-west corner
dst = int(pdist.network.nearest_nodes(gt, hosp.iloc[[0]])[0])  # the node nearest the first hospital
fast = pdist.network.shortest_path(gt, src, dst, compute="cpu")  # quickest route
short = pdist.network.shortest_path(g, src, dst, compute="cpu")  # shortest route
crow = float(np.hypot(*(gt.xy[src] - gt.xy[dst])))  # straight line
print(f"quickest: {fast['cost']:.1f} min over {shapely.length(fast['geometry']) / 1000:.1f} km | shortest: {short['cost'] / 1000:.1f} km | straight line {crow / 1000:.1f} km")  # compare
if caps["gpus"]:  # same route on the GPU
    gpu = pdist.network.shortest_path(gt, src, dst, compute="gpu")  # cuGraph SSSP
    print(f"cuGraph: {gpu['cost']:.1f} min, same nodes: {gpu['nodes'] == fast['nodes']}")  # check
fig, ax = plt.subplots(figsize=(8, 8))  # one map
roads.plot(ax=ax, color="lightgrey", lw=0.3)  # all roads
roads[roads.highway.str.contains("motorway|primary")].plot(ax=ax, color="grey", lw=0.8)  # main roads
gpd.GeoSeries([short["geometry"], fast["geometry"]], crs=5070).plot(ax=ax, color=["#2c7bb6", "#d7191c"], lw=[2.5, 2])  # routes
ax.plot(*gt.xy[src], "ko"); ax.plot(*gt.xy[dst], "r*", ms=14)  # ends
ax.set_title("Shortest (blue) and quickest (red) route to a hospital"); ax.set_axis_off(); plt.tight_layout(); plt.show()  # draw

The quickest route is longer than the shortest one but uses faster roads. Both are much longer than the straight line, which is the point of network analysis.

title: Shortest Paths, Centrality and Accessibility on Large Road Networks
section: Accessibility: travel time to the nearest school
text:
Accessibility: travel time to the nearest school
For every building in the network’s extent: snap it to the nearest node, then find the travel time from that node to the nearest school. One multi-source Dijkstra from all school nodes answers the second step for every node at once; shortest_path_lengths returns the time from each school to every node, and the minimum over schools is the time to the nearest one.


Code
schools = fac[fac.amenity == "school"].reset_index(drop=True)  # 171 schools
bld = pdist.vector.to_crs(pdist.read_vector(dd.BUILDINGS, bbox=tuple(gpd.GeoSeries(shapely.box(*roads.total_bounds), crs=5070).to_crs(4326).total_bounds)), 5070)  # buildings in the extent
bld = bld.set_geometry(bld.geometry.representative_point())  # one point per building
bld = bld[bld.within(shapely.box(*roads.total_bounds))].reset_index(drop=True)  # inside the road extent
school_nodes = np.unique(pdist.network.nearest_nodes(gt, schools))  # school locations on the graph
t = {}  # timings
t["nearest node of every building"], bnode = timed(lambda: pdist.network.nearest_nodes(gt, bld))  # snap buildings
t["Dijkstra from all schools, CPU"], d_cpu = timed(lambda: pdist.network.shortest_path_lengths(gt, school_nodes, compute="cpu"))  # SciPy
if caps["gpus"]:  # cuGraph, one SSSP per school
    t["SSSP from each school, GPU"], d_gpu = timed(lambda: pdist.network.shortest_path_lengths(gt, school_nodes, compute="gpu"))  # cuGraph
    print("GPU equals CPU:", bool(np.allclose(np.where(np.isinf(d_cpu), -1, d_cpu), np.where(np.isinf(d_gpu), -1, d_gpu), atol=1e-6)))  # check
bld["minutes"] = d_cpu.min(axis=0)[bnode]  # travel time to the nearest school
crow = pdist.vector.knn(bld, schools, k=1).distance.values  # straight-line distance to the nearest school
road_m = pdist.network.shortest_path_lengths(g, school_nodes, compute="cpu").min(axis=0)  # metres by road to the nearest school
bld["detour"] = road_m[bnode] / np.maximum(crow, 50)  # network / straight-line distance (at least 50 m)
print(f"{len(bld):,} buildings, {len(school_nodes)} school nodes")  # sizes
print(pd.Series(t, name="seconds").round(3).to_string())  # timings
print(bld[["minutes", "detour"]].describe(percentiles=[0.5, 0.9, 0.99]).round(2).to_string())  # distributions

Most buildings are within a few minutes’ drive of a school; the longest times are at the rural edges of the network. Network distance exceeded the straight line by about a third for the median building and by much more where rivers, railways and highways force detours. (The small spike at zero is buildings that snap to the same road node as a school, so their network distance is zero while the straight line is not.) On the CPU, SciPy’s multi-source Dijkstra handled all schools in one call; cuGraph ran one search per school, and on a road network of this size the GPU searches were slower, for the reasons given in the Overview. Both gave identical travel times. While this notebook was written they did not: the network contains 270 pairs of parallel segments (two roads joining the same two junctions), and cuGraph kept an arbitrary one of each pair where SciPy keeps the quicker, so some GPU travel times were up to 0.3 % too long. GeoLattice now passes only the quickest of parallel edges to cuGraph.

title: Shortest Paths, Centrality and Accessibility on Large Road Networks
section: Connected components and what they reveal
text:
Connected components and what they reveal
The OSMnx network is one connected component. Components become informative when something is removed: here, all motorway segments and their ramps, as if the freeways were closed.


Code
keep = ~roads.highway.str.contains("motorway")  # drop motorways and their links
g_closed = pdist.network.graph_from_lines(roads[keep])  # graph without them
lab = pdist.network.components(g_closed, compute="gpu" if caps["gpus"] else "cpu")  # component per node
sizes = np.bincount(lab)  # nodes per component
print(f"{g_closed.n_nodes:,} nodes in {len(sizes)} components; largest {sizes.max():,} nodes; "  # summary
      f"{(sizes < 10).sum()} components with fewer than 10 nodes")  # fragments
print("same labels on CPU:", bool((pd.factorize(pdist.network.components(g_closed, compute="cpu"))[0] == pd.factorize(lab)[0]).all()))  # check


15,729 nodes in 2 components; largest 15,727 nodes; 1 components with fewer than 10 nodes
same labels on CPU: True


The network barely changed: without the freeways it still holds together, apart from one two-node fragment that was reachable only by a ramp. Wichita’s street grid offers an alternative to every freeway, which is itself a useful finding about the network’s redundancy. Running components on a raw network in the same way finds digitizing errors (roads that should meet but do not) before they distort an accessibility analysis.

title: Shortest Paths, Centrality and Accessibility on Large Road Networks
section: Betweenness centrality on CPU and GPU
text:
Betweenness centrality on CPU and GPU
Exact betweenness of 16,000 nodes needs a shortest-path tree from every node. NetworkX does it in pure Python, so the comparison uses a sample of k source nodes (the approximation is unbiased and its error shrinks with k); cuGraph also computes the exact version.


Code
t = {}  # timings
t["CPU (NetworkX), k = 500"], b_cpu = timed(lambda: pdist.network.centrality(g, "betweenness", k=500, seed=0, compute="cpu"))  # sampled, CPU
if caps["gpus"]:  # cuGraph
    t["GPU (cuGraph), k = 500"], b_gpu = timed(lambda: pdist.network.centrality(g, "betweenness", k=500, seed=0, compute="gpu"))  # sampled, GPU
    t["GPU (cuGraph), exact"], b_exact = timed(lambda: pdist.network.centrality(g, "betweenness", compute="gpu"))  # all sources
    from scipy.stats import spearmanr  # rank correlation
    print("rank correlation with exact: CPU k=500", round(spearmanr(b_cpu, b_exact)[0], 3),  # sampling error
          "| GPU k=500", round(spearmanr(b_gpu, b_exact)[0], 3))  # same, GPU sample
print(pd.Series(t, name="seconds").round(2).to_string())  # timings


rank correlation with exact: CPU k=500 0.97 | GPU k=500 0.973
CPU (NetworkX), k = 500    16.09
GPU (cuGraph), k = 500      0.28
GPU (cuGraph), exact        3.60




Code
best = b_exact if caps["gpus"] else b_cpu  # the best available estimate
e = roads.copy()  # edges
e["btw"] = np.maximum(best.values[g.src], best.values[g.dst])  # edge score from its end nodes
fig, ax = plt.subplots(figsize=(9, 9))  # one map
e.plot(ax=ax, color="lightgrey", lw=0.3)  # all roads
top = e[e.btw > e.btw.quantile(0.95)]  # the top 5 %
top.plot(ax=ax, column="btw", cmap="inferno_r", lw=1.6)  # coloured by betweenness
ax.set_title("Road segments in the top 5 % of betweenness centrality"); ax.set_axis_off(); plt.tight_layout(); plt.show()  # draw









On this network the GPU computed the exact betweenness about four times faster than NetworkX computed a 500-node sample, and the sampled values already rank nodes almost like the exact ones (Spearman correlation 0.97). The highest values trace the freeway loop around central Wichita, the east-west Kellogg corridor (US 54) and the arterials that feed them: the routes that most shortest paths share. (This is unweighted betweenness, counted in hops; it describes the network’s structure, not traffic volumes.)

title: Shortest Paths, Centrality and Accessibility on Large Road Networks
section: When the GPU is not used
text:
When the GPU is not used
GeoLattice checks before sending betweenness to cuGraph. max_shortest_path_count probes how many equally short paths connect two distant nodes; above 10^18 cuGraph’s 64-bit counters could overflow and give wrong results, and GeoLattice runs the CPU version with a warning instead. A regular street lattice is the worst case: the number of shortest paths across an n x n grid grows like the binomial coefficient C(2n, n).


Code
lines = []  # a 70 x 70 lattice of 100 m streets
for i in range(71):  # rows and columns
    for j in range(70):  # segments
        lines.append(shapely.LineString([(j * 100, i * 100), ((j + 1) * 100, i * 100)]))  # east-west segment
        lines.append(shapely.LineString([(i * 100, j * 100), (i * 100, (j + 1) * 100)]))  # north-south segment
grid = pdist.network.graph_from_lines(gpd.GeoDataFrame(geometry=lines, crs=5070))  # the lattice graph
print(f"lattice: {grid.n_nodes:,} nodes | max shortest-path count {pdist.network.max_shortest_path_count(grid):.2e}"  # overflow probe
      f" | Wichita: {pdist.network.max_shortest_path_count(g):.2e}")  # the real network
with _w.catch_warnings(record=True) as caught:  # capture the warning
    _w.simplefilter("always")  # make sure it is recorded
    tb, bl = timed(lambda: pdist.network.centrality(grid, "betweenness", k=200, compute="gpu"))  # asks for the GPU
print(f"{tb:.1f} s;", caught[0].message if caught else "no warning (no GPU on this machine)")  # what happened


lattice: 5,041 nodes | max shortest-path count 9.38e+40 | Wichita: 1.11e+05
1.9 s; Graph has more than 1e18 equal-length shortest paths between some nodes (lattice-like network); cuGraph's int64 path counts would overflow, so betweenness runs on CPU.


The 70 x 70 lattice has about 10^40 equally short corner-to-corner paths, far beyond what a 64-bit integer holds, so the request for the GPU ran on the CPU with a warning. The Wichita network, with its irregular blocks, stays far below the limit. Silent overflow would have produced wrong centralities without any error; checking a cheap bound first is the safer design.

title: Shortest Paths, Centrality and Accessibility on Large Road Networks
text:
Summary and exercises

graph_from_lines turns noded road lines into a weighted graph; travel time weights come from posted or typical speeds.
Network distance to the nearest school was a third longer than the straight line for the median building, and much longer where barriers force detours.
A multi-source Dijkstra on the CPU answered accessibility for all 180,000 buildings at once; on a road network of this size it beat one cuGraph search per school.
Removing the freeways isolated only one two-node fragment: the street grid is redundant. Component labels find network errors and vulnerable links.
cuGraph computed exact betweenness four times faster than NetworkX computed a 500-node sample, and the sample ranked nodes almost like the exact result.
On lattice-like networks shortest-path counts overflow 64-bit integers; GeoLattice detects this and runs betweenness on the CPU.

Exercises

Compute travel time to the nearest hospital for every building. What share of buildings is more than 10 minutes away?
Compare betweenness weighted by travel time (build the NetworkX graph with g.to_networkx() and pass weight="weight") with the unweighted version. Which roads gain importance?
Remove the bridges over the Arkansas River (segments that cross it) and recompute school accessibility. Which neighbourhoods lose most?
Time exact betweenness on cuGraph for random subgraphs of 2,000, 4,000, 8,000 and 16,000 nodes and fit the growth exponent.

title: Training and Prediction at Scale: Random Forests, Boosting and Deep Learning on GPUs
text:
Overview

Where the work is








Stage
Size here
Parallel pattern




Training a tree ensemble
561 complete rows, 12 covariates
trees in parallel (random forest), split finding in parallel (boosting); a GPU helps for large tables


Cross-validation
5 folds x 3 models
each fold is independent


Predicting a raster
262 million pixels x 12 covariates
embarrassingly parallel: chunk by chunk, the model copied to each worker


Tiled inference of a CNN
18,510 x 24,400 pixels
overlapping tiles; batches spread over GPUs


Training a network on large data
many batches
data parallel: each device holds a model replica, sees a shard of the data, and gradients are averaged after every step





Spatial cross-validation
Random k-fold cross-validation puts neighbouring samples into training and test folds, and with spatially autocorrelated data it overstates accuracy. Spatial cross-validation groups samples into spatial blocks (here 5 clusters of the sample coordinates) and holds out one block at a time, which better reflects prediction into unsampled areas.


Tiles, overlap and receptive fields
A convolutional network sees a neighbourhood around each output pixel (its receptive field). At the edge of a tile part of that neighbourhood is missing and the network sees padding, so predictions near tile edges differ from those in the middle. Overlapping tiles and keeping only each tile’s centre (crop blending) remove the seams when the overlap covers the receptive field.


Distributed data parallel
DDP starts one process per device. Each process builds the same model, reads a different shard of each epoch’s data (DistributedSampler), and after every backward pass the gradients are averaged across processes (an all-reduce, NCCL on GPUs, Gloo on CPUs), so all replicas stay identical. With n devices an epoch takes about 1/n of the time.

Setup

import warnings  # warning control
warnings.filterwarnings("ignore")  # hide routine library warnings
import os  # environment and CPU count
import time  # wall-clock timing
from pathlib import Path  # file paths

import matplotlib.pyplot as plt  # figures
import numpy as np  # arrays
import pandas as pd  # tables
import geopandas as gpd  # vector data
import xarray as xr  # labelled rasters

import geolattice  # GeoLattice
import geolattice.distributed as pdist  # distributed and GPU spatial computing
import dist_data as dd  # chapter helper: paths, cached downloads, timers

plt.rcParams.update({"figure.dpi": 110})  # figure resolution
pd.set_option("display.width", 140)  # wider printed tables
OUT = Path("outputs")  # results and scratch files written by this chapter
OUT.mkdir(exist_ok=True)  # create it if needed
caps = pdist.capabilities()  # engines and GPUs on this machine
print("GeoLattice", geolattice.__version__, "|", os.cpu_count(), "CPU cores |", caps["gpus"], "GPU(s)",  # versions
      f"({caps.get('gpu_memory_total', 0) / 1e9:.0f} GB)" if caps["gpus"] else "")  # GPU memory

import sys  # module search path for the DDP script
import torch  # deep learning
from sklearn.cluster import KMeans  # spatial blocks for cross-validation
from sklearn.metrics import mean_squared_error, r2_score  # accuracy measures


def sync():  # wait for queued GPU work so timings are real
    if caps["gpus"]:  # only with a GPU
        import cupy as cp  # GPU arrays
        cp.cuda.Device().synchronize()  # block until done
    if torch.cuda.is_available():  # PyTorch work too
        torch.cuda.synchronize()  # block until done


def timed(fn):  # wall time and result of one call
    t = time.perf_counter(); out = fn(); sync(); return time.perf_counter() - t, out  # time it

title: Training and Prediction at Scale: Random Forests, Boosting and Deep Learning on GPUs
text:
The training table
The covariates are extracted at the 570 sampling points with pdist.extract_values (notebook 05); the response is log SOC, because SOC is right-skewed.


Code
soc = dd.gp_points()  # 570 sampling points
stack = dd.gp_stack()  # lazy (12, y, x) covariate stack on one grid
table = pdist.extract_values(soc, stack, name="v")  # one column per covariate
table = table.rename(columns=lambda c: c[2:] if c.startswith("v_") else c).dropna(subset=dd.PREDICTORS)  # tidy, complete rows
X = table[dd.PREDICTORS].to_numpy(np.float32)  # predictors
y = np.log(table.SOC.to_numpy())  # log SOC
xy = np.column_stack([table.geometry.x, table.geometry.y])  # coordinates
blocks = KMeans(5, random_state=0, n_init=10).fit_predict(xy)  # 5 spatial blocks
print(f"{len(table)} samples, {X.shape[1]} covariates; block sizes {np.bincount(blocks).tolist()}")  # sizes

title: Training and Prediction at Scale: Random Forests, Boosting and Deep Learning on GPUs
section: Models on CPU and GPU with spatial cross-validation
text:
Models on CPU and GPU with spatial cross-validation
Each model is fitted five times, holding out one spatial block each time, on the CPU and on the GPU where an implementation exists (cuML for the random forest, XGBoost’s CUDA backend; LightGBM here is CPU only).


Code
models = {"rf": dict(n_estimators=500, max_features=0.5, random_state=0),  # random forest
          "xgb": dict(n_estimators=400, learning_rate=0.03, max_depth=4, subsample=0.8, colsample_bytree=0.8),  # boosting
          "lgbm": dict(n_estimators=400, learning_rate=0.03, num_leaves=15, subsample=0.8, subsample_freq=1, colsample_bytree=0.8)}  # boosting
rows = []  # one row per model and target
for name, params in models.items():  # each model
    for c in (["cpu", "gpu"] if caps["gpus"] and name != "lgbm" else ["cpu"]):  # targets with an implementation
        pred = np.empty_like(y); fit_s = 0.0  # out-of-block predictions and fit time
        for b in range(5):  # hold out each block
            tr_, te = blocks != b, blocks == b  # split
            s, m = timed(lambda: pdist.ml.fit(name, X[tr_], y[tr_], task="regression", compute=c, **params))  # fit
            fit_s += s  # total fit time
            pred[te] = np.asarray(m.predict(X[te])).ravel()  # predict the held-out block
        rows.append({"model": name, "compute": c, "engine": m.geolattice_engine, "fit 5 folds (s)": fit_s,  # description
                     "RMSE (log)": mean_squared_error(y, pred) ** 0.5, "R2": r2_score(y, pred)})  # spatial CV accuracy
cv = pd.DataFrame(rows).set_index(["model", "compute"])  # table
cv.round(3)  # show

With 561 rows (the 570 samples less 9 with a missing covariate), training takes seconds everywhere and the GPU offers no advantage: there is too little work to fill it, and copying data and launching kernels cost more than they save. The GPU pays off for training on millions of rows (for example the pixels of a classified image), not for point samples. The accuracies are modest, as is typical for soil carbon at the regional scale under spatial cross-validation, and the three model types are close. The prediction step below is where scale matters.

title: Training and Prediction at Scale: Random Forests, Boosting and Deep Learning on GPUs
section: A soil carbon map of 262 million pixels
text:
A soil carbon map of 262 million pixels
The XGBoost model is refitted once on all samples, and pdist.ml.predict_raster applies it to every pixel of the 12-band stack, chunk by chunk, first on the CPU and then with the same trees moved to the GPU. (Comparing two separately trained models would mix the device with the random row and column sampling of training: a first version of this cell did that, and the two maps differed by up to 0.8 log units.) Pixels where any covariate is missing stay NaN.


Code
import copy  # copy a fitted model
final = {"cpu": pdist.ml.fit("xgb", X, y, task="regression", compute="cpu", **models["xgb"])}  # one model, fitted once
if caps["gpus"]:  # the same trees, predicting on the GPU
    final["gpu"] = copy.deepcopy(final["cpu"]); final["gpu"].set_params(device="cuda")  # move the booster to the device
    final["gpu"].geolattice_engine = "xgboost-cuda"  # predict_raster then feeds it CuPy chunks
print(f"stack: {dict(stack.sizes)}, {dd.gb(stack.nbytes)}, {stack.data.npartitions} chunks")  # size
t, maps = {}, {}  # timings and maps
for c, m in final.items():  # each model
    lazy = pdist.ml.predict_raster(m, stack)  # lazy map, one task per chunk
    with dd.PeakMemory() as pm:  # watch memory
        t[c], soc_map = timed(lambda: lazy.compute())  # read covariates and predict every pixel
    print(f"{m.geolattice_engine}: {t[c]:.1f} s, peak memory {pm.peak_gb:.1f} GB, "  # time and memory
          f"{int(np.isfinite(soc_map.values).sum()) / t[c] / 1e6:.1f} million predicted pixels per second")  # throughput
    maps[c] = soc_map  # keep it
if len(maps) == 2:  # compare the two
    d = np.abs(maps["gpu"].values - maps["cpu"].values)  # difference in log SOC
    print(f"largest |GPU - CPU| difference: {np.nanmax(d):.2e} (log units)")  # agreement

Prediction on the GPU was several times faster than on 24 CPU cores, and the two maps agree to float32 rounding: the GPU model receives each chunk as a CuPy array and predicts without copying the model back and forth. The map follows the covariates the samples tracked in notebook 05: higher carbon under the wetter, greener east and the cool, high mountains, low carbon on the warm and dry southern plains.

title: Training and Prediction at Scale: Random Forests, Boosting and Deep Learning on GPUs
text:
Class probabilities for every pixel
With proba=True, predict_raster returns one probability layer per class. Here SOC is split into terciles (low, medium, high) and an XGBoost classifier gives each pixel’s probability of belonging to the high class; for speed this runs on a 4096 x 4096 window of Kansas.


Code
cls = np.digitize(y, np.quantile(y, [1 / 3, 2 / 3]))  # 0 low, 1 medium, 2 high
clf = pdist.ml.fit("xgb", X, cls, task="classification", compute="gpu" if caps["gpus"] else "cpu", n_estimators=300, max_depth=3, learning_rate=0.05)  # classifier
win = stack[:, 8000:12096, 9000:13096]  # central Kansas window
t0 = time.perf_counter(); prob = pdist.ml.predict_raster(clf, win, proba=True).compute(); s = time.perf_counter() - t0  # probabilities
print(f"{dict(prob.sizes)} in {s:.1f} s; classes {prob['class'].values.tolist()}; probabilities sum to 1:",  # shape
      bool(np.allclose(prob.sum("class").values[np.isfinite(prob[0].values)], 1, atol=1e-5)))  # check
fig, ax = plt.subplots(1, 2, figsize=(13, 5.5))  # two maps
im = ax[0].imshow(prob.sel({"class": 2}), cmap="viridis", vmin=0, vmax=1); ax[0].set_title("P(high SOC)"); plt.colorbar(im, ax=ax[0], shrink=0.8)  # high class
ent = -(prob * np.log(prob.clip(1e-9))).sum("class").where(np.isfinite(prob[0]))  # entropy: uncertainty of the class
im = ax[1].imshow(ent, cmap="magma", vmin=0, vmax=np.log(3)); ax[1].set_title("class entropy (0 certain, 1.1 uniform)"); plt.colorbar(im, ax=ax[1], shrink=0.8)  # uncertainty
[a.set_axis_off() for a in ax]; plt.tight_layout(); plt.show()  # draw


{'class': 3, 'y': 4096, 'x': 4096} in 3.1 s; classes [0, 1, 2]; probabilities sum to 1: True

title: Training and Prediction at Scale: Random Forests, Boosting and Deep Learning on GPUs
section: A CNN over a 1.7 GB image in tiles
text:
A CNN over a 1.7 GB image in tiles
A tiny fully convolutional network learns to recognise vegetation from the red, green and blue bands alone. Its labels come from the near-infrared band (NDVI above 0.3), so no manual labelling is needed: the network must learn from colour and texture what the near-infrared band shows directly. It is trained on random patches, then pdist.ml.predict_tiles runs it over the whole image in 512 pixel tiles with 32 pixels of overlap.


Code
import rioxarray  # read the image
img = rioxarray.open_rasterio(dd.DATA / "08_remote_sensing" / "08_09_image_classification" / "Image_Fusion" / "HR" / "HR_Rural_July_14.tif")  # lazy
with dd.timer("read the 4-band 0.6 m image"):  # 1.8 GB of uint8
    arr = img.values  # (4, 24400, 18510)
rgb = (arr[:3].astype(np.float32) / 255.0)  # inputs: red, green, blue in 0..1
ndvi = (arr[3].astype(np.float32) - arr[0]) / (arr[3].astype(np.float32) + arr[0] + 1e-6)  # labels from near-infrared and red
label = (ndvi > 0.3).astype(np.float32)  # vegetation mask
print(f"image {arr.shape}, {dd.gb(arr.nbytes)}; vegetation share {label.mean():.1%}")  # sizes

dev = "cuda" if torch.cuda.is_available() else "cpu"  # training device
torch.manual_seed(0); rng = np.random.default_rng(0)  # reproducible
net = torch.nn.Sequential(  # 4 convolutions: receptive field of 9 x 9 pixels
    torch.nn.Conv2d(3, 16, 3, padding=1), torch.nn.ReLU(), torch.nn.Conv2d(16, 16, 3, padding=1), torch.nn.ReLU(),
    torch.nn.Conv2d(16, 16, 3, padding=1), torch.nn.ReLU(), torch.nn.Conv2d(16, 2, 3, padding=1)).to(dev)  # 2 classes
opt = torch.optim.Adam(net.parameters(), lr=3e-3)  # optimizer
t0 = time.perf_counter()  # start
for step in range(300):  # 300 batches of 16 random 128 x 128 patches
    r = rng.integers(0, arr.shape[1] - 128, 16); c = rng.integers(0, arr.shape[2] - 128, 16)  # patch corners
    xb = torch.from_numpy(np.stack([rgb[:, i:i + 128, j:j + 128] for i, j in zip(r, c)])).to(dev)  # inputs
    yb = torch.from_numpy(np.stack([label[i:i + 128, j:j + 128] for i, j in zip(r, c)])).long().to(dev)  # labels
    loss = torch.nn.functional.cross_entropy(net(xb), yb)  # pixelwise loss
    opt.zero_grad(); loss.backward(); opt.step()  # update
print(f"trained on {dev} in {time.perf_counter() - t0:.0f} s, final loss {float(loss):.3f}")  # training


read the 4-band 0.6 m image: 6.99 s
image (4, 24400, 18510), 1.81 GB; vegetation share 54.4%
trained on cuda in 2 s, final loss 0.074




Code
t = {}  # timings
with dd.PeakMemory() as pm:  # watch host memory
    t["whole image, tiles of 512, overlap 32"], out = timed(lambda: pdist.ml.predict_tiles(net, rgb, tile=512, overlap=32, batch_size=16))  # tiled inference
pred = out.argmax(0)  # predicted class per pixel
acc = (pred == label).mean()  # agreement with the NDVI labels
print(f"{out.shape[1]:,} x {out.shape[2]:,} pixels in {list(t.values())[0]:.0f} s, peak memory {pm.peak_gb:.0f} GB; "  # time and memory
      f"agreement with NDVI labels {acc:.1%}")  # accuracy
crop = rgb[:, 10000:12048, 8000:10048]  # a 2048 x 2048 crop
with torch.inference_mode():  # whole crop at once, no tiles
    whole = net(torch.from_numpy(crop[None]).to(dev)).float().cpu().numpy()[0]  # reference
tiled = pdist.ml.predict_tiles(net, crop, tile=256, overlap=32)  # the same crop in 81 tiles
naive = pdist.ml.predict_tiles(net, crop, tile=256, overlap=0)  # tiles without overlap
inner = (slice(None), slice(8, -8), slice(8, -8))  # away from the crop border
print(f"largest difference to whole-crop inference: overlap 32: {np.abs(tiled - whole)[inner].max():.1e}, "  # seamless
      f"no overlap: {np.abs(naive - whole)[inner].max():.2f}")  # seams


24,400 x 18,510 pixels in 13 s, peak memory 66 GB; agreement with NDVI labels 97.1%
largest difference to whole-crop inference: overlap 32: 0.0e+00, no overlap: 12.10




Code
fig, ax = plt.subplots(1, 3, figsize=(16, 5.5))  # three panels
z = (slice(10000, 11024), slice(8000, 9024))  # 1024 x 1024 pixels (614 m)
ax[0].imshow(np.moveaxis(rgb[(slice(None),) + z], 0, -1)); ax[0].set_title("true colour (0.6 m)")  # image
ax[1].imshow(label[z], cmap="Greens"); ax[1].set_title("label: NDVI > 0.3 (from near-infrared)")  # labels
ax[2].imshow(pred[z], cmap="Greens"); ax[2].set_title("CNN from red, green and blue, tiled")  # prediction
[a.set_axis_off() for a in ax]; plt.tight_layout(); plt.show()  # draw









The tiled run covered all 452 million pixels in well under a minute on the GPU. With 32 pixels of overlap the tiled result equals whole-crop inference to floating point rounding everywhere except the crop’s own border: the network’s receptive field (9 x 9 pixels) fits inside the 16 pixels each tile keeps as margin. Without overlap the tile edges see padding instead of their neighbours, and the predictions there differ. The CNN reproduces the NDVI mask closely from colour alone; trees, lawns and crops are green in the visible bands too.
Memory is the practical limit of this function: it holds the image as float32, its padded copy, the float64 accumulator and the output in host memory; with the training arrays the process peaked at about 65 GB here. For larger images, run it window by window, or wrap it in pdist.raster.map_tiles with an overlap.

title: Training and Prediction at Scale: Random Forests, Boosting and Deep Learning on GPUs
text:
Distributed data parallel training
pdist.ml.train_ddp starts one process per device and runs a training function in each. The function lives in scripts/ddp_soc.py (worker processes import it by name): it builds a small network for log SOC, wraps it with pdist.ml.ddp_model, and gives each rank its own shard of the data. With one GPU on this machine the GPU run uses one process; the CPU run uses two processes with the Gloo backend, which shows the mechanics of several ranks.


Code
sys.path.insert(0, str(Path("scripts").resolve()))  # make scripts/ddp_soc.py importable in the worker processes
import ddp_soc  # the training function
Xs = ((X - X.mean(0)) / X.std(0)).astype(np.float32)  # standardised predictors
runs = {}  # results per setup
if caps["gpus"]:  # one process on the GPU, NCCL
    t0 = time.perf_counter(); runs["1 GPU (NCCL)"] = pdist.ml.train_ddp(ddp_soc.train, nprocs=1, args=(Xs, y, 200)); runs["1 GPU (NCCL)"].append(time.perf_counter() - t0)  # train
t0 = time.perf_counter(); runs["2 CPU processes (Gloo)"] = pdist.ml.train_ddp(ddp_soc.train, nprocs=2, backend="gloo", args=(Xs, y, 200)); runs["2 CPU processes (Gloo)"].append(time.perf_counter() - t0)  # train
for name, r in runs.items():  # summarise
    *ranks, secs = r  # rank results and time
    print(f"{name}: {secs:.0f} s | " + " | ".join(f"rank {k['rank']} on {k['device']}: {k['rows']} rows, final loss {k['history'][-1]:.3f}, "
                                                    f"weights checksum {k['weights_checksum']:.6f}" for k in ranks))  # per rank


1 GPU (NCCL): 6 s | rank 0 on cuda:0: 561 rows, final loss 0.085, weights checksum -33.331352
2 CPU processes (Gloo): 5 s | rank 0 on cpu: 281 rows, final loss 0.101, weights checksum -21.550788 | rank 1 on cpu: 281 rows, final loss 0.110, weights checksum -21.550788


Each of the two CPU ranks trained on half of the rows per epoch, yet both ended with exactly the same weights (the checksums match): DDP averages the gradients after every step, so the replicas never diverge. The times are dominated by starting the processes and by communication; a network this small on 561 rows gains nothing from parallel training. DDP pays off when each step is expensive: large networks, large images, many batches. On a machine with n GPUs, train_ddp(fn) without nprocs starts one process per GPU with NCCL, and the same function runs unchanged; on a cluster torchrun or a SLURM job array starts the processes instead.

title: Training and Prediction at Scale: Random Forests, Boosting and Deep Learning on GPUs
text:
Summary and exercises

In spatial machine learning, training data are often small and prediction is large. With 570 samples the GPU did not speed up training; it sped up prediction of 262 million pixels several times, with results identical to the CPU’s.
Spatial cross-validation by blocks gave a realistic R2 for regional soil carbon.
predict_raster predicts values or class probabilities chunk by chunk; NaN pixels stay NaN.
predict_tiles ran a CNN over a 1.7 GB image; with an overlap at least twice the receptive-field radius the tiles left no seams.
train_ddp and ddp_model keep replicas identical by averaging gradients; parallel training pays off only when each step is expensive.

Exercises

Replace the random spatial blocks with 10 blocks and with leave-one-state-out cross-validation. How do RMSE and R2 change?
Predict the SOC map with the random forest on the GPU (cuML) and compare speed and map with XGBoost.
Run predict_tiles with tile=256 and tile=1024. How do time and GPU memory change?
Add a fifth convolution to the CNN. What is the receptive field now, and what overlap removes the seams?

title: Measuring, Checking and Tuning Distributed and GPU Workloads
text:
Overview

Correctness first
GPU kernels, chunked algorithms and parallel reductions all compute in a different order from the plain whole-array version, so results can differ by rounding, and bugs show up at chunk edges, at NaN values or with unusual geometries. Every operation should be checked against a reference on real data before it is trusted at scale: exactly for integers and geometries, within a tolerance for floating point.


Timing correctly

Laziness: a Dask call returns at once; time the .compute() (or the write) instead.
GPU queues: CuPy launches kernels asynchronously; synchronise the device before stopping the clock.
Warm-up: the first call compiles kernels, fills caches and loads files into the page cache; time later calls, or report the first separately.
Repeats: report the best or the median of several runs.



Strong and weak scaling

Strong scaling: fixed problem, more workers. Ideal: time falls as 1/n; Amdahl’s law (notebook 00) describes the shortfall.
Weak scaling: problem grows with the workers. Ideal: constant time. Weak scaling is what matters when the reason for more workers is more data.



Overheads that eat speed-ups
Task scheduling (about a millisecond per task on a cluster), serialization between processes, host-to-device copies over PCIe, Python code that holds the GIL, and reading the same data twice.

title: Measuring, Checking and Tuning Distributed and GPU Workloads
text:
Benchmarks done right
The cell below times the terrain ruggedness index (TRI, not used earlier in this notebook) on the GPU in three misleading ways, then with pdist.benchmark.


Code
if caps["gpus"]:  # needs a GPU
    g = pdist.to_gpu(win)  # data on the device
    t = time.perf_counter(); r = pdist.raster.tri(g); sync(); wrong1 = time.perf_counter() - t  # first call of TRI: includes kernel compilation
    t = time.perf_counter(); r = pdist.raster.tri(g); wrong2_launch = time.perf_counter() - t  # no sync: may return before the kernels finish
    t = time.perf_counter(); lz = pdist.raster.tri(dd.gp_raster("elev")); wrong3 = time.perf_counter() - t  # lazy: nothing ran
    bench = pdist.benchmark(pdist.raster.tri, win, computes=("cpu", "gpu"), repeats=5, warmup=1)  # warm-up, repeats, sync
    print(f"first call {wrong1 * 1000:.0f} ms | unsynchronised {wrong2_launch * 1000:.1f} ms | lazy call {wrong3 * 1000:.1f} ms")  # misleading numbers
    print(bench.round(4).to_string())  # the right numbers


first call 15 ms | unsynchronised 10.8 ms | lazy call 16.2 ms
         best_s  mean_s   std_s  repeats  speedup
compute                                          
cpu      0.0555  0.0606  0.0043        5   1.0000
gpu      0.0188  0.0242  0.0033        5   2.9515


The first call is the slowest because CuPy compiles TRI’s kernels then; an unsynchronised call can stop the clock before the queued kernels have finished (here the Dask machinery around each call dominates, so the error is small); and the lazy call measured only building a task graph for the whole DEM, not computing it. pdist.benchmark avoids all three: it runs a warm-up, materialises lazy results, synchronises the GPU and repeats.

title: Measuring, Checking and Tuning Distributed and GPU Workloads
text:
Strong and weak scaling
Strong scaling: slope of the full DEM, zonal statistics of NDVI by county and the point-in-county join, each with 1 to 24 threads. Weak scaling: slope with the DEM window growing in proportion to the threads, so each thread always has about 11 million pixels.


Code
ndvi = dd.gp_raster("ndvi").compute()  # NDVI in memory, so reading does not dominate
work = {"slope (raster, memory-bound)": lambda: pdist.raster.slope(dem, compute="cpu", chunks=(1024, 1024)),  # three workloads
        "focal median 5 (raster, compute-bound)": lambda: pdist.raster.focal(dem[:6000, :6000], "median", size=5, compute="cpu", chunks=(750, 750)),
        "points in counties (vector join)": lambda: pdist.vector.sjoin(pts, ks, predicate="within", compute="cpu", npartitions=48)}
threads = [1, 2, 4, 8, 16, 24]  # thread counts
strong = pd.DataFrame(index=threads, columns=list(work), dtype=float)  # seconds
for n in threads:  # each count
    with dask.config.set(scheduler="threads", num_workers=n):  # n threads
        for name, fn in work.items():  # each workload
            fn(); t = time.perf_counter(); fn(); strong.loc[n, name] = time.perf_counter() - t  # warm, then time
weak = {}  # seconds by thread count
for n in threads:  # each count
    side = int(np.sqrt(n * 11e6))  # pixels per side so each thread has about 11 million
    sub = dem[:min(side, dem.shape[0]), :min(side, dem.shape[1])]  # the window
    with dask.config.set(scheduler="threads", num_workers=n):  # n threads
        pdist.raster.focal(sub, "median", size=5, compute="cpu", chunks=(1024, 1024))  # warm-up

title: Measuring, Checking and Tuning Distributed and GPU Workloads
text:
Where the time goes: profiling
pdist.profile without a session uses Dask’s local profiler and returns a table of seconds by task type; with a session it writes Dask’s HTML performance report (task stream, worker profiles, bandwidth), which opens in a browser.


Code
lazy_chain = lambda: pdist.raster.hillshade(pdist.raster.focal(dd.gp_raster("elev"), "mean", size=5, compute="cpu"), compute="cpu")  # read, smooth, shade
res, table = pdist.profile(lazy_chain)  # local profiler
print(f"result {res.shape}; task time summed over threads: {table['sum'].sum():.1f} s")  # total
print(table.head(8).round(2).to_string())  # the most expensive task types
with pdist.start("local", n_workers=4, threads_per_worker=6) as s:  # a cluster for the HTML report
    _, report = pdist.profile(lazy_chain, path=str(OUT / "profile_hillshade.html"))  # performance report
print("performance report:", report, f"({Path(report).stat().st_size / 1e6:.1f} MB)")  # where it is


result (17196, 15245); task time summed over threads: 74.9 s
                 sum  count
task                       
getitem        66.66   1517
open_rasterio   3.79      9
rechunk         1.75    162
_trim           1.31    102
concatenate     0.65    396
finalize        0.38      1
overlap         0.29     16
repeat          0.05     22
performance report: outputs/profile_hillshade.html (0.6 MB)


Almost all of the task time is attributed to getitem tasks. That does not mean slicing is slow: Dask fuses each chunk’s read, halo slicing and the two computations into one task before running the graph, and the fused task keeps the name of its first step. The table is therefore a coarse view; the HTML report shows the same work as a timeline per thread and worker, which is where the real bottlenecks (idle threads, transfers, one slow chunk) become visible.

title: Measuring, Checking and Tuning Distributed and GPU Workloads
text:
Seven pitfalls, reproduced and fixed

1. Computing the same graph twice
Each .compute() runs its graph from the start. Two statistics of the same lazy array computed one after the other read the file twice; dask.compute (or pdist.compute) shares the work.


Code
lazy = dd.gp_raster("preci")  # lazy
t = time.perf_counter(); a, b = float(lazy.mean()), float(lazy.std()); twice = time.perf_counter() - t  # two passes
t = time.perf_counter(); a2, b2 = dask.compute(lazy.mean(), lazy.std()); once = time.perf_counter() - t  # one shared pass
print(f"two .compute() calls {twice:.2f} s | one dask.compute {once:.2f} s | same values: {np.isclose(a, a2) and np.isclose(b, b2)}")  # result


two .compute() calls 1.93 s | one dask.compute 1.37 s | same values: True




2. Tiny chunks
Notebook 01 measured it: 256 pixel chunks were about nine times slower than 2048 pixel chunks for the same slope. Check data.npartitions and the task count before running a big job.


3. Moving data to the host between GPU steps
A chain of GPU operations on host data copies every intermediate result to the host and back. Moving the input once and keeping intermediates on the device avoids that.


Code
if caps["gpus"]:  # needs a GPU
    chain = lambda d: pdist.raster.hillshade(pdist.raster.focal(d, "mean", size=5, compute="gpu"), compute="gpu")  # two GPU steps
    t = time.perf_counter(); chain(dem); sync(); host = time.perf_counter() - t  # host in, host between, host out
    t = time.perf_counter(); out = pdist.to_cpu(chain(pdist.to_gpu(dem))); sync(); device = time.perf_counter() - t  # one copy in, one out
    print(f"host input: {host:.2f} s | data kept on the GPU: {device:.2f} s")  # result


host input: 2.13 s | data kept on the GPU: 1.08 s




4. Reading a GPU result with NumPy
Results stay on the GPU when the input was on the GPU. NumPy cannot read CuPy memory directly; move results with pdist.to_cpu (or .get()), and check with pdist.is_gpu.


Code
if caps["gpus"]:  # needs a GPU
    r = pdist.raster.slope(pdist.to_gpu(win))  # a GPU result
    try:  # the mistake
        np.asarray(r.data)  # NumPy on CuPy memory
    except TypeError as e:  # what happens
        print("np.asarray on a CuPy array:", str(e)[:90])  # message
    print("is_gpu:", pdist.is_gpu(r), "| after to_cpu:", pdist.is_gpu(pdist.to_cpu(r)), type(pdist.to_cpu(r).data).__name__)  # the fix


np.asarray on a CuPy array: Implicit conversion to a NumPy array is not allowed. Please use `.get()` to construct a Nu
is_gpu: True | after to_cpu: False ndarray




5. compute="auto" on a machine with a GPU
"auto" picks the GPU whenever one exists, also inside the worker processes of a CPU cluster. While writing notebook 01 this silently turned a “CPU cluster” comparison into a GPU one, and four worker processes competed for the GPU’s memory. Pass compute="cpu" explicitly when measuring the CPU, or set the default for a whole session.


Code
print("auto on this machine:", pdist.explain("raster.slope")["uses"])  # GPU when present
pdist.set_defaults(compute="cpu")  # every call now defaults to the CPU
print("after set_defaults(compute='cpu'):", pdist.explain("raster.slope")["uses"])  # CPU
pdist.set_defaults(compute="auto")  # back to the default


auto on this machine: gpu
after set_defaults(compute='cpu'): cpu


Defaults(compute='auto', npartitions=None, chunks='auto')




6. Importing cuDF or cuML changes CuPy’s memory allocator
Importing cudf or cuml calls cupy.cuda.set_allocator(rmm_cupy_allocator). Without an RMM pool every CuPy allocation then becomes a cudaMalloc, which made chunked GPU work about four times slower while this chapter was written, and memory already cached by CuPy’s pool is stranded. GeoLattice imports RAPIDS libraries through geolattice.distributed._backend.rapids, which restores the previous allocator, and pdist.capabilities() only checks that the packages are installed. If you import cuDF yourself, restore the allocator afterwards or configure an RMM pool.


Code
if caps["gpus"]:  # needs a GPU and RAPIDS
    import subprocess, sys  # a fresh Python process, so cuDF is imported for the first time
    probe = """

7. Worker memory limits, GDAL’s cache and spilling
A worker that exceeds 60 % of its memory limit writes results to disk (spills), and at 95 % its nanny restarts it. While this notebook was written, workers limited to a few hundred megabytes or a gigabyte or two died again and again while doing nothing but reading GeoTIFFs. The cause was GDAL: it caches decoded raster blocks up to 5 % of the machine’s RAM in every process, here 6.6 GB per worker, far above the limit. pdist.start("local", memory_limit=...) now caps GDAL’s cache in the workers at a tenth of an explicit limit (set GDAL_CACHEMAX yourself to override). With that, a small limit produces what it should: spilling, and a slower job.

With 1.5 GB per worker part of the persisted DEM went to disk and the job took several times longer; with 6 GB nothing spilled. A job that spills constantly needs more workers, more memory per worker, smaller chunks, or less data persisted; a worker that dies while only reading files points to a library cache, not to your data.

title: Measuring, Checking and Tuning Distributed and GPU Workloads
text:
Summary and exercises

check_equivalence confirmed that every GPU implementation used in this chapter matched the CPU on real data: exactly for integers and geometries, to rounding for floating point.
Correct timing needs warm-up, synchronisation, materialised lazy results and repeats; pdist.benchmark does all four.
Strong scaling differed by workload: a compute-bound median scaled well, memory-bound slope did not, and the vector join was limited by its serial assembly step.
pdist.profile attributes time to task types, or writes Dask’s HTML performance report.
Seven pitfalls reproduced: repeated computes, tiny chunks, host round trips between GPU steps, NumPy on GPU memory, compute="auto" inside CPU clusters, RAPIDS imports changing CuPy’s allocator, and GDAL’s per-process cache breaking worker memory limits.

Exercises

Add pdist.network.shortest_path_lengths and pdist.analysis.dbscan (with compute="gpu") to the equivalence table. What tolerance does each need?
Measure strong scaling of pdist.zonal_stats for the counties with 1 to 24 threads. Where does it stop improving, and why?
Open the HTML performance report and identify the longest task in the task stream.
Repeat the spilling experiment with memory_limit="1GB" and with GDAL_CACHEMAX set to 2048 in the environment before starting the cluster. What happens to the workers?
